title_en: Philippine police file criminal complaints against Thomas Markle
content_en:
Police say the complaints accuse ‌Markle ‌of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation ‌of children.
Thomas Markle in a jail booking photograph after cutting off an electronic ankle monitor he was ordered to wear. Photo: Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office via Reuters
Philippine police said on Wednesday that ⁠criminal complaints ⁠had been filed against Thomas ⁠Markle, the estranged father of Britain’s Duchess of Sussex Meghan Markle, over alleged online child sexual abuse offences.
The filing of the complaints will enable prosecutors to examine ‌evidence and decide whether charges should be filed in court.
It came less than two weeks after US authorities arrested Thomas Markle in Florida on a federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs allegedly showing him with underage ⁠girls.
Thomas Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the ‌claims were untrue and describing them as “sick lies”.
Philippine police said complaints were filed before the prosecutor’s ‌office in Cebu province on Monday following an investigation last ⁠month into ⁠the alleged distribution and possession of child sexual abuse materials.
A private security guard stands beside a lit window outside Maravida Senior Living, where Thomas Markle was staying, in Lakeland, Florida, on November 6. Photo: AFP
Markle had lived in ‌Cebu for a period before returning to the United States.
Police said the complaints accuse Markle ‌of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation ‌of children.
Forensic examination of the remaining devices surrendered in the Philippines ⁠by Markle’s son, Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr, was ongoing and ⁠could yield further evidence to support the case or lead to additional charges, if warranted, police said.
Meghan, an American ‌actor, has been ‌estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles’ younger son, Harry, in 2018.
She has said she is “deeply distressed” over the matter.
By Reuters

title_en: From Shenzhen to Silicon Valley: Xi Jinping calls for global association of bay areas
content_en:
The Chinese president says cooperation between major coastal hubs could drive growth across the Asia-Pacific region.
Xi speaks at the 2026 Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen, southern China’s Guangdong province, on Wednesday. Photo: AP
President Xi Jinping has called for closer economic links between major coastal innovation centres across the globe – a proposal observers said could create new opportunities and exchanges for China and the United States.
Speaking at the opening of the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday, Xi used the address in the southern Chinese tech hub to strike an optimistic tone on China’s growth prospects, highlighting its strengths in innovation despite mounting economic challenges.
He urged closer cooperation between major metropolitan bay areas, arguing that deeper economic ties could help drive regional growth.
“The Pacific region is home to the world’s most important bay areas, notable for their open, interconnected economies with positive spillovers. Shenzhen, where we are now meeting, is part of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area (GBA),” he told business leaders from 21 Apec economies.
“China supports the establishment of a world association of bay areas to deepen exchanges and strengthen economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region,” he said, without offering further details.
Observers said the proposal reflected Beijing’s interest in building lasting economic links between China and the United States, including through regional and local-level cooperation.
“Traditional sub-national exchanges are limited by administrative boundaries. Bay areas may transcend city and regional borders, allowing diverse enterprises and institutions to participate and swap ideas,” said Guo Hai, dean of the South China University of Technology’s Institute of Public Policy.
There is tremendous complementarity among China’s GBA and the bay areas surrounding San Francisco, New York and TokyoGuo Hai, South China University of Technology’s Institute of Public Policy
Such cooperation, Guo said, could make business and people-to-people exchanges less vulnerable to political tensions by institutionalising local-level cooperation and keeping such dealings separate from disputes between the two central governments.
“Local authorities are less politically driven, more pragmatic and pro-business. There is tremendous complementarity among China’s GBA and the bay areas surrounding San Francisco, New York and Tokyo,” he said.
However, Guo noted that Beijing still needed to flesh out the details and consult potential partners on the proposed association’s membership and governance structure.
Xi’s call for closer ties between bay areas drew support from some business representatives in the United States. Antonio Yung, an envoy and business representative for the government of Sacramento, California’s capital, welcomed deeper cooperation between the San Francisco Bay Area and China’s GBA.
“The two bay areas are uniquely linked culturally, and there is mutually beneficial business. Now that Xi has underscored bay-to-bay ties, there’s an expectation [that more can be done for] exchanges to expand substantially,” Yung said.
Zak Dychtwald, founder of BridgeWorks, a consultancy that advises American companies operating in China, said Shenzhen and Silicon Valley had similarities and competitive strengths.
“Silicon Valley has been Chinese tech’s ‘innovation city on a hill’ for decades. Walk into any Chinese innovation centre, and you’ll see Silicon Valley’s history on the wall. Proposing a partnership of bay areas signals a new sense of parity,” Dychtwald said.
[embedded media]
“The bay area push is sincere but is foremost in China’s interest. Silicon Valley can’t easily replicate Shenzhen’s hardware innovation strengths. Still, China has a lot to learn from the US on software,” he added.
In his speech, Xi also pointed to innovation as a way to shore up growth. While the performance of the world’s second-largest economy has become increasingly uneven, the Chinese leader called the country a “vast testing ground”, saying it offered an unusually large environment to develop and refine cutting-edge technologies.
“From factory and farm robots to autonomous driving and drone delivery, China is a supersized innovation testing ground where frontier technologies are tested and improved in real-world scenarios,” Xi said. “New technologies will be turned into growth drivers.”
Xi also stressed that China’s 4.6 per cent economic growth in the first three quarters was a sign of strength.
“The economy maintains a strong momentum, demonstrating great resilience and vitality … The green and low-carbon transition is also picking up speed,” he said. “The 15th five-year plan has got off to a good start,” he added, referring to Beijing’s half-decade-long blueprint for socio-economic development.
But while Beijing’s 4.5 to 5 per cent growth target for 2026 appeared within reach, October retail sales and industrial output both trailed expectations. Consumer spending growth slowed to 0.4 per cent from 1.1 per cent in September, while industrial output growth fell to 4.8 per cent from 5.5 per cent.
Against this backdrop, Xi signalled that China wanted to expand market access and increase imports, saying Beijing would accelerate efforts to develop a large, open market for overseas businesses.
By Frank Chen

title_en: Democrats nominate Jeffries to be first black US House speaker
content_en:
Despite facing opposition from some progressive colleagues, Jeffries secured 251 votes in a closed-door, secret ballot, with 11 against.
US congressman Hakeem Jeffries speaks with reporters ahead of Democratic leadership elections at the Capitol on Tuesday. Photo: AP
Hakeem Jeffries is on the cusp of becoming the first black speaker of the US House of Representatives after Democrats elected him their leader on Wednesday following a sweeping midterm election triumph.
The 56-year-old New Yorker secured 251 votes in a closed-door, secret ballot, with 11 cast against his nomination, according to US media.
Jeffries faced no declared challenger, although opposition from some newly elected progressives had exposed divisions over how Democrats should wield their new-found power.
His nomination puts him on course to preside over a commanding Democratic majority during the final two years of US President Donald Trump’s term, as his party prepares to reverse Republican policies and investigate the administration.
Jeffries must still win a formal vote of the full House when the new Congress convenes on January 3, when he would become the first black politician to hold the powerful post. With a large Democratic majority, this is seen as something of a formality.
US congresswoman Nancy Pelosi arrives for the House leadership elections on Capitol Hill on Wednesday. Photo: EPA
Both returning Democrats and incoming lawmakers took part in Wednesday’s election, including progressives who had sought concessions on issues ranging from US military support for Israel to the influence of money in politics.
Jeffries had requested a recorded vote rather than a nomination “by acclamation” – without a formal ballot – as some allies had hoped.
He argued that every Democrat should have an opportunity to weigh his experience, record and vision, citing the precedent set when the party last took control of the House in 2018.
The ballot remained secret, with the overall tally made public but individual votes kept anonymous.
Ahead of the election, Jeffries met progressive lawmakers to discuss issues including Israel and healthcare, with proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand coverage among the topics discussed.
The Democratic leader has also sought to shift attention to the party’s plans for governing after voters handed Republicans a crushing defeat amid anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel costs.
“Folks are drowning in this Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning that situation around, beginning on day one,” he told reporters on Tuesday.
“We’re going to relentlessly fight for an affordable America.”
A protester holds a sign outside US Senator Chuck Schumer’s office in New York on Tuesday. Photo: EPA
Raised in Brooklyn’s working-class Crown Heights neighbourhood, Jeffries trained as a lawyer before entering the New York state legislature in 2007 and winning election to Congress in 2012.
Known for his measured manner, sharp rhetoric and penchant for quoting hip-hop artists, he became the first black politician to lead a party in either chamber of Congress when Democrats chose him to succeed Nancy Pelosi in 2022.
He also served as a House prosecutor during Trump’s first impeachment trial in 2020.
As speaker, Jeffries would preside over one of Washington’s most powerful institutions and stand second in line to the presidency behind the vice-president.
But he would face a formidable task in managing a Democratic coalition spanning centrists and an increasingly assertive left flank.
His party has promised investigations into Trump and his administration, while lawmakers remain divided over Israel, healthcare and how aggressively to pursue their agenda against a president who retains veto power.
Jeffries’s nomination contrasts with a more competitive leadership contest among Senate Democrats, where veteran party chief Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from progressive Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen.
Van Hollen has attracted support from prominent left-wing figures, including Bernie Sanders, but acknowledges he is the underdog. Senate Democrats will elect their leader in early December.
Republicans chose their own congressional leaders last week, elevating Trump ally Jim Jordan in the House and retaining John Thune in the Senate.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Japan’s Takaichi meets Putin in rare talks amid strained ties with Russia
content_en:
First meeting between the countries’ leaders in seven years comes amid tensions over Ukraine, an espionage arrest and a territorial dispute.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi (left) and Russian President Vladimir Putin met on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China. Photo: AP
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday, marking a rare high-level contact at a time of deeply strained relations over Moscow’s war in Ukraine and the recent arrest of a Japanese journalist on espionage allegations.
The talks, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, lasted about 30 minutes.
It was the first face-to-face encounter between the leaders of the two countries in seven years, since the late Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe last met Putin in 2019.
Bilateral ties have deteriorated sharply since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with Tokyo joining Western allies in imposing sweeping sanctions on Moscow.
Relations have been tested further recently by a series of diplomatic and commercial flashpoints – most notably the detention of Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun.
The reporter was arrested in October on accusations of gathering information on Moscow’s defence capabilities for Tokyo.
[embedded media]
Earlier this month, Moscow placed local subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco under temporary management, prompting a formal diplomatic protest from Tokyo.
Beyond these recent frictions lies a decades-old sovereignty row that has prevented the two nations from signing a formal peace treaty since the end of World War II.
The dispute centres on a chain of islands off Japan’s northernmost Hokkaido, administered by Russia as the Southern Kurils and claimed by Tokyo as the Northern Territories.
Tensions over the archipelago flared in August when Putin travelled to Etorofu – known as Iturup in Russia – one of the four contested islands.
The trip, his first inspection of the territory since taking office in 2000, drew swift protest from Tokyo.
By Alyssa Chen

title_en: Islam projected to surpass Christianity as world’s largest religion by 2035
content_en:
Pew Research Centre’s new projections forecast that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035.
Muslim pilgrims perform Umrah around the Kaaba, Islam’s holiest shrine, at the Grand Mosque complex in Saudi Arabia’s holy city of Mecca on October 20. Photo: AFP
Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world’s largest religion by 2035, according to detailed projections released on Wednesday by the Pew Research Centre.
Pew, which has been issuing authoritative reports on religious demography for 25 years, said both Islam and Christianity were growing, but Islam was growing much faster. A key reason, Pew said, was that Muslims tended to have more children than other major religious groups.
“It’s the babies,” said Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett, explaining that conversion and other ways of changing religious identity were much smaller factors than fertility rates.
During 2020 to 2025, the fertility rate for Muslims was 3.1 children per woman, followed by the rate for Christians at 2.5, according to Pew. The average fertility rate for all other women was 1.6, below the level of 2.1 that is considered necessary for each generation to replace itself.
A Christian worshipper lights a candle in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in the Old City of Jerusalem on Sunday. Photo: AFP
According to Pew’s latest estimates, there were 2.27 billion Christians and 2.02 billion Muslims worldwide in 2020. Pew’s new projections forecast that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035. By 2070, if recent trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under 3 billion Christians worldwide.
The estimates are part of a broader Pew project examining how the size of major religious groups could change between 2020 and 2070. The projections take into account recent differences between religious groups’ age profiles, fertility rates, and patterns of religious switching and migration.
Among the many notable findings: Pew projects that the United States, within 40 years, will no longer have a Christian majority. Christians now account for 62 per cent of the population, according to Pew, and will fall below 50 per cent by 2065.
In neighbouring Canada, Christians were expected to drop below 50 per cent by 2030, Pew said.
In both countries, a significant reason for the drop is the concurrent increase in the number of people with no religious affiliation. By 2070, they are projected to account for 41 per cent of the US population and to outnumber Christians in Canada.
The world’s population is projected to increase by 29 per cent between 2020 and 2070, according to Pew. Of the religious groups it analysed, Muslims and Christians are the only ones expected to keep pace, with Christians growing by 30 per cent and Muslims by 80 per cent.
Hindus light oil lamps as they celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, in Srinagar, Indian-controlled Kashmir, on November 8. Photo: AP
Although Hindus and Jews are growing in absolute numbers, they are projected to decline as a percentage of the global population, Pew noted. It forecasts that Buddhists would shrink both in number and as a portion of the world’s population, in part due to expected declines in the overall populations of China, South Korea and Japan.
According to Pew, over the coming decades most of the world’s population growth is expected to occur in Africa, particularly south of the Sahara Desert, where most people are Christians or Muslims. The region’s high fertility and rising life expectancy would boost the global numbers of both faiths, Pew predicted.
By 2070, Pew said, more than half of the world’s Christians would live in sub-Saharan Africa, and Congo would surpass the US as the country with the most Christians, with their ranks increasing threefold to 270 million.
The populations of other major regions are expected to grow more modestly, or even decline.
For example, the number of people living in Europe would shrink by 17 per cent by 2070, Pew said, and the number of Christians there would drop by a third, from 505 million to 324 million. Over the same period, the percentage of Europe’s population that is Muslim is expected to increase from 6 per cent to 13 per cent.
In the US, Pew projects that the number of Christians will decline from about 217 million in 2020 to about 174 million in 2070.
Several mainline Protestant denominations in the US have faced declining membership over many years. However, Jeffrey Brodd, a religious studies professor at California State-Sacramento, suggested a rebound was possible following congressional election victories this month by several Democrats active in these moderate-to-liberal denominations.
Indonesian Muslims take part in the Istisqa rain prayer at a field in Surabaya, East Java province, on October 23. Indonesia currently has the most Muslims. Photo: AFP
Fertility rates a driving factor
By Pew’s estimates, Muslim women gave birth to more babies than women in any other religion during 2020 to 2025. About 252 million babies were born to Muslim mothers, compared with 208 million born to Christian mothers.
Muslims are the only major religious group expected to have growing numbers of births in the decades ahead. The other groups are projected either to have steady numbers of births or to experience gradual decline.
If recent trends continue, according to Pew, Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population by 2070, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia – which currently has the most Muslims.
Gina Zurlo, a senior researcher at Harvard Divinity School specialising in religious demographics, said Christian-Muslim relations were “extremely important” in light of the evolving trends.
“The ‘clash of civilisation’ theory still looms large in some religious communities and there is a lot of misunderstanding of both religions from both sides,” she said via email. “Many Christians are not happy to see that Islam will be the world’s largest religion and it’s causing even more angst.”
“I hope people seek opportunities for greater interreligious education,” she added. “Personal contact is important – when people have personal relationships across religious differences, it ‘humanises’ the ‘other’ in fruitful ways.”
Thai Buddhist devotees carry a long red robe to wrap and cover the pagoda during the Golden Mountain Pagoda Red Robe Wrapping rite ceremony at Wat Saket temple in Bangkok on Tuesday. Photo: EPA
Alan Cooperman, Pew’s director of religion research, notes that most of the projected proliferation of Muslims and Christians is occurring in countries where they already are the majority – with conversion playing only a minor role.
“I don’t think this is a situation in which the growth of Muslims is coming at the expense of Christians,” he added. “I do worry about mischief being made with headlines or narratives that take this finding and portray it as sort of a clash where Christians are losing to Muslims.”
Many countries have also seen a steady proliferation of the “nones” – people who are atheist, agnostic or religiously unaffiliated.
Excluding China, which has a high proportion of “nones” but faces a sharp decline in overall population, the ranks of “nones” elsewhere will grow by more than 180 million by 2070, Pew noted.
The “nones” already account for most of the population in 10 countries, including the Czech Republic, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Uruguay and Vietnam, according to Pew. South Korea, France and the United Kingdom are forecast to join this group by 2070.

title_en: Rare hug and roaring flyover set stage for historic firsts at Apec in Shenzhen
content_en:
China gears up for a display of major-power diplomacy in unprecedented talks with Russia and the United States.
US President Donald Trump walks with China’s President Xi Jinping after arriving at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: pool via AFP
It was a day of firsts in Shenzhen on Wednesday when Chinese President Xi Jinping personally greeted his American counterpart Donald Trump at the city airport, setting up a historic start to the Apec summit.
It was the first time in nearly seven decades that China’s top leader had welcomed a visiting foreign head of state at an airport, and it set the stage for an international event that is likely to lead to a joint declaration by the 21 Apec members on Thursday.
Earlier in the day, Xi hosted Vladimir Putin, the first serving Russian president to visit the southern Chinese hi-tech capital, and on Thursday, the two leaders will take part in another first – a trilateral summit with Trump.
In yet another unprecedented event, Xi will also hold his third bilateral summit this year with Trump.
[embedded media]
The last time a Chinese head of state greeted a visiting counterpart on the tarmac was in 1959 when paramount leader Mao Zedong was at Beijing’s airport to welcome the Soviet Union’s Nikita Khrushchev for a secret trip during a time of strategic distrust.
But this time it was different. After Trump walked down the staircase of Air Force One, the leaders of the two most powerful countries in the world hugged before the cameras – a rare display of physical affection by Xi.
Then five Chinese J-10C fighter jets from the PLA Air Force’s August 1st Aerobatic Team roared past, trailing coloured smoke across the sky at the airport.
China wants to make the message clear – the unparalleled honour given to Trump was a show of how it values the principle of reciprocity.
Reciprocity has become a key element in China-US relations and was articulated by Xi during his state visit to the US two months ago.
“When I visited the United States in September this year, President Trump and the first lady specially went to the airport to welcome me and held a grand welcome ceremony. China is a nation of etiquette and has a tradition of reciprocity,” Xi said to Trump as the two were on the tarmac, according to state news agency Xinhua.
He added that he looked forward to discussing bilateral ties, Asia-Pacific cooperation and global issues.
Wednesday marked the start of what promises to be two days of intense summitry.
The world is eagerly waiting to see how the trilateral meeting of the three largest powers will unfold, particularly regarding any impact on the Ukraine war, North Korea and even the Middle East.
Kremlin senior adviser Yuri Ushakov was quoted by Russia’s official Tass news agency as saying the three sides were working intensively on a joint statement and that the parties would touch on a wide range of issues, “taking into account the conflicts tormenting the world”.
[embedded media]
Those talks will be preceded by a bilateral meeting between Xi and Trump – the US president’s first such discussion since his Republican Party’s bruising midterm electoral defeats.
Analysts and business sectors are also watching closely for any concrete progress on the Boards of Trade and Investment agreed by the two countries earlier this year, potential AI cooperation, and any possible fallout from the scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
A wild card for Thursday is whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will join any of the talks. Kim is not taking part in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit but earlier this week Trump floated the idea that the two might meet in Shenzhen.
Putin’s early arrival, warm words for Xi
Wednesday’s official activity began in the early hours, with Putin among the first leaders to arrive in the city.
He was greeted on arrival by Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi. Xi and Putin then met for a two-hour bilateral meeting followed by a working breakfast.
The relationship between the two countries stood “as firm as a mountain amid wind and rain” and provided stability and certainty to a volatile and changing world, he said, according to a report by state news agency Xinhua.
Putin also gave a keynote address at the Apec CEO summit, during which he said Western sanctions were “failed attempts”.
He argued that “instruments of economic dominance” – including sanctions, tariffs and export restrictions – had lost their intimidating effect and could not stop Russia’s national growth. Instead, they were only hurting the European Union’s industrial capacity and competitiveness.
In his opening speech to the CEO summit, Xi called for cooperation and innovation to bring prosperity to the Asia-Pacific region to weather the turbulent world at a time when “global growth lacks momentum, and unilateralism and protectionism are rampant”.
He also assured world leaders that China would continue to open up, positioning the country as a “supersize market” and “a promised land of development” for the global business community through innovation.
[embedded media]
“China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access but also go a step further – we will carry out reform in challenging areas, such as rules, regulation and standards, in order to fully ensure market access and an accommodating operating environment in the manufacturing sector, to steadily expand opening up in the service sector, and to foster a more stable and more predictable first-class environment for companies from around the world to invest and do business in China,” Xi said.
Xi added that China would support the establishment of a World Association for Bay Area Economic Cooperation “to deepen exchanges among bay areas from across the world”.
Canada’s Carney attends Apec amid US trade war
While the big powers are soaking up most of the attention in Shenzhen, Apec is also a platform for middle powers to exert influence on the world stage.
Among them is Canada, which has been drawn into a trade war with the United States. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met Trump later in the day to discuss trade issues.
Carney said the two discussed ongoing work towards a mutually beneficial trade agreement aimed at creating quality jobs, boosting affordability and fully respecting Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty.
Earlier he said that ties with China were “growing on every front” but brushed off suggestions that it was a threat to the US.
Carney also said he raised the issue of AI global governance when he met Xi in Shenzhen on Tuesday, setting out Canada’s “model for how this governance can be developed”.
China’s South Korea, Japan relations on show at Apec
China’s relations with South Korea have also been improving.
“I hope that South Korea-China ties will move beyond full recovery to become a more mature strategic partnership,” South Korean President Lee Jae Myung told Xi in talks on Wednesday.
Lee was given a lavish reception at the airport early that morning, with more than 100 dancers waiting to greet him. The warm reception was a stark contrast to the low-key welcome given to Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi walks toward Xi before the Apec welcome banquet on Wednesday. Photo: AFP
It is the first time a Japanese leader has visited China in seven years, but Takaichi’s welcome party consisted of a retired diplomat and the Japanese ambassador.
Still, courtesy prevailed. Ahead of the Apec “family photo” preceding the state dinner, Takaichi shook hands with Xi – their first in-person interaction since her remarks on Taiwan last year soured ties dramatically.
She said a few words to the Chinese leader, but Xi only smiled and did not respond. Xi’s wife, Peng Liyuan, also appeared to say nothing beyond a greeting.
More telling was the unusual photo taken of Xi, Trump and Putin. Putin walked over to Xi and Trump as they chatted briefly before the general photo of all the Apec leaders.
At the state dinner, Xi took the chance to tout Shenzhen as an example of the country’s innovation and international cooperation.
“Shenzhen’s story is a microcosm of China’s reform and opening-up,” Xi said in his toast to the guests, adding that the city’s development was “a successful example of Asia-Pacific cooperation”.
Yun Sun, an expert at the Washington-based Stimson Centre, said it was the first time a sitting US president had visited Shenzhen, a venue that “brings out the importance of the AI and chips discussion”.
She said recent events in the US would not greatly affect Beijing’s approach to ties. “I don’t think [the] midterm results or Nvidia has a major impact on how China will handle Trump,” she said.
“The key for China is what choices Trump will make.”
Additional reporting by Amber Wang, Dewey Sim, Cao Jiaxuan, Alyssa Chen, Fan Chen, Orange Wang and Khushboo Razdan
By Josephine Ma

title_en: Israel’s parliament moves to roll back Netanyahu’s divisive legacy
content_en:
With new speaker Matan Kahana at the helm, Gadi Eisenkot’s camp has an opportunity to deal early blows to Netanyahu’s legislative agenda.
Israeli lawmakers attend a parliamentary session at the Knesset in Jerusalem, during a vote to elect Matan Kahana as the new speaker, on Tuesday. Photo: AP
Israel’s parliament met under a new speaker from the anti-Benjamin Netanyahu bloc on Wednesday, as opponents of the caretaker prime minister began a legislative offensive to roll back his divisive legacy.
In the vote for parliament speaker late on Tuesday, 66 lawmakers out of 120 voted in favour of Matan Kahana, an ally of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot who has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu.
The speaker is an important office as it sets the timetable for parliamentary business and can therefore speed up or delay debates or votes on proposed legislation.
With Kahana at the helm, Eisenkot’s camp has an opportunity to deal blows to Netanyahu’s legislative agenda even before a possible government is formed.
High on the list is repealing the sweeping reforms to reduce the independence of the judiciary that were advanced by Netanyahu, who has been enraged over corruption charges against him that could land him in prison if he loses power.
Gadi Eisenkot (right) and new Knesset Speaker Matan Kahana after a voting session for the new speaker at the Israeli parliament, in Jerusalem on Tuesday. Photo: EPA
On Wednesday, a temporary committee in charge of organising parliamentary business approved waiving the usual 45-day waiting period for a series of private members’ bills put forward by both Eisenkot and Netanyahu’s blocs.
The Knesset held preliminary votes on bills from Eisenkot’s camp to reverse Netanyahu-era legislation aimed at increasing political influence over the judiciary and broadcast media, as well as weakening the role of the attorney general.
All passed the preliminary readings, but must still clear several parliamentary stages and be put to three votes before becoming law.
Netanyahu’s bloc put forward bills seeking to revoke the rights of lawmakers who do not recognise Hamas as a “terrorist organisation” and to ban interfering with the Jewish religious practice of laying tefillin – binding small boxes containing Torah scrolls to the arm or head – in public spaces or educational settings.
Both also passed preliminary readings after Eisenkot’s bloc said it would not take part in those votes and left the chamber.
“We will have no part in Likud’s political theatre,” Eisenkot’s Yashar party said in a statement, referring to Netanyahu’s right-wing party.
Kahana, a 54-year-old former special forces soldier who is now a member of Yashar, was elected on Tuesday with the backing of the two Arab-majority lists, who won an unprecedented number of seats in the October 27 election.
“I intend to serve as speaker for everyone, regardless of religion, race or gender,” Kahana said during his inauguration speech immediately after the vote.
Benjamin Netanyahu and other lawmakers attend a parliamentary session at the Knesset in Jerusalem on Tuesday. Photo: AP
The October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either Eisenkot or Netanyahu’s bloc.
Netanyahu on Tuesday acknowledged the result in a rare statement free from political attacks on his opponents.
“The results of these elections are not what I wanted, nor are they what others wanted, but they are what the people want,” he told journalists, calling for unity.
Netanyahu, who has reportedly been urging US President Donald Trump to resume war on Iran, has talked up the threat from Tehran as he insists on the need for a unity government with Eisenkot.
As well as repealing Netanyahu’s divisive judicial reforms, Eisenkot has also vowed to quickly set up a state commission of inquiry to investigate security failures that led to Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack – the deadliest day in Israel’s history.
Netanyahu, who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel’s security, has refused an independent probe, instead proposing one whose members would be chosen by politicians.

title_display: Israel’s parliament moves to roll back Netanyahu’s divisive legacy
content_display:
With new speaker Matan Kahana at the helm, Gadi Eisenkot’s camp has an opportunity to deal early blows to Netanyahu’s legislative agenda.
Israeli lawmakers attend a parliamentary session at the Knesset in Jerusalem, during a vote to elect Matan Kahana as the new speaker, on Tuesday. Photo: AP
Israel’s parliament met under a new speaker from the anti-Benjamin Netanyahu bloc on Wednesday, as opponents of the caretaker prime minister began a legislative offensive to roll back his divisive legacy.
In the vote for parliament speaker late on Tuesday, 66 lawmakers out of 120 voted in favour of Matan Kahana, an ally of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot who has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu.
The speaker is an important office as it sets the timetable for parliamentary business and can therefore speed up or delay debates or votes on proposed legislation.
With Kahana at the helm, Eisenkot’s camp has an opportunity to deal blows to Netanyahu’s legislative agenda even before a possible government is formed.
High on the list is repealing the sweeping reforms to reduce the independence of the judiciary that were advanced by Netanyahu, who has been enraged over corruption charges against him that could land him in prison if he loses power.
Gadi Eisenkot (right) and new Knesset Speaker Matan Kahana after a voting session for the new speaker at the Israeli parliament, in Jerusalem on Tuesday. Photo: EPA
On Wednesday, a temporary committee in charge of organising parliamentary business approved waiving the usual 45-day waiting period for a series of private members’ bills put forward by both Eisenkot and Netanyahu’s blocs.
The Knesset held preliminary votes on bills from Eisenkot’s camp to reverse Netanyahu-era legislation aimed at increasing political influence over the judiciary and broadcast media, as well as weakening the role of the attorney general.
All passed the preliminary readings, but must still clear several parliamentary stages and be put to three votes before becoming law.
Netanyahu’s bloc put forward bills seeking to revoke the rights of lawmakers who do not recognise Hamas as a “terrorist organisation” and to ban interfering with the Jewish religious practice of laying tefillin – binding small boxes containing Torah scrolls to the arm or head – in public spaces or educational settings.

title_en: North Korean enrichment facility extension ‘externally complete’: IAEA
content_en:
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi says the ongoing expansion of North Korea’s uranium enrichment programme ‘remains a cause for serious concern’.
A satellite image shows a nuclear material production factory in Yongbyon, North Korea, on May 17. Photo: 2026 Planet Labs PBC/Handout via Reuters
A further extension of an enrichment facility in North Korea has been “externally complete” since last month, UN nuclear watchdog head Rafael Grossi has said.
Inspectors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) have not had access to North Korea since 2009, with the agency relying on satellite imagery and open sources to monitor the country’s nuclear programme.
“Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late-October 2026,” Grossi said on Wednesday in his opening statement at this week’s Board of Governors meeting.
“The ongoing expansion of the DPRK’s uranium enrichment programme remains a cause for serious concern,” he added, referring to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, the country’s official name.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un (right) inspecting a uranium enrichment facility in September 2024. Photo: KCNA/KNS/dpa
North Korea, under rafts of UN sanctions for its development of banned weapons, is believed to operate uranium enrichment facilities at sites in Yongbyon, Kangson and Kusong.
In September, IAEA members expressed “growing concern” in a resolution passed at the agency’s annual conference about increased atomic activity in North Korea.
The IAEA’s annual conference has repeatedly passed resolutions raising fears over North Korea’s nuclear weapons programme.
Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, said in a statement that the country’s nuclear-armed status was “absolute”, calling those hoping for its denuclearisation “idiots” and dismissing the “familiar silly talk” of efforts to denuclearise the country at the IAEA conference.
In a report ahead of the conference, Grossi said the IAEA had identified an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, which Pyongyang purportedly decommissioned after talks but later reactivated in 2021.
US President Donald Trump has hinted at a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un this week as Trump heads to Asia.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: A tarmac hug with Xi and a handshake with Putin, how Trump began his China visit
content_en:
The Chinese leader broke with decades of protocol by greeting the US president at the airport and recalling his own welcome to Washington.
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump briefly hugged on the tarmac at Shenzhen’s airport. Photo: Reuters
Handshakes, warm welcomes and carefully staged photo opportunities defined US President Donald Trump’s first day in Shenzhen on Wednesday, as China showcased its diplomatic priorities ahead of a planned three-way summit with Russia.
Here are the key moments from the day.
Xi’s personal welcome for Trump
Chinese President Xi Jinping broke with decades of protocol by personally greeting Trump at Shenzhen Baon Airport.
Their handshake quickly turned into a brief hug, while five J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, trailing red, yellow and blue smoke across the sky to welcome the US president.
[embedded media]
State news agency Xinhua reported that Xi recalled his September visit to the US, when Trump and his wife Melania welcomed the Chinese leader at the airport, saying: “China is a nation that values courtesy and has a tradition of reciprocating it.”
Xi also called for a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”, while his guest praised Xi as a “great leader”.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin, who arrived earlier, was welcomed by Cai Qi, a member of the Politburo Standing Committee.
Big three in the frame
At the Apec gala dinner, Putin approached Trump for a handshake and brief discussion, with Xi standing nearby.
It was the first time all three leaders had appeared together in public. They also joined other Apec leaders for the official group photograph.
Trump shakes hands with Vladimir Putin while Xi looks on. Photo: Reuters
The encounter came ahead of Thursday’s planned meeting between the trio. Washington has said nuclear arms reduction and Iran would be high on the agenda.
One senior US official said Ukraine would not be discussed because “China is not really a part of that track”, but Trump has said he wanted to discuss denuclearisation, Iran and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”.
Xi and Putin’s vision
Xi and Putin met earlier and set out their shared vision of a multipolar world. Xi called on both countries to “lead and advance the multipolarisation of the world and the democratisation of international relations”.
Putin said they were working towards “a fairer multipolar world order” and described economic coercion as “a thing of the past”.
Regional ties
Trump arrived in Shenzhen fresh from Manila, where he pursued stronger US trade and security ties with the Philippines and renewed cooperation with America’s Quad partners Japan, India and Australia.
His Asian tour has also drawn criticism at home. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer accused Trump of treating Manila as “little more than a layover on his way to meet with Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and potentially even Kim Jong-un”.
Trump has floated the possibility of meeting the North Korean leader but nothing has been announced officially.
[embedded media]
Meanwhile, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, whom Trump met in Manila, received a lower-level airport welcome in Shenzhen.
She later exchanged greetings with Xi at the banquet, marking their first official contact since her comments last year that a crisis in the Taiwan Strait may trigger military intervention by Japan.
Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Japan and the US, in common with most countries, do not recognise the island as independent.
By Khushboo Razdan

title_en: How China’s ‘carrier nannies’ are powering the Liaoning’s long Pacific push
content_en:
Replenishment ships made at least eight crossings through two major waterways around Japan between October 16 and Wednesday.
China’s Liaoning aircraft carrier transited the Miyako Strait near Japan into the Pacific Ocean on October 14. Photo: Reuters
Chinese replenishment ships were seen repeatedly transiting two major waterways around Japan as the Liaoning aircraft carrier conducted an extended western Pacific Ocean deployment that could test its 40-day endurance record.
According to Japanese defence ministry statements, the ships made at least eight crossings through the Miyako Strait and the Osumi Strait between October 16 and Wednesday, the South China Morning Post calculated.
The straits are strategically important in southwestern Japan and provide passage between the East China Sea and the western Pacific.
Chinese naval replenishment ships made repeated crossings between the two bodies of water, Japanese officials said.
The Chinese naval supply ship Hulunhu resupplies the destroyer Wuxi at sea during a western Pacific training exercise involving the aircraft carriers Liaoning and Shandong in June 2025. Photo: Handout
The vessels included the 50,000-tonne Type 901 ship Hulunhu alongside three 23,000-tonne Type 903A replenishment ships Taihu, Chaohu and Kekexilihu.
The Hulunhu accounted for four crossings, and the Taihu, Chaohu and Kekexilihu made the other four combined.
The Hulunhu is the lead vessel of China’s Type 901 fast combat support ships, capable of conducting alongside, astern and vertical replenishment. It can simultaneously supply warships with dry and liquid cargo, including ammunition, fresh water and fuel.
The ships are particularly important for aircraft carrier strike groups, which require aviation fuel to sustain carrier-based aircraft operations. This has earned them the nickname “carrier nannies”.
Meanwhile, the Liaoning is on pace to break its own record for longest Pacific deployment – surpassing the 40-day mark set in June – as the PLA Navy increases transits of large replenishment ships sailing between the East China Sea and the western Pacific to sustain the strike group’s operations.
After transiting the Miyako Strait into the Pacific Ocean on October 14, the Liaoning aircraft carrier group sailed into the South China Sea and passed through the Sulu and Celebes seas, completing an anticlockwise loop around the Philippines.
Following that transit, the group spent late October and early November conducting training operations in the Philippine Sea east of the Philippines.
The four-ship Liaoning strike group includes the Type 055 large guided-missile destroyers Wuxi and Anshan, and the Type 052D guided-missile destroyer Huainan.
[embedded media]
The formation did not include replenishment ships for the long operational period, with China instead deploying them separately.
Modern comprehensive replenishment ships, ranging from smaller supply vessels supporting coastal operations to large, fast combat support ships designed to accompany aircraft carrier strike groups on extended deployments, are indispensable for large-scale, prolonged and high-intensity combat operations in distant waters.
During the Liaoning’s exercise, an H-6K bomber pilot said he used numerous coded phrases to coordinate with pilots aboard the aircraft carrier, state broadcaster CCTV reported last month.
Military analyst Du Wenlong said the use of coded phrases to coordinate with carrier-based pilots, particularly those flying J-15 and J-35 fighter jets, could vastly improve coordination in providing aerial cover, according to the CCTV report.
Separately, China’s Type 003 aircraft carrier, the Fujian, returned from a recent drill in the South China Sea, according to satellite images. The images showed the Fujian was sailing back to its homeport Yulin Naval Base in Hainan province on Tuesday.
The Fujian will conduct more frequent and complex joint exercises with escorting destroyers, frigates and submarines to develop a stronger, more integrated naval combat system, according to military analyst Wei Dongxu in a CCTV report.
The Fujian will also undergo more coordinated ship-aircraft training, Wei said, adding that “we may see full-deck aircraft launch operations in the future”.
China’s other aircraft carrier, the Type 002 Shandong, has been under maintenance since January at Yulin. A satellite image on October 17 showed it was still in dry dock.
By Albee Zhang

title_en: Asean, Canada speed up trade pact over Trump, but can it curb US reliance?
content_en:
The agreement could establish a common framework, extending preferential market access to countries not covered by existing trade pacts.
Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr and First Lady Louise Araneta-Marcos greet Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney (right) as he arrives for the Asean Summit in Pasay City, Metro Manila, on Sunday. Photo: EPA
Canada and Asean are closing in on a free-trade agreement after five years of negotiations – a potential breakthrough that could deepen their economic ties and give businesses more opportunities amid growing uncertainty over global trade.
Its greatest value, though, might come from strengthening supply chains rather than reshaping trade, according to analysts.
Ottawa and the bloc announced the “substantial conclusion of negotiations” of the Asean-Canada Free Trade Agreement (ACAFTA) on Sunday, raising hopes that the agreement could be signed next year under Singapore’s chairmanship.
The announcement, made on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit, marked a significant step towards an agreement that has been under negotiation since November 2021.
In a joint statement released over the weekend, Asean leaders and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the progress, saying it “marks a significant milestone in the Asean-Canada relationship”.
“It reflects both sides’ ambition to deepen economic integration, expand trade and investment, and strengthen economic connectivity amid an evolving global economic landscape,” the leaders said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney (centre) and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (left) pose for a group photo with Southeast Asian leaders on the sidelines of the Asean summit on Sunday. Photo: dpa
Once implemented, the agreement is expected to reduce trade barriers, strengthen supply chains and provide businesses and investors with greater certainty.
Barrett Bingley, Asia regional director of the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, said ACAFTA negotiations had accelerated this year as leaders on both sides increasingly recognised the need to reduce their exposure to the United States.
“You could say that President Trump has accelerated the conclusion of the ACAFTA … with his effective attacks on the trade architecture of both Asean and Canada,” he said.
Asean was Canada’s fifth-largest merchandise trading partner last year, but the United States remains by far Ottawa’s most important.
The agreement would give Canada greater access to Asean’s nearly 700 million consumers and opportunities in agriculture, manufacturing, resources and services, said Ahmed Albayrak, a research associate at the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre.
“Broader trade relationships can reduce exposure to American tariffs and policy changes,” he said.
Robert Walker, a research fellow at the same institute, said Asean’s trade-intensive economies and integration with Chinese supply chains offered Canada opportunities to broaden its economic relationships – although the pact’s impact on diversification away from the US would be “marginal”.
“What is notable is that this would be Asean’s first trade agreement with a North American economy,” he said.
But outstanding provisions still need to be settled before the pact can be signed and ratified. Albayrak expects the process to continue up to next year, with Singapore at the helm. “Singapore would help advance the agreement,” he said.
“How soon the FTA is concluded and then ratified is totally dependent on the willingness of both sides to make further concessions on the areas of trade and investment that have not been concluded,” Walker said.
Another reason 2027 looks more likely is that it is the 50th year of relations between both parties, according to Bingley.
“We are hoping there is an announcement around the ACAFTA at that time. We don’t know if it will be ready for signing … you might see a political moment, for instance, in November at the leaders summit in 2027, where the signing is actually done, if it’s held that long,” he said.
Extending access
The agreement could establish a common framework for economic ties across Southeast Asia, extending preferential market access to countries that are not covered by existing trade pacts with Ottawa, such as Cambodia and Laos, Albayrak said.
Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore and Vietnam are already trade partners with Canada under the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership.
Ottawa has also recently signed bilateral trade deals with the Philippines and Indonesia, with the latter set to take effect on December 1.
Even for countries already covered by existing agreements, the new pact could give businesses greater flexibility, Bingley said.
One potential benefit for manufacturers is the accumulation of rules of origin, which could allow materials and production processes from different Asean members to count towards the requirements for preferential tariff treatment.
This could help industries such as electronics, automotive parts, semiconductors and processed agricultural products maintain supply chains across Southeast Asia without facing higher tariffs because various stages of production take place in different countries.
Workers assemble electric cars at a factory in Hai Phong, Vietnam, in September 2023. Photo: AP
“Asean is already quite a substantial exporter into Canada,” Bingley said. “So I suspect there’ll be even more of that, especially as certain types of manufacturing move out of China and deeper into Asean supply chains.”
Greater certainty for investors could also encourage businesses to establish operations in both markets, he said. “The additional investment certainty that’s going to come with that should spur establishment in both places.”
Agriculture – particularly sanitary and phytosanitary measures governing food products – could be another priority area, alongside services and energy, he added.
Canada has also expressed interest in supporting the Asean Power Grid, an initiative aimed at improving electricity connectivity in the region, potentially creating opportunities for Canadian technology and engineering firms.
The free trade agreement could support these ambitions, Bingley said, but cautioned that governments and businesses would still need to invest in physical infrastructure to unlock its full potential.
He pointed to Canadian energy exports as an example of how the lack of suitable facilities could constrain trade even if market access improved.
“At the moment, Asean is buying very, very little Canadian oil. Brunei is buying some. Singapore is buying a little bit, because the refineries are not in the right configuration or metallurgy to take large amounts of Canadian oil,” he said.
“So the trade deals are great. They’ve laid down excellent optionality. And now it’s for both sides to put in place the hard infrastructure.”
By Sam Beltran

The agreement could establish a common framework, extending preferential market access to countries not covered by existing trade pacts.
Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr and First Lady Louise Araneta-Marcos greet Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney (right) as he arrives for the Asean Summit in Pasay City, Metro Manila, on Sunday. Photo: EPA
Canada and Asean are closing in on a free-trade agreement after five years of negotiations – a potential breakthrough that could deepen their economic ties and give businesses more opportunities amid growing uncertainty over global trade.
Its greatest value, though, might come from strengthening supply chains rather than reshaping trade, according to analysts.
Ottawa and the bloc announced the “substantial conclusion of negotiations” of the Asean-Canada Free Trade Agreement (ACAFTA) on Sunday, raising hopes that the agreement could be signed next year under Singapore’s chairmanship.
The announcement, made on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit, marked a significant step towards an agreement that has been under negotiation since November 2021.
In a joint statement released over the weekend, Asean leaders and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the progress, saying it “marks a significant milestone in the Asean-Canada relationship”.
“It reflects both sides’ ambition to deepen economic integration, expand trade and investment, and strengthen economic connectivity amid an evolving global economic landscape,” the leaders said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney (centre) and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (left) pose for a group photo with Southeast Asian leaders on the sidelines of the Asean summit on Sunday. Photo: dpa
Once implemented, the agreement is expected to reduce trade barriers, strengthen supply chains and provide businesses and investors with greater certainty.
Barrett Bingley, Asia regional director of the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, said ACAFTA negotiations had accelerated this year as leaders on both sides increasingly recognised the need to reduce their exposure to the United States.
“You could say that President Trump has accelerated the conclusion of the ACAFTA … with his effective attacks on the trade architecture of both Asean and Canada,” he said.
Asean was Canada’s fifth-largest merchandise trading partner last year, but the United States remains by far Ottawa’s most important.
The agreement would give Canada greater access to Asean’s nearly 700 million consumers and opportunities in agriculture, manufacturing, resources and services, said Ahmed Albayrak, a research associate at the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre.
“Broader trade relationships can reduce exposure to American tariffs and policy changes,” he said.
Robert Walker, a research fellow at the same institute, said Asean’s trade-intensive economies and integration with Chinese supply chains offered Canada opportunities to broaden its economic relationships – although the pact’s impact on diversification away from the US would be “marginal”.
“What is notable is that this would be Asean’s first trade agreement with a North American economy,” he said.
But outstanding provisions still need to be settled before the pact can be signed and ratified. Albayrak expects the process to continue up to next year, with Singapore at the helm. “Singapore would help advance the agreement,” he said.
“How soon the FTA is concluded and then ratified is totally dependent on the willingness of both sides to make further concessions on the areas of trade and investment that have not been concluded,” Walker said.
Another reason 2027 looks more likely is that it is the 50th year of relations between both parties, according to Bingley.
“We are hoping there is an announcement around the ACAFTA at that time. We don’t know if it will be ready for signing … you might see a political moment, for instance, in November at the leaders summit in 2027, where the signing is actually done, if it’s held that long,” he said.
Extending access
The agreement could establish a common framework for economic ties across Southeast Asia, extending preferential market access to countries that are not covered by existing trade pacts with Ottawa, such as Cambodia and Laos, Albayrak said.
Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore and Vietnam are already trade partners with Canada under the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership.
Ottawa has also recently signed bilateral trade deals with the Philippines and Indonesia, with the latter set to take effect on December 1.
Even for countries already covered by existing agreements, the new pact could give businesses greater flexibility, Bingley said.
One potential benefit for manufacturers is the accumulation of rules of origin, which could allow materials and production processes from different Asean members to count towards the requirements for preferential tariff treatment.
This could help industries such as electronics, automotive parts, semiconductors and processed agricultural products maintain supply chains across Southeast Asia without facing higher tariffs because various stages of production take place in different countries.
Workers assemble electric cars at a factory in Hai Phong, Vietnam, in September 2023. Photo: AP
“Asean is already quite a substantial exporter into Canada,” Bingley said. “So I suspect there’ll be even more of that, especially as certain types of manufacturing move out of China and deeper into Asean supply chains.”
Greater certainty for investors could also encourage businesses to establish operations in both markets, he said. “The additional investment certainty that’s going to come with that should spur establishment in both places.”
Agriculture – particularly sanitary and phytosanitary measures governing food products – could be another priority area, alongside services and energy, he added.
Canada has also expressed interest in supporting the Asean Power Grid, an initiative aimed at improving electricity connectivity in the region, potentially creating opportunities for Canadian technology and engineering firms.
The free trade agreement could support these ambitions, Bingley said, but cautioned that governments and businesses would still need to invest in physical infrastructure to unlock its full potential.
He pointed to Canadian energy exports as an example of how the lack of suitable facilities could constrain trade even if market access improved.
“At the moment, Asean is buying very, very little Canadian oil. Brunei is buying some. Singapore is buying a little bit, because the refineries are not in the right configuration or metallurgy to take large amounts of Canadian oil,” he said.
“So the trade deals are great. They’ve laid down excellent optionality. And now it’s for both sides to put in place the hard infrastructure.”
By Sam Beltran

title_en: Xi greets Takaichi with a smile – but no words – as China-Japan freeze lingers
content_en:
The encounter before Apec welcome banquet is their first in-person interaction since Takaichi’s controversial comments on Taiwan a year ago.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi (left) and Chinese President Xi Jinping exchange smiles after shaking hands at the Apec summit welcome banquet in Shenzhen on November 18, 2026. Photo: Reuters
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Chinese President Xi Jinping had their first in-person interaction in Shenzhen since last autumn, when ties froze due to her controversial remarks on Taiwan.
Takaichi shook hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, as they posed for greeting photos ahead of the customary Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) “family photo” on Wednesday evening, according to a live feed of a welcome dinner for the Apec gathering.
Takaichi, dressed in a fluorescent pink blazer, said a few words to Xi after their handshake, to which Xi responded only with a smile.
Peng likewise appeared to remain silent after greeting her. After posing for the photograph, the trio exchanged nods, and the Japanese leader walked away. There was no interpreter on the stage with them.
This marked the first interaction between the two leaders since bilateral ties plunged to a historic low following Takaichi’s remarks that a crisis in the Taiwan Strait could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, potentially paving the way for military intervention.
It was the first time a sitting Japanese leader had spoken so explicitly about how the country might react in such a situation, drawing fierce rebukes from Beijing, including repeated demands for a retraction, export restrictions and the cancellation of flights, multiple high-level engagements and cultural events.
Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited – by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise the island as an independent state, though Washington is committed to supplying it with defensive weapons and opposes any forcible takeover.
[embedded media]
Earlier in the day, Takaichi made a low-key arrival in Shenzhen, beginning the first China visit by a Japanese leader in seven years.
She was greeted by retired Chinese diplomat Zhang Qiyue and Japanese ambassador to China Kenji Kanasugi on the tarmac before nodding briefly to ground staff.
Upon her arrival, there were no young Chinese greeters waving bouquets or national flags and chanting “welcome”. It was a stark contrast to the receptions given to other leaders, including South Korea’s presidential couple, who received a warm and exuberant welcome even at midnight, and US President Donald Trump, who was met with a historic greeting by Xi as fighter jets trailed colourful smoke overhead.
By Fan Chen
Sections: News / China / Diplomacy | Topics: China-Japan relations, 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen, Shenzhen, China, Japan, Sanae Takaichi, Peng Liyuan, Xi Jinping

title_en: US seeks stronger Southeast Asia ties to keep sensitive technology out of ‘wrong hands’
content_en:
US Ambassador to Asean Kevin Kim says Southeast Asia will be ‘at the heart of the superintelligence industry’, amid new chip export rules.
The United States has announced new restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips. Photo: Shutterstock
The United States wants to strengthen its cooperation with Southeast Asian governments to prevent sensitive technology from falling “into the wrong hands”, its envoy to Asean has said, as new restrictions on advanced chips raise concerns about the region’s access to cutting-edge artificial intelligence infrastructure.
US Ambassador to Asean Kevin Kim on Wednesday said the new measures highlighted Washington’s belief that Southeast Asia would be “at the heart of the superintelligence industry” looking ahead.
The US Commerce Department on Monday announced the new rules, which require companies to obtain a licence to “export, re-export or transfer [in-country]” advanced semiconductors to Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Brazil, saying the countries “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion”.
The measures also restrict data centres from remotely supplying high-volume compute to companies headquartered in, or with an ultimate parent in, these countries to train hi-tech models.
Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong arrives for the Asean summit in Pasay City, Metro Manila, the Philippines, on Sunday. Photo: EPA
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong separately told local media on Tuesday that his government could help the US run checks on companies in the city state to address concerns over how the chips were deployed and take firm action against businesses using Singapore to circumvent export controls.
“We want to uphold the rule of law, and we want to uphold Singapore’s reputation as a trusted business hub,” Wong told Singapore media after the Asean-US Special Summit in Manila on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, at a virtual press conference, Kim said the restrictions highlighted Southeast Asia’s importance to AI development.
“Given the importance that the United States, President Trump, and the entire government place on winning the superintelligence race, it’s very, very important for the United States to build a regulatory framework, processes, building trusted partnerships throughout the world that will ensure that American technology, American capabilities … are getting into the right hands,” said Kim, who presented his credentials in June.
“We want to be able to work with governments in Southeast Asia to ensure that the right technology, the right capabilities, do not fall into the wrong hands, so it’s very important for the US government to know how we can build trust; how we can build cooperation moving forward,” he added.
Kim also noted that Washington would maintain all communication channels to ensure concerns and information were exchanged between the US and its Southeast Asian partners.
Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said on Wednesday at the Singapore FinTech Festival that the city state was an international business hub and a trusted partner of many American enterprises.
“We value our international reputation, and we do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries in their international business activities,” Gan said, warning that the country would act against those who flouted its laws.
He added that Singapore was working with affected companies to assess the implications for their businesses and was engaging US authorities on the new rules and how Singapore could facilitate access for its companies.
[embedded media]
Under the new rules, shipments to the four Southeast Asian nations will be exempt from licensing requirements if they are destined for companies headquartered in the US or whose ultimate parent is US-based, provided the exporter submits monthly reports detailing the parties involved and the nature of the chips.
Existing data centre operators already supplying remote compute to covered entities have 90 days from the rule’s effective date, on Thursday, to obtain a licence to continue those services, while new shipments of advanced chips to the five countries require a licence once the rule takes effect.
The new measures come amid a scandal that led Jensen Huang to resign as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and former senior executive at Singapore-headquartered technology firm Megaspeed whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspect of spying for Beijing.
China has rejected the espionage allegations as groundless, accusing Washington of using the claims as a pretext to tighten technology restrictions against Beijing.
The controversy has fuelled recriminations in Washington as US authorities investigate whether advanced semiconductors used to power AI were diverted to China in violation of export controls through Megaspeed and its network of subsidiaries across Southeast Asia.
Alice Huang left Megaspeed in August 2025, while the company has denied wrongdoing and said it takes compliance with US export controls seriously.
By Jean Iau

title_en: Ship captain to set sail home after Hong Kong drops HK$400m pipeline damage case
content_en:
Prosecution drops criminal damage case against former captain of the Newnew Polar Bear after failing to contact witnesses from the mainland.
Finnish Border Guard photo of the cargo ship Newnew Polar Bear moving near the Balticconnector gas line in October 2023. Photo: Reuters
Marine authorities have withdrawn the prosecution of the captain of a Hong Kong-flagged container ship who was accused of severing a critical Baltic Sea gas pipeline linking Estonia and Finland three years ago, despite the court hearing that the incident caused HK$400 million in damage.
Proceedings against 43-year-old Wan Wenguo for alleged criminal damage were discontinued on Wednesday after a prosecutor from the Hong Kong Marine Department told Eastern Court that several witnesses from mainland China could not be contacted.
Wan, who had been in custody since December 2024, was expected to be deported to the mainland.
He had been charged with damaging a section of the 77km (47.8-mile) Balticconnector, a natural gas undersea pipeline that supplies Finland, and a nearby telecommunications cable linking Finland and Estonia. The damage occurred on October 8, 2023, when the Newnew Polar Bear was sailing through the Gulf of Finland.
The incident made international headlines after Finnish authorities said they suspected that an anchor of a Chinese container ship had been dislodged and damaged the pipeline.
Wan was also alleged to have violated navigation safety rules during the voyage from October to December 2023 by failing to ensure that the vessel had enough anchors and by not submitting daily reports to its owner. Both are also offences under the Merchant Shipping (Safety) Ordinance.
Underwater view of the damage sustained by the 77km Balticconnector natural gas pipeline. Photo: Handout
In the first hearing in December 2024, the presiding magistrate described the prosecution as a “special case” with no precedent in Hong Kong.
In subsequent hearings, the parties discussed legal issues including whether Hong Kong had the jurisdiction to handle a case that involved the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea.
They also touched on whether the case should be tried in the lowest level of court in Hong Kong after a magistrate revealed that the incident caused HK$400 million (US$51.3 million) in damage.
Wan’s lawyer prepared statements from maritime law specialists from overseas. The prosecution received documents from Finnish and Estonian authorities.
Wan had indicated that he would plead not guilty to the criminal damage offence, which was originally set for trial in December.
But the case took an unexpected turn on Wednesday when the prosecutors said they would not continue with the criminal prosecution after failing to summon several witnesses from the mainland. The South China Morning Post learned that one of the witnesses was an employee of the shipping company.
However, Wan still faced two summary charges, to which he had pleaded guilty, related to his failure to ensure that his ship complied with certain requirements.
The Eastern Law Courts Building in Sai Wan Ho, where proceedings against captain Wan Wenguo took place. Photo: Eugene Lee
The ship, Newnew Polar Bear, began its voyage in Kaliningrad and arrived in St. Petersburg, Russia, in early October 2023. It was supposed to sail through the North Sea, arriving at Vostochny, an international container port in the Russian Far East, before docking at its final destination in Tianjin, mainland China, in December.
On October 8, Wan found out that an anchor was missing and told the shipping company about it. He had tried but been unable to source parts from ports in Russia.
The company confirmed that he should carry on the journey because Newnew Polar Bear was scheduled to rendezvous with other icebreakers.
As the ship continued to sail without an anchor between October 28 and November 3, Wan failed to report his location and speed to the company, which is a standard procedure required under international maritime rules.
Jerry Chung Ming-shing, Wan’s lawyer, told the court that two telecommunication systems were affected by the weather in the Arctic area, and it had not crossed his client’s mind that he could use an iridium satellite phone – which uses a network that converges at the North and South Poles – to reach his company.
Wan admitted to breaching the law because of his negligence and said he intended to take responsibility by paying fines for the two summary offences.
Chung said Wan, a native of Northeast mainland China, did not have any friends or relatives in Hong Kong to help settle the fines for him.
Magistrate Kestrel Lam Tsz-hong noted that Wan would be deported after the hearing and that it would be difficult for the court to trace whether the seafarer would return and pay off the penalties.
The prosecution did not object to preposition of “unconditional release”, but Lam insisted on handing down a fine of HK$4,000 for the two charges.
The judge ordered Wan to clear the fines before June 30 next year, having noted that the owner of the ship company had earlier paid HK$1,500 for similar offences.
By Fiona Chow

title_en: Xi’s speech at Apec gathering puts spotlight on cooperation
content_en:
Stressing the importance of openness, the president set out specific steps that China is taking that are positive for regional and global shared prosperity.
Chinese President Xi Jinping speaks at the opening ceremony of Apec CEO summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18. Photo: dpa
China is hosting its third Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, having hosted the event in Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. Past themes of these events have been inclusive, featuring terms like “partnership”, “participation” and “together”. Apec 2026 in Shenzhen is no exception; it’s theme is “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”. President Xi Jinping reflected it in his keynote address. The word “cooperation” appeared up to 19 times in the English translation. The contrast with the prevailing volatile global climate of geopolitical tension, armed conflict, protectionism and unilateralism is very obvious.
Apec’s 21 member economies together account for more than 61 per cent of global gross domestic product and 36 per cent of the world’s population, representing high growth potential. From day one, Apec has advocated sustainable development for this region.
The world has changed politically and economically since the first time China hosted Apec. Yet China’s commitment to multilateralism remains the same.
In his address, Xi cited specific steps that would be positive for Asia-Pacific – and global – shared prosperity. China would cut tariffs and expand market access while going further to reform rules and regulations for foreign businesses, fostering a more stable and predictable environment for companies to invest and do business.
Xi called for deeper cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI), saying China supports establishing a World Association for Bay Areas’ Economic Cooperation. This would deepen exchange and interaction among various bay areas and help explore new paths of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation. The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area would have an even bigger role to play, one that is to be expanded to a global level. Xi emphasised Shenzhen’s status as a part of China’s Greater Bay Area.
Without naming the United States, Xi warned against rising “unilateralism and protectionism” and called on Asia-Pacific economies to remove trade and investment barriers. Xi pledged to further open China’s vast consumer market to global businesses and pointed to China’s 15th five-year plan as a source of economic opportunity and cooperation. He urged support for “free and open trade” without investment barriers, and called for upholding a World Trade Organization-centred multilateral trading system and stable supply chains. He argued that openness brought progress while isolation inevitably led to “falling behind”, and called for building a “bridge of openness and cooperation” across the Asia-Pacific. Xi described the current geopolitical situation as “complex and volatile”, citing rising protectionism, weak growth momentum and new challenges from emerging technologies.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted that economic ties between China and Canada were getting closer, and said China had restored market access for more than 90 per cent of the Canadian trade that had faced tariffs. Russian President Vladimir Putin said sanctions, tariffs and export curbs could hold back development but were not capable of fully stopping growth or destroying economies. Europe and the US have “punished themselves” with such measures, he said.

It is expected that China’s initiatives will pave the way for more regional and global collaborations amid the challenges of protectionism and unilateralism. In that regard, Xi’s initiatives are critical for the future of the region.
