title_display: Xi’s speech at Apec gathering puts spotlight on cooperation
content_display:
Stressing the importance of openness, the president set out specific steps that China is taking that are positive for regional and global shared prosperity.
Chinese President Xi Jinping speaks at the opening ceremony of Apec CEO summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18. Photo: dpa
China is hosting its third Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, having hosted the event in Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. Past themes of these events have been inclusive, featuring terms like “partnership”, “participation” and “together”. Apec 2026 in Shenzhen is no exception; it’s theme is “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”. President Xi Jinping reflected it in his keynote address. The word “cooperation” appeared up to 19 times in the English translation. The contrast with the prevailing volatile global climate of geopolitical tension, armed conflict, protectionism and unilateralism is very obvious.
Apec’s 21 member economies together account for more than 61 per cent of global gross domestic product and 36 per cent of the world’s population, representing high growth potential. From day one, Apec has advocated sustainable development for this region.
The world has changed politically and economically since the first time China hosted Apec. Yet China’s commitment to multilateralism remains the same.
In his address, Xi cited specific steps that would be positive for Asia-Pacific – and global – shared prosperity. China would cut tariffs and expand market access while going further to reform rules and regulations for foreign businesses, fostering a more stable and predictable environment for companies to invest and do business.
Xi called for deeper cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI), saying China supports establishing a World Association for Bay Areas’ Economic Cooperation. This would deepen exchange and interaction among various bay areas and help explore new paths of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation. The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area would have an even bigger role to play, one that is to be expanded to a global level. title_en: Just whose interests do those who ‘stand with Taiwan’ serve?
content_en:
It is important to separate Taiwanese people’s interests from the familiar Western narratives around the Taiwan Strait.
Supporters of Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an, who is seeking re-election, march through the rain in Taipei on November 14. Many supporters of Taiwan speak of preserving the “Taiwanese way of life”. A scenario involving war will not help. Photo: AFP
Many Westerners, from professional commentators to enthusiastic youth, like to “stand with Taiwan” in their public comments. But is their aim to actually support the best possible future for the people of the island, even if it manifests itself in peaceful reunification, or do they simply intend to counter Beijing, as a conscious or unwitting part of Washington’s geopolitical endeavours?
For decades, the magic term for closing every public discussion on the issue of Taiwan has been “status quo”. Every opinion or analysis circled back to the status quo, knowing well it was a comfortable middle ground serving as peaceful management of the situation.
Recent developments suggest mounting tensions may not allow this convenient avoidance to survive for long. Will it be the increasingly blatant separatist rhetoric of the leaders in Taipei that causes an irreversible reaction? Will it be the militarisation of some close neighbours that eventually forces countermeasures? Will it be either side seeing an unexpected tactical or geopolitical opportunity to settle the question once and for all? We don’t know. But the stability of the status quo has been quietly eroding, and with every tension-filled news headline, it gets closer to crumbling.
To avoid bias, it would help to look beyond the familiar narratives, because global public forums have been saturated with American (not Taiwanese) commentary about the past, present and future of the island.
There is very little, if any, knowledge in the West of the fact that both constitutions across the Taiwan Strait, despite their different interpretations, consider Taiwan part of China, and neither establishes a country called Taiwan.
Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te delivers a speech, next to a portrait of Sun Yat-sen, the revolutionary who helped topple China’s last imperial dynasty, during Double Tenth celebrations in Taipei on October 10. Photo: Reuters
Quite the contrary: in recent years, more Western news outlets and commentators seem to be blurring lines, relativising facts. Some now routinely call Taiwan a country, brushing aside constitutional realities and adding unnecessary provocation to an already sensitive issue. And while unknowing sympathisers may be credited with uninformed goodwill, when serious analysts talk like this, it is dangerously irresponsible. One may even ask, whose interests does such behaviour really serve?
Many genuinely well-meaning supporters will confirm that the core ideal they aim to preserve is the sociopolitical progress that the people of Taiwan have achieved, often called the “Taiwanese way of life”. And that, just like the progress and development of mainland China, it is worth respecting and preserving.
If the status quo collapses and the question is forced into a definitive settlement, three outcomes are possible: negotiated reunification, reunification through war, or independence through war. It has been declared and confirmed several times: any declaration of independence will lead to armed conflict. It is not unnatural: most countries would react that way if a part of them unilaterally claimed independence.
So here we are at the original question: Which scenario offers the best chance of preserving the Taiwanese way of life? Given not only the immeasurable human cost, but also the unpredictability of any war, and presuming that reunification after a war would not be based on upholding the political system, one may come to the conclusion that the best chance that the Taiwanese way of life will endure is if the parties on both sides of the Taiwan Strait agree on it as part of a comprehensive, foundational deal.
[embedded media]
It has been a widespread narrative that Taiwan’s democracy is at risk from reunification, but Beijing has, time and again, confirmed that in case of a peaceful agreement, the political and governance system of the island will be respected.
More importantly, Beijing would have no reason or interest in undermining it at the cost of widespread unrest. For Beijing, reunification is way too important to be jeopardised in unnecessary ways.
And for those who fear the concessions would be temporary, it is important to emphasise: the parties need not follow historical examples. Negotiations can start with a clean sheet, with enforceable safeguards and independent compliance reviews built into the agreement, protecting its terms for generations to come.
More people in Taiwan ask themselves if Washington is just using the island as a tool to contain its rising adversary. If so, then war or peace may be decided by others’ interests, perhaps with the sole aim of weakening China, regardless of how many locals’ lives it may cost. So one hopes that those who “stand with Taiwan” consider what it is they are standing with or for. Because if the people matter less than the geopolitical narratives surrounding them, then perhaps they are merely pieces in someone else’s chess game.
By David Gorombolyi

title_en: Sign of the times? How China is quietly shifting global trade onto yuan payments
content_en:
China now settles nearly 30 per cent of its trade in yuan as both Beijing and grass-roots traders push to increase use of the currency.
Illustration: Brian Wang
When accountant Shao Bo visited a branch of Russia’s VTB Bank in Shanghai recently, she was surprised to find the place was packed with representatives of exporters from all over China.
“Everyone was there for the same purpose: setting up accounts to accept yuan payments from Russian buyers,” she said.
That “everyone” includes Shao. The company she works for in Shanghai produces and exports zips to fashion and apparel companies across Asia. The firm had started working with two new Russian buyers last year, and it was keen to stop settling transactions in roubles.
“Several months back, we proposed to our Russian clients that they pay in yuan rather than roubles,” she said. “I thought we might have some negotiations ahead, but they agreed to use yuan without much pushback.”
Companies across the world are making the same switch, as the Chinese yuan quietly but rapidly emerges as a popular currency for global payments.
Five years ago, only 17 per cent of China-Russia trade was settled in yuan, according to data from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. By June this year, that figure had jumped to 62 per cent.
Russia, hobbled by US sanctions, is an outrider when it comes to embracing the yuan. But the Chinese currency is also gaining ground across the board.
Nearly 30 per cent of China’s cross-border goods trade was settled in yuan during the first half of the year, according to the People’s Bank of China – more than 18 percentage points higher than its share a decade ago.
What is driving the increase?
The shift is partly being driven by grass-roots Chinese exporters like Shao’s company, which are eager to avoid foreign exchange losses.
The onshore yuan has been steadily appreciating in recent months, notching several four-year highs against the US dollar in October. Last week, it was trading at about 6.65 per dollar.
It looks like the yuan will probably keep strengthening, so using yuan for settlement is a natural call for our businessShao Bo, employee at Shanghai-based export company
For Chinese exporters who are paid in US dollars or other foreign currencies, a stronger yuan can be a major problem – squeezing their margins at a time when many are already under severe pressure amid a domestic economic slowdown.
“Clients won’t make up for our foreign exchange losses,” Shao said. “It looks to me like the yuan will probably keep strengthening. Using yuan for settlement is therefore a natural call for our business.”
That is especially true in the apparel industry, where Shao’s firm operates. The yuan has gained about 4.6 per cent so far this year – a figure that exceeds the net profit margins for many exporters in the industry.
The average profit margin in the knitwear sector, for example, was just 3.58 per cent in the first nine months of last year, according to the China National Textile and Apparel Council.
“Textile export markets are plagued by fierce, cutthroat competition,” Shao said. “That is why we need to try our best to guard against foreign exchange losses.”
Overseas buyers, meanwhile, are becoming more willing to accept demands to pay in yuan as China’s exporters gain greater influence in the global market.
Zhang Bin is the general manager of Solidware, a Shanghai-based firm that designs, manufactures and exports stainless steel drinkware. Most of its customers are based in Europe. For decades, euro or US dollar settlement was the norm, but Zhang recently achieved a milestone.
[embedded media]
“Two buyers in Sweden and Austria accepted yuan settlement this year,” Zhang said. “What won them over was our products – we own proprietary patents and unique designs for the items we supply.
“Our technical edge and reasonable pricing naturally put us in a stronger bargaining position at the negotiating table,” he added.
Shao echoed that view. “When it comes to our Russian clients, they struggle to find more competitive suppliers than us on both pricing and quality,” she said.
This ground-level trend dovetails with a long-term push by Beijing to internationalise the yuan.
China has been following a policy strategy of “encircling cities from the countryside”, according to Hu Jie, professor and executive director of the Southeast Asia Centre at the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance.
During the Chinese Civil War, the Communist Party focused on building rural bases in areas with weak central state control, consolidating their strength, and only then surrounding and seizing control of major cities.
According to Hu, Beijing is following a similar approach in boosting global use of the yuan: first moving to strengthen financial linkages with countries across the Global South.
“This boils down to economic clout,” Hu said. “The sequence starts with less developed economies and countries with strong trade links to China, before moving on to developed ones.”
A major target of China’s efforts has been the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) – China’s largest regional export market.
[embedded media]
“China and Asean rank as each other’s top trading partners, laying a foundation for financial connectivity,” Hu said. “Cross-border people flows are frequent, too. Put plainly, that creates another avenue for them to spend or even invest the yuan they hold.”
Having travelled extensively across Southeast Asia and spoken with local officials, Hu said another factor was driving the deepening ties: local views of China remained broadly optimistic, a marked contrast to sentiment in Europe.
Several Asean economies have already incorporated the yuan into their official foreign reserve portfolios. Meanwhile, Chinese financial institutions are expanding their footprints in the region.
More than 140 Asean institutions have connected to China’s Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), which enables banks to clear and settle cross-border payments directly in yuan, according to official data. Chinese banks are active in every Asean member nation.
Zhang Jun, chief economist at Beijing-based China Galaxy Securities, said he expected yuan internationalisation to continue gaining traction within the region.
“With spillover effects from global geopolitical risks and mounting trade protectionism, the strategic value of China-Asean economic and trade cooperation is being redefined,” he noted.
How far can the yuan go?
Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People’s Bank of China, said in mid-October that 6 to 7 per cent of global payments are now settled in yuan – making the Chinese currency the third most popular worldwide – when figures from the CIPS and Swift (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication) payment systems are taken together.
Even so, analysts cautioned that the yuan’s growth in trade settlement could hit a ceiling.
Zhang, the drinkware exporter, has first-hand experience of the currency’s limited appeal for some buyers. He made a breakthrough by convincing clients in Austria and Sweden to pay in yuan, but he has since been unable to build on that momentum.
For more developed economies to adopt the yuan, China has to open up more investment avenuesHu Jie, Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance
“One European buyer told me he turned down yuan settlement because the currency serves little purpose for him,” Zhang said. “He does not keep track of China’s financial opening-up or the financial framework, which he finds overly complicated.
“More importantly, his own end customers in Europe have no demand for yuan either,” he added.
According to Hu at the Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance, China must create more channels for foreign investors to deploy yuan capital to make them more willing to accept the currency.
Mainland financial regulators recognise this dynamic and have ramped up sovereign bond issuance in 2026. The planned treasury bond supply for the year has reached 84 billion yuan, 24 per cent higher than a year earlier.
China’s Ministry of Finance also issued yuan green sovereign bonds in Canada this month, marking the first issuance of yuan-denominated sovereign bonds in North America.
Yet, fundamental issues still arise when yuan flows across borders.
While overseas investors can use channels such as the Stock Connect and qualified foreign institutional investor schemes, these arrangements remain “cumbersome”, according to Hu. They are held back by “trading limits, a narrow set of investment instruments and restrictions” on the strategies investors may deploy.
“The yuan’s share in international trade settlement will continue to climb, yet there is an upper bound,” Hu said. “The core constraint is that the currency is not fully freely convertible.
“For more developed economies to adopt the yuan, China has to open up more investment avenues,” he said. “Capital-account liberalisation is still incomplete.”
By Emma Ma

title_en: South Korean first lady Kim Hea Kyung’s warmth and style captivate Chinese social media
content_en:
Visiting Shenzhen for Apec, the president’s wife is greeted with praise for her ‘natural poise and ease that simply cannot be faked’.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung (left) and his wife, Kim Hea Kyung, pose with children after receiving flowers during a meeting with South Korean residents in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: EPA/Yonhap
South Korean first lady Kim Hea Kyung has charmed Chinese social media users with her warmth towards ground staff, personal style and affection for her husband – fuelling online “shipping” of Seoul’s first couple.
Accompanying South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Kim arrived in Shenzhen early on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.
Like other visiting dignitaries, Lee and Kim received a red-carpet welcome with an honour guard. More than 100 dancers dressed in white shirts and pink skirts waved flower bouquets on the tarmac.
But what caught attention on Chinese social media was the South Korean first couple’s reactions to those greeting them.
Lee and Kim began to applaud the greeters as they walked on the red carpet, and Kim continued to clap her hands and wave at the staff behind her car’s tinted closed window once inside.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and first lady Kim Hea Kyung arrive at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport on Wednesday for the Apec leaders’ meeting. Photo: AFP
In a social media post, one commenter said the couple’s conduct showed “none of the anticipated solemnity or stiffness”, singling out the applause that went on for several seconds and their eyes “brimming with genuine gratitude”.
The post described the South Korean first lady as showing “natural poise and ease that simply cannot be faked”.
“Accustomed as we are to the meticulously choreographed protocols of diplomatic occasions and the grand narratives of major-power rivalry, we often overlook these small yet heartwarming moments,” the commenter added.
“The true essence of international relations can be the simplest goodwill between people.”
Beyond her warm gestures, Kim has also drawn praise for her attire: a light pink dress upon stepping off the aircraft, a light green traditional Korean hanbok for a lunch later in the day and a white hanbok at the welcome dinner.
Seoul’s first lady has a large fan base in China, with a dedicated “super topic” on Weibo, one of China’s largest social media platforms. The feature allows users of the site to build and join interest-based communities. Another super topic dedicated to the presidential couple has drawn thousands of followers and posts.
In these online communities, users praise Kim’s style, closely track her schedule and share photos of the couple’s public interactions.
Some have taken to affectionately calling Lee and Kim “Mom and Dad”, a term used by “shippers” – fans who cheer a couple’s romance – to express their fondness for the two.
Fans in these channels have also written fan fiction about the couple, with some even using photos of the pair as their phone-lock screens.
On Wednesday, Lee and Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks, with Xi urging his counterpart to safeguard global supply chains, deepen economic policy coordination and foster cooperation on artificial intelligence.
By Fan Chen

title_en: Xi-Trump ties tested as calls grow in Washington for tougher China policy
content_en:
Experts claim Trump will face increasing pressure to take a more uncompromising approach with Beijing despite encouraging rapport with Xi.
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes US President Donald Trump upon his arrival in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. Photo: AP
The personal rapport between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping is being put to its sternest test yet amid growing congressional pressure over AI chip curbs and broader calls in Washington for a more assertive policy on China, according to experts.
The two leaders are set to hold formal talks on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen.
While Trump may want to preserve a cordial rapport with Xi and a tactical thaw between Washington and Beijing, he faces “enormous pressure from the US Congress and more confrontation-minded advisers within his administration to tighten export controls on high-end chips”, said Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser at the International Crisis Group.
Wyne noted that Trump was also facing renewed demands to unfreeze stalled arms sales to Taiwan and pursue a broader, more assertive pushback against Beijing.
“Trump will face growing pressure to take a tougher approach to China,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington.
“But I think Beijing sees Trump holding the line on keeping the relationship on a stable path through the end of his term,” he added.
[embedded media]
Since May, the administration has put on hold a US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan that the US Congress had cleared.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.
Leaders’ good relationship eases trade, technology tensions
Over the past year, direct leader-to-leader ties have acted as the primary stabiliser in a fractious relationship marked by intensifying trade, technology and strategic rivalry.
That buffer is now under strain as fallout from the Nvidia scandal and allegations of advanced AI chip smuggling into China fuel congressional demands for stricter export curbs.
Meanwhile, calls within the administration for a tougher stance on China and persistent frustration over a fragile rare earth truce have cast doubt on whether personal goodwill at the top can still keep ties on course.
On Wednesday, Beijing put on an elaborate show of that goodwill as Trump arrived in Shenzhen to attend the Apec summit.
Breaking with decades of protocol, Xi personally welcomed Trump on the airport tarmac with a handshake that turned into a brief hug, returning the rare gesture the Chinese leader received when he arrived in Washington for a state visit in September.
The reception marked the first time in nearly seven decades that a Chinese leader had personally received a visiting head of state on arrival. The last time it happened was in 1959, when Mao Zedong greeted Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev.
According to state news agency Xinhua, Xi recalled how Trump and first lady Melania Trump had greeted him at the airport during his US visit, noting that “China is a nation that values courtesy and has a tradition of reciprocating it”.
[embedded media]
Xi went on to call for a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”, while Trump hailed his host as a “great leader”.
Chan said Xi’s gesture came down to diplomatic reciprocity.
“Xi was put into a difficult position because this meant going against protocol,” Chan said.
“If Xi didn’t match this symbolic gesture, it might be treated as a personal slight by Trump.”
The bonhomie in Shenzhen belied mounting calls in Washington to tighten AI chip controls on China – pushing Nvidia, the administration and lawmakers into lockstep.
On Tuesday, Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress announced that the company would no longer ship Hopper data centre chips to China, despite US government approval.
The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday moved to block Chinese firms from remotely accessing advanced AI chips via overseas data centres, closing a major export-control loophole.
On Wednesday, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission urged Congress to require chip exporters to China to provide auditable data proving shipments do not divert US manufacturing capacity.
A bipartisan group of lawmakers is also preparing to fold several measures tightening export controls on AI chips into the final version of the National Defence Authorisation Act in December.
Nvidia scandal unlikely to be discussed at talks in Shenzhen
The multi-front push comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive following allegations of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, as the chipmaker faces accusations of facilitating AI chip smuggling to China through the company.
According to US media reports, American intelligence officials suspected Alice Huang of working for Beijing, which China has denied.
“The Nvidia scandal is unlikely to be a major topic of discussion between Trump and Xi,” Chan said.
Senior US officials, too, on Friday said the “situation with Nvidia” may not affect the trip.
Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), said both sides accepted that key supply chains, particularly in AI, would remain separate as the technology became more critical.
On whether they could sustain that divide without a blow-up over rare earths, he said: “It seems like the answer is yes, but it is getting tenser and tenser.”
Washington has repeatedly pressed Beijing to increase rare earth shipments, calling on China to speed up export licence approvals for the strategic minerals and honour commitments under the trade truce signed in Busan, South Korea, last year.
Under the one-year deal, Washington reduced tariffs on certain Chinese imports and suspended additional trade restrictions in return for a pause on China’s rare earth export controls. The agreement was extended by two months, to January 10, 2027.
“I think it is very tenuously holding,” McGuire added.
According to David Sacks, a senior fellow at CFR, Beijing sees Trump as an outlier against Washington’s bipartisan China consensus, which the next US president in 2028 is likely to return to.
That dynamic, he said, “puts a premium on China extending this so-called detente for two years, and locking in whatever advantages they can achieve over the next two years as they prepare for President Trump’s successor and look past his presidency”.
By Nayan Seth

title_en: US court convicts Florida pastor over plot to assassinate Haiti’s president
content_en:
⁠Christian Emmanuel Sanon was accused of seeking to replace Jovenel Moise as the Caribbean nation’s leader.
Haiti’s President Jovenel Moise speaks during an interview at his home in Petion-Ville, a suburb of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, in February 2020. Photo: AP
⁠Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a ⁠US-Haitian pastor accused of conspiring ⁠to assassinate and usurp the Caribbean nation’s last sitting president, has been convicted of all charges linked to the murder by a judge in Miami, the Miami Herald reported on Wednesday.
Sanon, 68, could face up to life ‌in prison. Prosecutors say the conspirators had for a time planned to replace President Jovenel Moise – who was shot in his bedroom in 2021 – with Sanon, though he was later sidelined in favour of another candidate.
Sanon has maintained his innocence throughout.
Prosecutors accused Sanon of seeking to replace Moise as president in a conspiracy concocted across ⁠both Haiti and Florida, which involved using US companies to hire Colombian mercenaries to impersonate US ‌Drug Enforcement Administration agents and storm Moise’s home the night of July 7, 2021.
Moise was shot dead in his bedroom that night ‌and his wife, Martine Moise – a key witness in the trial – was flown ⁠to Florida for treatment ⁠for bullet wounds she sustained in the attack. She has now registered as a presidential candidate for Haiti’s ‌first election in more than 10 years.
Haiti’s President Jovenel Moise sits with his wife, Martine, during his swearing-in ceremony in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, in February 2017. Photo: AP
The years since his death have seen violent gangs expand their influence across ‌Haiti, taking ‌control of most of the capital and many surrounding regions, forcing some 1.5 million from ‌their homes.
Those still to face trial include Joseph Felix Badio, a former government anti-corruption ⁠official whom other suspects’ defence lawyers accused of masterminding the operation, and 17 Colombian former soldiers ⁠flown in from Haiti in September.
Seven more have been charged for their roles in facilitating the funding of the plot and helping those responsible evade justice ‌after the killing, including ‌Vitel’homme Innocent, a gang leader tied to the kidnapping of 17 US and Canadian missionaries later in 2021, and who has yet to be arrested.
A new list of indictments US prosecutors released in September included four people whose names were redacted.
By Reuters
Sections: News / World / Americas / United States & Canada | Topics: Americas and the Caribbean, Haiti, Florida, Crime, United States, Colombia, Drug Enforcement Administration

title_en: Huawei case enters jury deliberations after 2-month battle in US courtroom
content_en:
Chinese tech giant faces 12 counts, including racketeering conspiracy, trade secret theft and bank fraud, in a nearly eight-year case.
Huawei has been at the centre of longstanding tensions between Washington and Beijing over technology and national security. Photo: AP
Jurors began deliberating on Wednesday in the US government’s criminal case against Huawei Technologies, following a two-month trial that has been one of the most high-profile prosecutions of a Chinese technology giant in recent years.
Huawei, a Shenzhen-based company, is the world’s largest telecoms equipment maker and a major smartphone manufacturer. It faces 12 criminal counts, including racketeering conspiracy, stealing trade secrets, bank fraud and obstruction of justice.
US prosecutors have accused Huawei and three affiliated companies of operating a criminal enterprise over two decades, allegedly stealing trade secrets from other technology companies, including internet router source code and robotics equipment, rewarding employees for obtaining competitors’ confidential information, defrauding banks about its business in Iran and obstructing investigations.
Huawei has been effectively barred from selling telecommunications equipment to US carriers since 2019. If convicted, it could face substantial fines and forfeiture of proceeds from the alleged crimes.
After both parties presented their closing arguments on Monday and Tuesday, Wednesday’s proceedings started with the government’s rebuttal to defence lawyers’ closing arguments.
Huawei’s lawyer has pushed back on the theft allegations, framing them as isolated acts by individual employees that did not represent the company as a whole.
[embedded media]
Robert Pollack, an assistant US attorney, said the employees’ acts represented the company and called the defence’s argument, which focused on the “idea of bad apples and good” ones, an effort to distract the jury.
“The defence wants to make it seem more complicated than it is,” he added.
Pollack said Huawei had a corporate culture that emphasised: “nobody owns anything we can’t take and there is nothing wrong with that”.
The rebuttal was finished at 11am US Eastern time (12am Tuesday, Hong Kong time), followed by Judge Ann Donnelly’s charging instructions to jurors for more than three hours. The jurors left for their deliberations just after 2.45pm.
It’s unclear how long the jurors will take to reach a decision on the 12 counts.
The case has dragged on for nearly eight years, and the trial has been under way since September, with prosecutors calling 61 witnesses and Huawei presenting 15 witnesses.
Prosecutors also say Huawei used Hong Kong-registered Skycom as an unofficial subsidiary to conduct business in Iran and concealed its relationship with the company from banks including HSBC.
Huawei denies the charges. In closing arguments, defence lawyer Brian Heberlig said prosecutors had constructed a “fictionalised portrait”. He disputed the allegation that the company deceived banks, saying financial institutions were aware of its business in Iran and chose to continue working with Huawei.
He argued that employees responsible for the misconduct were disciplined or fired. Pollack dismissed the explanation of firing an employee who wrote a memo that encouraged stealing confidential secrets, saying that what happened after the memo doesn’t matter, and the key is the memo being written and sent out.
Heberlig also argued that Huawei’s growth was driven by engineering, investment and innovation rather than theft.
The case has drawn international attention since the 2018 arrest in Canada of Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou, the daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei, at the request of the US.
Meng spent nearly three years in Canada before reaching a deferred prosecution agreement with US authorities in 2021 and returning to China.
Meng’s confession before her release became a key part of the debate in the courtroom as she admitted to misleading the HSBC on Huawei’s relations with Skycom and the company’s business in Iran.
By Han Li, Lucy Quaggin

Meng’s confession before her release became a key part of the debate in the courtroom as she admitted to misleading the HSBC on Huawei’s relations with Skycom and the company’s business in Iran.

title_en: US and Venezuela sign deal to re-establish military ties during Hegseth visit
content_en:
The US defence chief says that since Maduro’s ousting, the nation has gone from regional threat to ‘compliant’ security partner.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks to the media at the US embassy in Caracas, Venezuela, on Wednesday. Photo: Reuters
The United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to re-establish military ties, from training to intelligence sharing, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday on a visit with the South American nation’s interim leaders.
Hegseth said that following the January capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro by the US military, the country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner”.
He also praised the “close cooperation” with interim President Delcy Rodriguez that allowed officials “to stabilise Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all”.
The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.
Rodriguez separately lauded the opportunity to strengthen the military partnership. “I hope that this technical-military cooperation … can be brought to its highest possible level, so that … we may address common threats,” she said.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth meets with Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez at the Miraflores Presidential Palace in Caracas on Wednesday. Photo: Venezuelan Presidency via AFP
Hegseth’s visit underscores efforts by President Donald Trump’s administration to deepen its influence in the South American country since US forces ousted Maduro in January.
Hegseth is the latest member of Trump’s cabinet to travel to Venezuela following visits this year by the Interior and Energy secretaries, who have focused on efforts to tap its oil reserves and critical minerals.
Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the US to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves.
The head of US military operations in Latin America, General Francis Donovan of US Southern Command, also has met interim authorities in Venezuela at least twice this year.
The US military has been expanding its attention on the region since Trump returned to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the western hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels.
To try to stem the flow of narcotics into the US and the scourge of fatal overdoses, American forces have been attacking what the Trump administration says are boats smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.
At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” in September 2025, although US officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims the vessels were carrying drugs.
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado greets a relative of a political prisoner outside El Rodeo prison in Guatire, Venezuela, on November 6. Photo: AP
Hegseth’s visit comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years. Rodriguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro’s capture. Rodriguez’s court-allowed term expired in July, but she continues to function as Venezuela’s head of state.
Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the “safe” return of the politician was the result of “reconciliation talks” supported by his country, which he considered “the best opportunity” Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy.
The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment towards Trump.
While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House’s decision to prioritise reviving Venezuela’s oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country.
The Trump administration says it has returned more than US$12 billion, or almost 99 per cent, of the revenue obtained from the sales of Venezuelan oil back to the country under the terms of the energy deal reached with Rodriguez’s government, according to a report released this month.
By Associated Press

title_en: El Salvador’s Bukele says his troops destroyed gang leader’s mansion in Haiti
content_en:
It wasn’t immediately clear if Jeff, one of the country’s most powerful gang leaders, was killed in the attack on his home in Port-au-Prince.
Residents take to the streets to demonstrate their support for Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and the deployment of Salvadoran soldiers to fight armed gangs in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Tuesday. Photo: AP
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said on Wednesday that his troops had demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It was not immediately clear if he was killed.
Bukele posted a video on social media that begins with old footage of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadorean helicopters flying towards it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home.
“My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele said.
The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti’s independence from France and transforming it into the world’s first black republic.
It was not immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A UN-backed gang suppression force said that it was not involved.
Jeff is considered one of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he is known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban.
Salvadorean President Nayib Bukele released footage on social media on Wednesday of two helicopters blasting the large Port-au-Prince house of Haiti gang leader Jeff. Image: X/nayibbukele
His so-called Taliban gang, which has a couple hundred members, has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince.
“It is one of the most organised gangs, with the strictest territorial control,” said Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group.
Da Rin said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations.
Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo.
“It’s very easy to identify it by satellite,” Da Rin said. “It was a very defiant act by him.”
He noted that Jeff’s home was very vulnerable to an aerial attack, but it was built in a place where attacking it by land would have been extremely difficult.
Da Rin said Jeff was among a handful of gang leaders who have built mansions in recent years. “In a way, they felt untouchable in their territory,” he said.
The use of explosive drones and helicopters, which Haitian police and military lack, has changed that.
While it has allowed forces to chase after gangs more efficiently, it also has multiplied the number of innocent victims and prompted gangs to retaliate against civilians.
“It is not surprising that gangs would seek to undermine enthusiasm for the arrival of new forces by targeting civilians who have expressed support for security operations,” said Sandra Pellegrini, a senior analyst with Armed Conflict Location and Event Data.
Residents take to the streets to demonstrate their support for Salvadorean President Nayib Bukele and the deployment of Salvadorean soldiers to fight armed gangs in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on Tuesday. Photo: AP
She and Da Rin warned that despite Bukele’s attacks against Haitian gangs, one persistent challenge is forces retaining long-term control over territories recaptured from gangs, further placing civilians at risk.
Da Rin said he doubts Jeff was staying at the mansion when it was attacked early Wednesday given that on November 8, Salvadorean troops attacked the home of Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmo San Jou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang. He was not killed in the attack.
Da Rin said gang leaders have several residences and can always seek shelter in any home within the territory they control.
He noted that Jeff and Lanmo San Jou are allies and control the main roads north and east of Port-au-Prince that lead to other cities and towns, charging tolls that have become their main source of revenue.
“He and Lanmo San Jou are arguably the most powerful warlords in Port-au-Prince,” Da Rin said.
Canaan was established as an informal community after a devastating earthquake hit Haiti in January 2010. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to now live there.
The attack came a day after thousands of Haitians in Port-au-Prince and beyond marched in favour of Bukele, thanking him and his troops for fighting violent gangs.
On Wednesday, Haitians were again celebrating.
“Jeff is a criminal and I hope he died,” said Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old salesman in Port-au-Prince. “We asked for help; Bukele answered us.”
Last month, Bukele deployed around 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on October 18 while deep in gang territory. They remain missing.
By Associated Press

title_en: Chinese executive convicted in case linked to Bangkok tower collapse
content_en:
At least 92 people were killed when an earthquake struck the partially built high-rise building in Thailand’s capital last year.
Rescuers work at the site of a high-rise building under construction that collapsed after an earthquake in Bangkok, Thailand, in March 2025. Photo: AP
A court in Thailand on Wednesday found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders of a Thai subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned construction company guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand in a case related to the collapse of a Bangkok office building last year.
At least 92 people died on March 28, 2025, when an earthquake struck the partially built high-rise, which was to house the State Audit Office.
It was the only building in Thailand to collapse completely due to the 7.7-magnitude quake, which was centred in neighbouring Myanmar.
The tower was being built by a joint venture between China Railway No 10 (Thailand) and Italian-Thai Development. Executives from both companies are also facing separate proceedings over alleged wrongdoing related to the building’s collapse.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and its director, Zhang Chuanling, were found guilty of violating Thailand’s Foreign Business Act by using Thai nominee shareholders to conceal the company’s foreign ownership and operating a construction business without the required permission.
The Criminal Court in Bangkok fined the company and Zhang 1 million baht (US$30,00) each and sentenced Zhang to three years in prison, while also ordering the company to cease operations.
[embedded media]
The defendants had denied the charges and were granted bail.
China Railway No 10 (Thailand) is a Thai-registered affiliate of China Railway No.10 Engineering Group, part of the Chinese state-owned China Railway group, which operates internationally.
The involvement of Chinese companies in the building collapse and other construction-related accidents has drawn considerable attention.
The most notable other accident took place in January this year on a line that is part of a Thai-Chinese high-speed railway project linking the capital to northeastern Thailand.
At least 32 people were killed and dozens injured when a construction crane crashed onto a moving passenger train, derailing it.
Italian-Thai Development was also the construction contractor for the railway project, and a Chinese company handled design and construction supervision.
After the train accident, China’s ambassador to Thailand, Zhang Jianwei, said that China requires its companies to follow the rules when taking part in overseas projects, and that Beijing is willing to “guide Chinese companies to actively cooperate with the Thai authorities’ investigation”.
Wednesday’s court case also saw three Thai shareholders found guilty of acting as nominees for China Railway No 10 (Thailand). Two were sentenced to six years in prison each and fined 2 million baht (US$60,000), while the third received a three-year prison term and a 1-million-baht fine.
However, the court reduced their sentences and their fines by one-fifth after they confessed to the offences.
By Associated Press

title_en: Indonesia has had a tough year but don’t write off Prabowo Subianto yet
content_en:
The president is pursuing ambitious changes, which will take time to bear fruit, and he still has two years left to do it.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto arrives for a welcome banquet in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: Xinhua
Superficially, the case against Indonesia and its president, Prabowo Subianto, writes itself. Still, a nation of 285 million people should not be judged by one tough year.
Admittedly, recent news from Indonesia – the world’s fourth-most-populous country and its largest Muslim democracy – has been concerning.
After years as a Southeast Asian investment darling cum natural resources powerhouse, it has been beset by economic turbulence and renewed political intrigue that recalls the turmoil of the 1998 Asian Financial Crisis, when its survival was in doubt.
In the last few months, smoke from forest and peat fires in Borneo and Sumatra has closed schools and drifted into neighbouring countries.
Then, there are the mounting anxieties about our economy. Despite attempts at reform, global index provider MSCI has proposed moving Indonesia from emerging to stand-alone market status over alleged opaque share ownership and coordinated trading.
The Jakarta Composite Index is displayed on an LCD board at the Indonesian Stock Exchange building on Wednesday. Photo: EPA
Indonesian stocks by late October dropped around 40 per cent. The Jakarta Composite Index shed around 6 quadrillion rupiah (US$330 billion) in market value.
Meanwhile, Prabowo’s signature initiative, Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG), or the free nutritious meals for schoolchildren, has been beset by teething difficulties. In September, it resulted in some 560 incidents of food poisoning involving 50,000 people.
Then there are the legacy grouses about resource nationalism and Prabowo’s focus on international affairs, with his approval rating below 50 per cent for the first time.
The recent resignation of vice-president Gibran Rakabuming Raka, son of former President Joko Widodo, whose support was crucial for Prabowo’s 2024 victory, has also led to fears that this once-stabilising coalition is fracturing.
Ambitious changes
But those troubling headlines tell only part of the story. Prabowo is pursuing ambitious changes, which will take time to bear fruit, and the search for a new vice-president offers an opportunity to strengthen his administration and help turn those ambitions into results.
The government has, for example, revoked land-use permits linked to forest fires in Kalimantan and reclaimed more than 6 million hectares (15 million acres) of oil palm plantations illegally cultivated inside the national forest estate.
For decades, Indonesia’s land-use map was, mildly put, a fiction: concessions granted on paper, forests felled in fact, and nobody prosecuted. Prabowo’s administration is seeking to change that through tougher enforcement.
Volunteers spray water on a fire at Terantang in Indonesia’s Barito Kuala regency, South Kalimantan province, on November 7. Photo: AFP
Beyond its forests, Indonesia supplies more than half the world’s mined nickel. Add geothermal, hydro and solar power, and the country holds resources that could play a major role in global decarbonisation. Prabowo is seeking to harness that potential, launching an ambitious programme to develop 100 gigawatts of solar power over the next three years.
Though not as exciting as comparisons with 1998, through the three quarters of 2026, Indonesia’s economy grew 5.45 per cent, including 5.47 per cent in the third quarter, while the world managed about 3.1 per cent.
As for the MBG, which cost around 268 trillion rupiah this year and reached 60 million people, Indonesia has little need to apologise for spending on its children. A child stunted at two is a worker who earns less at 40. States that neglect their children pay the difference in healthcare and imported food.
What the MBG needs is safety at an industrial scale, with kitchen audits published and a dashboard no minister can bury.
A student carries trays of food supplied by the Indonesian government’s free meal programme at a primary school in Garot on the outskirts of Banda Aceh on Friday. Photo: AFP
For decades, our commodities left port at prices that suited buyers and came back as someone else’s profits.
Our Finance Ministry estimates that suspected under-invoicing has cost Indonesia US$908 billion since 1991, with US$150 billion a year leaking through mispricing, transfer pricing and earnings that never came home.
The governments of Indonesia and Singapore are now discussing greater cooperation on tax data sharing to help identify such practices and recover lost revenue. It is a step towards addressing a problem that has persisted for decades.
Meanwhile, our president is Indonesia’s most visible leader in generations. Under him, we joined Brics last year. He says “Free Palestine” in rooms where the phrase is unwelcome.
Gibran resigned after months of lawfare over his educational credentials. Prabowo will need to name two potential replacements for our legislature to pick. He has said he will need to consult his coalition first – because that is how it works in Indonesia, like most democracies.
Talent first
But there are certain fixes that Indonesia and his administration need.
As a Special Forces operator – who won office in 2024 with more than 96 million votes – Prabowo knows that a nation, like an army, runs on logistics. You need big-picture people but also someone to keep the ledger, to ensure programmes like the MBG work.
Indonesia’s next vice-president should arrive with a filing system, be able to read a cold-chain audit, a budget and a fire-risk map, and understand what matters.
They should be the kind of person whom you can say no to on Tuesday and still eat dinner with on Friday.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto (left) embraces Gibran Rakabuming Raka after a press conference announcing Gibran’s resignation as vice-president on November 12. Photo: AFP
In short, the primary consideration should be talent.
After decades of trauma, our people deserve much, much more than bare survival.
Prabowo has perhaps two years left to show that his focus on meals, minerals and reclaimed forests is the foundation for better, more dignified lives for all Indonesians.
He must win, and win now.
For that, he needs a vice-president who will not flatter him, and Indonesians should want him to find one. I certainly do.
By Muhammad Lutfi

Meanwhile, Prabowo’s signature initiative, Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG), or the free nutritious meals for schoolchildren, has been beset by teething difficulties. In September, it resulted in some 560 incidents of food poisoning involving 50,000 people.
Then there are the legacy grouses about resource nationalism and Prabowo’s focus on international affairs, with his approval rating below 50 per cent for the first time.
The recent resignation of vice-president Gibran Rakabuming Raka, son of former President Joko Widodo, whose support was crucial for Prabowo’s 2024 victory, has also led to fears that this once-stabilising coalition is fracturing.
Ambitious changes
But those troubling headlines tell only part of the story. Prabowo is pursuing ambitious changes, which will take time to bear fruit, and the search for a new vice-president offers an opportunity to strengthen his administration and help turn those ambitions into results.
The government has, for example, revoked land-use permits linked to forest fires in Kalimantan and reclaimed more than 6 million hectares (15 million acres) of oil palm plantations illegally cultivated inside the national forest estate.
For decades, Indonesia’s land-use map was, mildly put, a fiction: concessions granted on paper, forests felled in fact, and nobody prosecuted. Prabowo’s administration is seeking to change that through tougher enforcement.
Volunteers spray water on a fire at Terantang in Indonesia’s Barito Kuala regency, South Kalimantan province, on November 7. Photo: AFP
Beyond its forests, Indonesia supplies more than half the world’s mined nickel. Add geothermal, hydro and solar power, and the country holds resources that could play a major role in global decarbonisation. Prabowo is seeking to harness that potential, launching an ambitious programme to develop 100 gigawatts of solar power over the next three years.
Though not as exciting as comparisons with 1998, through the three quarters of 2026, Indonesia’s economy grew 5.45 per cent, including 5.47 per cent in the third quarter, while the world managed about 3.1 per cent.
As for the MBG, which cost around 268 trillion rupiah this year and reached 60 million people, Indonesia has little need to apologise for spending on its children. A child stunted at two is a worker who earns less at 40. States that neglect their children pay the difference in healthcare and imported food.
What the MBG needs is safety at an industrial scale, with kitchen audits published and a dashboard no minister can bury.
A student carries trays of food supplied by the Indonesian government’s free meal programme at a primary school in Garot on the outskirts of Banda Aceh on Friday. Photo: AFP
For decades, our commodities left port at prices that suited buyers and came back as someone else’s profits.
Our Finance Ministry estimates that suspected under-invoicing has cost Indonesia US$908 billion since 1991, with US$150 billion a year leaking through mispricing, transfer pricing and earnings that never came home.
The governments of Indonesia and Singapore are now discussing greater cooperation on tax data sharing to help identify such practices and recover lost revenue. It is a step towards addressing a problem that has persisted for decades.
Meanwhile, our president is Indonesia’s most visible leader in generations. Under him, we joined Brics last year. He says “Free Palestine” in rooms where the phrase is unwelcome.
Gibran resigned after months of lawfare over his educational credentials. Prabowo will need to name two potential replacements for our legislature to pick. He has said he will need to consult his coalition first – because that is how it works in Indonesia, like most democracies.
Talent first
But there are certain fixes that Indonesia and his administration need.
As a Special Forces operator – who won office in 2024 with more than 96 million votes – Prabowo knows that a nation, like an army, runs on logistics. You need big-picture people but also someone to keep the ledger, to ensure programmes like the MBG work.
Indonesia’s next vice-president should arrive with a filing system, be able to read a cold-chain audit, a budget and a fire-risk map, and understand what matters.
They should be the kind of person whom you can say no to on Tuesday and still eat dinner with on Friday.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto (left) embraces Gibran Rakabuming Raka after a press conference announcing Gibran’s resignation as vice-president on November 12. Photo: AFP
In short, the primary consideration should be talent.
After decades of trauma, our people deserve much, much more than bare survival.
Prabowo has perhaps two years left to show that his focus on meals, minerals and reclaimed forests is the foundation for better, more dignified lives for all Indonesians.
He must win, and win now.
For that, he needs a vice-president who will not flatter him, and Indonesians should want him to find one. I certainly do.
By Muhammad Lutfi

title_en: Danny Quah on Asean’s middle course and a prisoner’s dilemma for US, China
content_en:
Singapore economist discusses US-China friction over trade, why Asean avoids picking sides and how China’s export prowess benefits Southeast Asia.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
Danny Quah is an economics professor at the National University of Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy. He served as the school’s dean between 2018 and 2025, and has consulted for, among others, the World Bank, the Bank of England and the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
Here, he discusses how the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) navigates the US-China rivalry, yuan internationalisation in the region and why the “China shock” has played out differently in Southeast Asia.
This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
You have introduced the concept of a “G-minus” world. How do you define this model, and what does it mean for global trade?
The G-minus concept is the idea that global rules, norms and institutions need to operate well even without great-power permission. For the last eight decades, nations maintained sovereignty under an architecture supported and created by the United States – a great power that has largely been a benevolent hegemon.
But circumstances now reflect how the world no longer has access to that kind of benevolent leadership from the United States. It is time for us to think how, in the absence of a great power – or perhaps even against a great power’s obstructions – we can still have a system that is multilateral enough, that has a level playing field, a system for peaceful dispute resolution, and a commitment to cooperation in the face of common challenges.
In economic terms, we might say the G-minus world is an attempt to reduce the great-power elasticity on world order, that the rest of us can continue to function even if the great power behaves in unexpected ways.
Right now, the G-minus idea is an aspiration. But I think Asean is an example of something that almost has a G-minus architecture, because Asean has spent the last six decades trying to get 10 – now 11 – very different nations to work with one another, without there being a leader that tells everybody what to do.
The RCEP (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership) is a good example of Asean success in trade. Many out there think of RCEP as a China-led grouping – it is not. It is an Asean-initiated grouping that happens to include China; it also happens to include Japan and South Korea.
One might ask: how were nations brought together when relations are sometimes quite tense? My suspicion: because Asean leads itself. If this were China-led, I think it would be much more awkward for other nations that might feel certain kinds of discord with China to become full-blown members. It is Asean’s ability to act in a way that fosters and encourages collaborative behaviour, without relying on a leader telling everybody else what to do, that has made RCEP a success.
[embedded media]
But if tensions heighten, could Asean be forced to pick sides? For instance, is the region re-examining its supply chains and Chinese ties because of Washington’s scrutiny of transshipments?
What Asean has done is allow its member states to navigate this rivalry without choosing sides. It has an architecture that encourages engagement with both great powers, while minimising the strategic vulnerability associated with them.
America’s official policy is that its large trade deficit with China is harmful, and it has taken to levying tariffs on imports from China and taking action against third countries for transshipment or chain-washing. A knee-jerk reaction is to assume that you must pick a side: choosing America by helping to contain China’s rise and not doing business with China, or picking China by paying no attention to America’s tariffs because you think China is the winning side.
Asean is doing neither of these. Instead, it is deepening economic integration with China in a way that escapes the charge of transshipment. By ensuring that there is enough value added when goods pass from China through Asean to the United States, a piece of product that leaves Asean for the United States is identifiably Asean rather than Chinese.
For example, one of Asean’s largest exports is in electronics. Chinese technology is important for semiconductors. But we assemble the semiconductors in Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, and those semiconductors are then put into electronic goods higher up the value chain that are exported to the rest of the world. This is a case of significant Asean integration in addressing the rules of origin challenge from the United States.
And right now, America is scrambling because unless its administration sees a way to get around its own laws, it will no longer be allowed to charge Asean with transshipment. That is why it is appealing to Section 301 and other kinds of trade policies.
You will notice that in doing this, Asean did not require a leader. No one said that Asean should import these things from China, add value in Thailand, ship it to Malaysia, add further value in Singapore, before exporting from Indonesia. It emerged from nations figuring out that they could inadvertently cooperate with one another through Asean rules – another example of a G-minus narrative in managing US-China relations.
So Asean is deepening integration, not decoupling from China. But it is also not decoupling from the United States. America is a really important part of Asean’s economic journey. America accounted for 16 per cent of Asean’s exports in 2024 – it’s probably a little more now. America invests hugely in foreign direct investment in Singapore, notably, and across the rest of Asean. Asean has figured out how to work with both powers, without antagonising either.
On the subject of trade deficits, surging exports this year – particularly in hi-tech industries – have fuelled concerns of a “China Shock 2.0”. What’s your take on this?
On the America front, the tensions are between America’s consumers – who want to have cheap, high-quality Chinese goods in greater quantity – and the parts of America’s industry that compete directly with Chinese industry and want to have less competition. What America is seeing now is an ascendancy of America’s competitor industries, and American consumers are – for the time being – keeping relatively quiet despite being sidelined.
Europe has a similar mix of this. Its positioning in the industrial landscape makes it more similar to the United States, and so it too finds competition with China’s similarly placed industries painful.
With the US side, there is an additional complication which is geopolitical and not purely economic. America’s difficulties with China are bipartisan. The traditional Republican position says that America needs to be number one in the world and right now, they feel that American strength is being challenged – it doesn’t matter to them that this alternative hegemon happens to be China. On the other hand, the Democrats feel an awkwardness with China because they continue to have a vision of China as being a communist country that is authoritarian and disrespects human rights.
The Trump administration actually subscribes to neither of these views. [US President] Donald Trump himself says that President Xi Jinping is his great friend, and he loves the way China does things. But he is set against China on the economic front because his Maga base loves the idea that it is someone else’s fault that jobs are not plentiful in America. Jobs actually are plentiful, just not in those industries and not in those geographies.
The rest of the world does not subscribe to either the American or European view on this. In South America, Africa and much of Asia, the way we see it, China’s goods are high quality and affordable. We are not rich like the West. We can’t afford to see these prices rise and we’re glad that Chinese goods are cheap.
I want to be clear that China has also faced its own version of a China shock, or the World Trade Organization (WTO) shock to China. Many Americans and Western observers say China’s accession to the WTO was what accorded its most-favoured-nation status, and that was what allowed China to succeed so spectacularly in exporting to the rest of the world.
But in China’s accession to the WTO, China had to adjust as well, and its state-owned enterprises and its old way of manufacturing all had to be re-engineered. China did not move from a low-level developing economy to having sleek Shenzhen factories that assemble iMacs and iPhones overnight. It had to re-engineer its production processes, and in doing that, it laid off hundreds of thousands of workers in the northeast – jobs which never came back to China.
When you speak to industrialists in Heilongjiang, they will describe an experience of WTO accession that is very different from how the rest of the world thinks of China. They suffered deeply. For them that was the “China Shock”.
So, China’s coming into the world came at considerable pain to itself, and that is another reason it keenly feels the double standards that the West has imposed on it – in that we too felt that pain, we swallowed it and we re-engineered because you told us that is what we should do.
You should do that too. You taught Asia’s emerging economies that competition makes us all better if only we adjust. You lectured us that creative destruction means we have to let go of lagging economic activity, freeing up those resources so they can move on to more productive use. Economic awkwardness is the signal that tells us to shift to doing something else. Apply these lessons now to yourself.
[embedded media]
So why haven’t the “China shock” narratives been as prominent in Asean, despite Chinese exports to the region rising more than to the US and the EU this year?
In Asia, we have the consumers who want cheap, high-quality goods, and the competitor industries – similar to America and Europe. But we also have a third kind of key stakeholder: those downstream from what America produces and from what China produces.
This group is part of industry, but they see cheap and high-quality Chinese products as good because they use them as inputs. So China’s technology and export prowess make it possible for them to also produce things that are cheaper and higher quality. This group adds a voice that is parallel to the consumer voice. They are quite pleased at China’s manufacturing prowess, and they don’t think of it as overcapacity or a China shock.
Again, using electronics and semiconductor manufacturing as an example: a lot of us have Nvidia on our minds when we think of chips, but there is also a thriving industry beyond those frontier chips. They are not any less useful to us – we have them in our cars, in our computers, in the shipping industry – and China does these really well and affordably.
There is also energy. Southeast Asia needs the kind of energy that allows us to meet our carbon commitments, and China provides the technology to help us do that. On top of Chinese electric batteries, solar panels and wind turbines, we have built an ecosystem of electricity transmission that plugs into everything else that we do.
To be very clear, there are also Asean voices talking about the China shock – Indonesian industry, for instance. I am politically and socially very sympathetic with those in societies that need help. But I have much less sympathy for tycoons whose business is now being undermined by cheap imports.
If you have been undermined by a competitor, you need to figure out what to do next to win back the market. In economics, we think of this as creative destruction. These are the forces of market competition. You cannot just sit on what you are currently doing and complain about China taking away your business.
[embedded media]
So how did the world manage past trade shocks, and what do you make of our way out of the current one?
In an earlier time, it was Japan that was Asia’s champion in advancing technology. What Japan did was that it later moved on to higher value industries and it kept moving on. This created space in the industries it had left behind, with technology available for the rest of Asia to leverage. That was how a lot of the rest of Asia built out our jobs. If Chinese technology does not continue to advance and move up the value chain to create space, there will be problems.
Other observers might also say that the Japan shock was disrupted by America’s actions on the Plaza Accord and the resulting yen appreciation, and America’s trade sanctions against Japan. A lot of the American rhetoric against China now resembles American rhetoric against Japan then, but the circumstances are very different.
China is much larger than Japan. On the geopolitical front, Japan had its entire military defence outsourced to the United States, which had been the case since the end of World War II. China is in a very different position, and its military defence capabilities in some dimensions are comparable to those of the United States. China will never agree to the kind of currency recalibration that Japan did.
I don’t see a clean resolution to the economic challenges that the US and China face. They are now stuck in a prisoner’s dilemma-type situation, where America will continue to draw on investment sanctions, export controls, import quotas, tariffs – many different ways to directly or indirectly disrupt the flow of Chinese goods to the US.
China, in turn, has now found the critical minerals and rare earths card to be a reliable way in which it practises economic statecraft. It has used that against Japan, and it could also potentially use that against the United States.
If the stand-off continues, the great fear is that the world would go into a Smoot-Hawley type situation, and it becomes an arms race in tariffs – which first occurred in 1930s America at the start of the Great Depression. Thankfully, that has not featured since “Liberation Day”. Countries have taken different approaches to this.
Malaysia has done a lot of acquiescence. It has agreed to many things that America wanted, to a point where there was actually domestic popular pushback against what had been agreed by the political leaders in Malaysia. But nothing disastrous has emerged from that; Malaysia is now in the midst of an economic boom. The semiconductor industry and the AI data centre race have been very good for Malaysia. And now the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade is no longer binding because the US Supreme Court has struck down Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs.
The worry about the world falling into a Smoot-Hawley situation has not materialised, and perhaps the world can tolerate this for a little bit longer.
China is actively promoting yuan usage across Asean countries through trade settlements, panda bonds and cross-border payment systems, with Singapore serving as a top offshore yuan hub in the region. Why is Beijing focusing so heavily on Southeast Asia for its currency roll-out, and how successful have its yuan internationalisation goals been so far?
One natural question that comes out of this is: Is China setting up a replacement to the world reserve currency? I think that China is not, because China still has concerns about the convertibility of the yuan. It does not want its currency to float entirely freely on an open market, and it worries that its economy is not robust enough to withstand the potential destabilisation of highly volatile yuan. It also recognises that the presence of the Chinese yuan out there, while growing, is not that large at this point.
But that might not be the right question to ask. The notion of the world reserve currency being the US dollar has always featured prominently in geopolitical discussion, because it means that America has access to specific policies like financial sanctions that other nations do not. The recalibration of the Japanese yen also reflected how America controlled the international financial system. But America can lose that power of control over the world’s economy, even with the US dollar still being the world reserve currency.
So the right question could be: Can the rest of the world, for its own self-protection – not because it is trying to replace the American dollar – build enough structure so that it is no longer so vulnerable? This is what we’re seeing with the yuan in Southeast Asia. The ventures are implicitly attempts to build alternatives, not replacements, that will give all of us greater control over our financial business instead of ceding entirely to the United States.
Currency is one part of the problem. The other part is the pipes through which that currency flows. There is a Brics-plus counterpart to Swift emerging and China has the alternative CIPS, which is also a clearance and settlement system. There is mBridge and Project Nexus, which are more Southeast Asia-centred. They are multilateral and involve China, but they are not controlled by China.
I think for many Southeast Asian countries, this is a way to leapfrog the building of the international financial system, so we are keen to join in on these. We went from using currency – bypassing credit cards to a great degree – immediately into fintech and digital payment systems.
And for China, if its trade with Asean continues to grow – and it looks like it will – there is every reason to use the local currencies rather than go through the intermediary of the US dollar.
[embedded media]
During his visit to the US in September, Xi asserted that the Thucydides Trap can be overcome. Is this possible? What does an economic relationship of managed competition without escalating to confrontation look like in practice?
I am torn on this. I want to believe that as long as we are trading, no matter other disagreements, we would feel compelled to keep this economic relationship going and build institutions and norms that help us cooperate. But I also believe that trade can create tensions, such as the China shock.
Graham Allison, who coined the term Thucydides Trap, told me that America will not be happy until it is surrounded only by friends and fish. That is because America is a large enough place; it can actually contemplate economic isolationism. But for the rest of us – especially small states like the member states of Asean – we cannot. So for us, trade is central and existential.
But for America and China, trade need not be. China’s growth trajectory was one that relied on exporting to the rest of the world, but China too is a continent-sized nation. Continent-sized nations can imagine being isolated from the rest of the world. I think the world will be poorer for it, but those two great powers can imagine that.
That is why we need to advance the G-minus agenda urgently. Because if those two great powers cannot reconcile these issues and they are forced into choosing isolationism, the rest of us – that’s 80 per cent of the world – have to figure out how to manage this.
What role, then, does Asean play in great power rivalry?
For a while, it looked like the great powers viewed great power rivalry as imposing a choice that Asean needed to take sides. Asean has been very clear it will not.
What Asean is doing now is trying to expand optionality by economically integrating with China’s supply chain, and improving its own economic strength and resilience by adding value in that supply chain. We are telling America that we respect its right to impose sanctions because it has concerns. While respecting those rights, we are able to adapt in a way that keeps us on the right side of your sanctions. We are economically resilient.
Asean is trying to work with both great powers and increase its range of options, but keep from being vulnerable to either one. I think implicit in your question is: what happens if the great power rivals then act in a way that shrinks Asean’s options? This is like the ISEAS questionnaire, which asked if forced to choose a side, which side would you choose? For the past few years, the margins have been tight.
And if we get to that point, that would mean the world would have already shrunk its optionality in ways that western Europe does not figure. Africa, Latin America and the rest of Asia does not figure for Southeast Asia any more. It would mean that everything has just merged into a background and it is only America and China left.
If we come to that point, we have lots of other things to worry about. So, we need to make sure that all of the world continues to play a role in Asean’s economic landscape. We cannot allow the great powers to shrink our optionality.
By Xinyi Wu
