You lectured us that creative destruction means we have to let go of lagging economic activity, freeing up those resources so they can move on to more productive use. Economic awkwardness is the signal that tells us to shift to doing something else. Apply these lessons now to yourself.
[embedded media]
So why haven’t the “China shock” narratives been as prominent in Asean, despite Chinese exports to the region rising more than to the US and the EU this year?
In Asia, we have the consumers who want cheap, high-quality goods, and the competitor industries – similar to America and Europe. But we also have a third kind of key stakeholder: those downstream from what America produces and from what China produces.
This group is part of industry, but they see cheap and high-quality Chinese products as good because they use them as inputs. So China’s technology and export prowess make it possible for them to also produce things that are cheaper and higher quality. This group adds a voice that is parallel to the consumer voice. They are quite pleased at China’s manufacturing prowess, and they don’t think of it as overcapacity or a China shock.
Again, using electronics and semiconductor manufacturing as an example: a lot of us have Nvidia on our minds when we think of chips, but there is also a thriving industry beyond those frontier chips. They are not any less useful to us – we have them in our cars, in our computers, in the shipping industry – and China does these really well and affordably.
There is also energy. Southeast Asia needs the kind of energy that allows us to meet our carbon commitments, and China provides the technology to help us do that. On top of Chinese electric batteries, solar panels and wind turbines, we have built an ecosystem of electricity transmission that plugs into everything else that we do.
To be very clear, there are also Asean voices talking about the China shock – Indonesian industry, for instance. I am politically and socially very sympathetic with those in societies that need help. But I have much less sympathy for tycoons whose business is now being undermined by cheap imports.
If you have been undermined by a competitor, you need to figure out what to do next to win back the market. In economics, we think of this as creative destruction. These are the forces of market competition. You cannot just sit on what you are currently doing and complain about China taking away your business.
[embedded media]
So how did the world manage past trade shocks, and what do you make of our way out of the current one?
In an earlier time, it was Japan that was Asia’s champion in advancing technology. What Japan did was that it later moved on to higher value industries and it kept moving on. This created space in the industries it had left behind, with technology available for the rest of Asia to leverage. That was how a lot of the rest of Asia built out our jobs. If Chinese technology does not continue to advance and move up the value chain to create space, there will be problems.
Other observers might also say that the Japan shock was disrupted by America’s actions on the Plaza Accord and the resulting yen appreciation, and America’s trade sanctions against Japan. A lot of the American rhetoric against China now resembles American rhetoric against Japan then, but the circumstances are very different.
China is much larger than Japan. On the geopolitical front, Japan had its entire military defence outsourced to the United States, which had been the case since the end of World War II. China is in a very different position, and its military defence capabilities in some dimensions are comparable to those of the United States. China will never agree to the kind of currency recalibration that Japan did.
I don’t see a clean resolution to the economic challenges that the US and China face. They are now stuck in a prisoner’s dilemma-type situation, where America will continue to draw on investment sanctions, export controls, import quotas, tariffs – many different ways to directly or indirectly disrupt the flow of Chinese goods to the US.
China, in turn, has now found the critical minerals and rare earths card to be a reliable way in which it practises economic statecraft. It has used that against Japan, and it could also potentially use that against the United States.
If the stand-off continues, the great fear is that the world would go into a Smoot-Hawley type situation, and it becomes an arms race in tariffs – which first occurred in 1930s America at the start of the Great Depression. Thankfully, that has not featured since “Liberation Day”. Countries have taken different approaches to this.
Malaysia has done a lot of acquiescence. It has agreed to many things that America wanted, to a point where there was actually domestic popular pushback against what had been agreed by the political leaders in Malaysia. But nothing disastrous has emerged from that; Malaysia is now in the midst of an economic boom. The semiconductor industry and the AI data centre race have been very good for Malaysia. And now the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade is no longer binding because the US Supreme Court has struck down Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs.
The worry about the world falling into a Smoot-Hawley situation has not materialised, and perhaps the world can tolerate this for a little bit longer.
China is actively promoting yuan usage across Asean countries through trade settlements, panda bonds and cross-border payment systems, with Singapore serving as a top offshore yuan hub in the region. Why is Beijing focusing so heavily on Southeast Asia for its currency roll-out, and how successful have its yuan internationalisation goals been so far?
One natural question that comes out of this is: Is China setting up a replacement to the world reserve currency? I think that China is not, because China still has concerns about the convertibility of the yuan. It does not want its currency to float entirely freely on an open market, and it worries that its economy is not robust enough to withstand the potential destabilisation of highly volatile yuan. It also recognises that the presence of the Chinese yuan out there, while growing, is not that large at this point.
But that might not be the right question to ask. The notion of the world reserve currency being the US dollar has always featured prominently in geopolitical discussion, because it means that America has access to specific policies like financial sanctions that other nations do not. The recalibration of the Japanese yen also reflected how America controlled the international financial system. But America can lose that power of control over the world’s economy, even with the US dollar still being the world reserve currency.
So the right question could be: Can the rest of the world, for its own self-protection – not because it is trying to replace the American dollar – build enough structure so that it is no longer so vulnerable? This is what we’re seeing with the yuan in Southeast Asia. The ventures are implicitly attempts to build alternatives, not replacements, that will give all of us greater control over our financial business instead of ceding entirely to the United States.
Currency is one part of the problem. The other part is the pipes through which that currency flows. There is a Brics-plus counterpart to Swift emerging and China has the alternative CIPS, which is also a clearance and settlement system. There is mBridge and Project Nexus, which are more Southeast Asia-centred. They are multilateral and involve China, but they are not controlled by China.
I think for many Southeast Asian countries, this is a way to leapfrog the building of the international financial system, so we are keen to join in on these. We went from using currency – bypassing credit cards to a great degree – immediately into fintech and digital payment systems.
And for China, if its trade with Asean continues to grow – and it looks like it will – there is every reason to use the local currencies rather than go through the intermediary of the US dollar.
[embedded media]
During his visit to the US in September, Xi asserted that the Thucydides Trap can be overcome. Is this possible? What does an economic relationship of managed competition without escalating to confrontation look like in practice?
I am torn on this. I want to believe that as long as we are trading, no matter other disagreements, we would feel compelled to keep this economic relationship going and build institutions and norms that help us cooperate. But I also believe that trade can create tensions, such as the China shock.
Graham Allison, who coined the term Thucydides Trap, told me that America will not be happy until it is surrounded only by friends and fish. That is because America is a large enough place; it can actually contemplate economic isolationism. But for the rest of us – especially small states like the member states of Asean – we cannot. So for us, trade is central and existential.
But for America and China, trade need not be. China’s growth trajectory was one that relied on exporting to the rest of the world, but China too is a continent-sized nation. Continent-sized nations can imagine being isolated from the rest of the world. I think the world will be poorer for it, but those two great powers can imagine that.
That is why we need to advance the G-minus agenda urgently. Because if those two great powers cannot reconcile these issues and they are forced into choosing isolationism, the rest of us – that’s 80 per cent of the world – have to figure out how to manage this.
What role, then, does Asean play in great power rivalry?
For a while, it looked like the great powers viewed great power rivalry as imposing a choice that Asean needed to take sides. Asean has been very clear it will not.
What Asean is doing now is trying to expand optionality by economically integrating with China’s supply chain, and improving its own economic strength and resilience by adding value in that supply chain. We are telling America that we respect its right to impose sanctions because it has concerns. While respecting those rights, we are able to adapt in a way that keeps us on the right side of your sanctions. We are economically resilient.
Asean is trying to work with both great powers and increase its range of options, but keep from being vulnerable to either one. I think implicit in your question is: what happens if the great power rivals then act in a way that shrinks Asean’s options? This is like the ISEAS questionnaire, which asked if forced to choose a side, which side would you choose? For the past few years, the margins have been tight.
And if we get to that point, that would mean the world would have already shrunk its optionality in ways that western Europe does not figure. Africa, Latin America and the rest of Asia does not figure for Southeast Asia any more. It would mean that everything has just merged into a background and it is only America and China left.
If we come to that point, we have lots of other things to worry about. So, we need to make sure that all of the world continues to play a role in Asean’s economic landscape. We cannot allow the great powers to shrink our optionality.
By Xinyi Wu

title_en: New US chip restrictions could cool Southeast Asia’s booming M&A market, bankers warn
content_en:
Foreign investment has flooded into Southeast Asia’s AI ecosystem this year, but tighter US chip export curbs could chill activity, bankers warn.
Southeast Asian countries including Malaysia have attracted a flood of foreign direct investment this year. Photo: Shutterstock
The latest US export restrictions on AI chips might affect valuations in Southeast Asia’s booming mergers and acquisitions (M&A) market, which has attracted a flood of foreign investment as China’s market has cooled, according to M&A bankers.
China’s M&A activity had only reached US$225 billion by the end of August this year – trailing the US$484 billion total for the whole of 2025 – according to a report released by French investment bank Natixis on Wednesday.
Inbound deals were outpacing outbound activity, with deal value growing in technology, healthcare and energy.
“This is in line with China’s K-shaped economy,” said Miranda Zhao, head of M&A for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East at Natixis, referring to the contrast between China’s booming tech and export sectors and its sluggish consumption levels.
“China has been going through a transformation or inward alignment to drive innovation, to drive efficiency instead of just fitting scale and growth,” she added.
A visitor plays chess with an AI robot at the AI Expo Thailand on November 5, 2026. Photo: EPA
Southeast Asia, meanwhile, has seen record inflows of foreign investment. The region’s foreign direct investment reached US$236 billion in 2025 – double China’s total, according to the report. And its M&A activity this year had already surpassed last year’s total by the end of September.
Part of the region’s appeal stemmed from the “China+1” strategy, in which businesses move parts of their supply chains and capital from China to nearby Southeast Asian countries to hedge against rising geopolitical risks.
This trend has fuelled the buildout of Southeast Asia’s artificial intelligence ecosystem, with the rise of data centres a notable example. Between 2023 and September this year, one-third of M&A deals in Southeast Asia were in digital infrastructure and the energy transition.
In an effort to curb China’s access to advanced AI, however, the US tightened restrictions on chip exports to third countries this week, which could affect Southeast Asia’s burgeoning AI ecosystem.
“Valuations will start diverging,” said Abbas Rangwala, head of M&A for Southeast Asia and India at Natixis. So far, a lot of Southeast Asian suppliers could “simultaneously serve both Western and Chinese hyperscalers”, but the new American regulation might change that, he added.
M&A transactions in the region might take longer because “people will spend a lot more time on due diligence”, according to Rangwala.
But Rangwala said he did not expect a deep shift in the region’s M&A market, only “a bit of a slowing down” until there was more clarity on how the latest American restrictions would affect transaction structures.
By Tim Yuen Lingk

title_en: France, China and Japan drive US$75.5 billion paring of US Treasuries holdings
content_en:
Japan’s holdings hit lowest level since late 2024, as China’s drop to lowest since July 2008 amid US monetary policy and inflation concerns.
The US Department of the Treasury building is seen from the top of the Washington Monument in Washington on October 22. Photo: AFP
Japan, the largest foreign holder of US Treasuries, reduced its holdings in September to the lowest level since the end of 2024, as France joined China in offloading US debt amid growing global concerns over Washington’s fiscal outlook.
Japan’s holdings in September fell by US$5.2 billion to US$1.063 trillion, compared with August, leaving them just above the US$1.062 trillion recorded in December 2024, according to data released by the US Treasury Department on Wednesday.
The data also showed that China pared its holdings by US$26.8 billion to US$563.9 billion in September – its fourth consecutive month of decline. This marked the lowest level since July 2008, when its holdings stood at US$550 billion, according to Chinese financial data provider Wind.
Overall foreign holdings of US Treasuries fell by US$75.5 billion to US$9.24 trillion in September, the lowest level since October 2025. France recorded the largest monthly decline among major holders, shedding US$31.4 billion to US$332 billion, followed by China.
Among other major foreign holders, the UK, the second-largest holder of US debt, reduced its holdings by US$8.7 billion to US$985.8 billion in September, data from the US Treasury Department showed.
By contrast, Belgium increased its holdings by US$17.4 billion to US$507.9 billion, while Canada added US$3.1 billion to reach US$467.7 billion.
The figures came as concerns over US monetary policy and inflation continued to weigh on global bond demand. In September, the Federal Reserve raised the target range for its federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 to 4 per cent to curb elevated inflation.
Yields on 30-year US Treasuries climbed to around 5.7 per cent in early October before retreating, but began rising again in November as investors reassessed the outlook for US interest rates.
Japan has also been reassessing its overseas debt exposure as rising domestic bond yields make Japanese government securities more attractive. Bank of Japan data showed that Japanese investors sold a net 6.06 trillion yen (US$38 billion) in US bonds in the first nine months of the year.
The US Treasury Department said in early November that it expected to keep its auction sizes for notes and bonds unchanged for the next several quarters, while continuing to “evaluate potential future changes”.
Some market participants had anticipated that Washington would scale back 20- and 30-year bond sales, leaning more heavily on shorter-dated debt instead, to slow the rise in long-term yields.
Later in the month, the US Treasury sold US$42 billion in 10-year notes at a yield of 5.02 per cent, higher than the 5.01 per cent yield on the long-end debt on the secondary market before the end of subscription.
China slipped to third place among foreign holders of US Treasuries in March last year, behind Japan and the UK, continuing a gradual but uneven retreat that began during US President Donald Trump’s first term amid rising tensions and concerns over the weaponisation of the US dollar.
In contrast to its broader reduction in US debt holdings, China has steadily increased its gold reserves, widely viewed as a hedge against geopolitical and financial risks.
China’s central bank increased its gold reserves by 830,000 troy ounces in October to 78.3 million ounces, extending its buying streak to 24 consecutive months, according to official data released earlier this month.
By Sherry Wang, Mia Nurmamat

title_en: US unlikely to catch China on rare earths in 10 months, but its friends may offer a lift
content_en:
While US President Donald Trump says America is catching up, analysts say his time frame is ‘simply unrealistic’.
US President Donald Trump walks to board Air Force One at Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila on Wednesday. Photo: AP
Despite a prediction by US President Donald Trump this week, American supplies of rare earth metals are unlikely to “catch up” with China within 10 months, analysts said, while adding that Beijing should not underestimate US progress as cooperation with third countries, including mineral-rich partners in Southeast Asia, would give it a lift.
“The US has indeed made considerable progress,” said Wang Yingliang, a Shanghai-based political economist and chief editor of the economic analysis platform Sharp Voices.
“But catching up with China’s production capacity and influence within 10 months is simply unrealistic. There is currently no clear pathway for the US to secure all the rare earth resources it needs within that time frame.”
Trump made the prediction in Manila on Tuesday, before a scheduled meeting with President Xi Jinping on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen.
China got its start in rare earths – critical inputs in the production of a range of high-value goods – decades ago, with the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, a US-based think tank, saying it now accounted for about 70 per cent of global rare earth mining and 90 per cent of processing output.
According to analysts, it supplied 71 per cent of US rare earth imports between 2021 and 2024.
The United States began a major ramp-up just last year.
“However, if the US continues to step up its efforts through political mobilisation, industrial investment and economic diplomacy, it could gain short-term advantages in certain specialised areas,” Wang said.
They included innovations by US national laboratories, research into rare earth substitutes and the recycling of rare earth materials, he said.
The situation on the ground in the US has not changed. We still need rare earth imports from ChinaDexter Roberts, Atlantic Council
“But turning these breakthroughs into commercial applications at scale is another matter, and that ultimately depends on market demand,” Wang said, adding that China was not only a major producer of rare earths and related products, but also a major consumer.
The 10-month pledge sounded “out of the realm of possibility”, said Dexter Roberts, a US-based senior fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank’s Global China Hub.
“The situation on the ground in the US has not changed,” he said. “We still need rare earth imports from China.”
The Trump administration had invested US$18.6 billion in critical minerals production in the US by the middle of this year, according to industry news outlet The Northern Miner. The 17 rare earth elements – deemed “rare” because they are hard to extract and process – are among the critical minerals.
US mines’ rare earth production rose 12 per cent to an estimated 51,000 tonnes (56,217 short tons) last year.
Analysts said the US could make headway in 10 months with help from abroad.
The US was looking for a “diversified supply model” to cut reliance on any single supplier, said Liu Wenjing, a member of the Astana International Financial Centre’s executive council for the mining sector and principal adviser at Elistra Advisory, which she founded.
“If the 10-month target is understood as accelerating investment, bringing some additional capacity online and building a more resilient alternative supply network with allies, we can see tangible progress,” Liu said.
Among the bigger Chinese rare earth firms, China Northern Rare Earth’s net profit attributable to shareholders rose 136.55 per cent in the first nine months of this year and China Rare Earth Resources and Technology’s rose 112.37 per cent, according to calculations by research and market-data company MLQ.ai.
The trade war between China and the US has seen Beijing add to restrictions on US-bound rare earth exports, prompting Washington to look for other sources of the metals, which play key roles in hi-tech hardware and aerospace gear.
Trump may have been seeking support in Southeast Asia by making his prediction in Manila this week, said Liang Yan, a professor of economics at Willamette University in the US. Trump attended a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders in Manila on Tuesday.
Several Southeast Asian countries have vast deposits of rare earth elements but could be reliant on foreign capital to get them out of the ground.
Myanmar was Southeast Asia’s largest rare earth miner last year, producing 22,000 tonnes, according to the US Geological Survey. It said Vietnam held an estimated 3.5 million tonnes of reserves but mined just 150 tonnes that year.
“One thing is really to rally a strong coalition on rare earths,” Liang said, adding that Trump’s remark gave “allies more confidence that Trump is going to work with them”.
Wang said the US might find short-term advantages abroad through “economic diplomacy”, such as by sharing rare earth recycling and research on rare earth substitutes.
Trump and Xi are expected to discuss China’s rare earth exports to the US at the Apec summit, with Liang saying Trump may have made the 10-month remark to “calm the market a little bit” in case he made no progress with Xi this week.
By Ralph Jennings, Mia Nurmamat

“If the 10-month target is understood as accelerating investment, bringing some additional capacity online and building a more resilient alternative supply network with allies, we can see tangible progress,” Liu said.
Among the bigger Chinese rare earth firms, China Northern Rare Earth’s net profit attributable to shareholders rose 136.55 per cent in the first nine months of this year and China Rare Earth Resources and Technology’s rose 112.37 per cent, according to calculations by research and market-data company MLQ.ai.
The trade war between China and the US has seen Beijing add to restrictions on US-bound rare earth exports, prompting Washington to look for other sources of the metals, which play key roles in hi-tech hardware and aerospace gear.
Trump may have been seeking support in Southeast Asia by making his prediction in Manila this week, said Liang Yan, a professor of economics at Willamette University in the US. Trump attended a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders in Manila on Tuesday.
Several Southeast Asian countries have vast deposits of rare earth elements but could be reliant on foreign capital to get them out of the ground.
Myanmar was Southeast Asia’s largest rare earth miner last year, producing 22,000 tonnes, according to the US Geological Survey. It said Vietnam held an estimated 3.5 million tonnes of reserves but mined just 150 tonnes that year.
“One thing is really to rally a strong coalition on rare earths,” Liang said, adding that Trump’s remark gave “allies more confidence that Trump is going to work with them”.
Wang said the US might find short-term advantages abroad through “economic diplomacy”, such as by sharing rare earth recycling and research on rare earth substitutes.
Trump and Xi are expected to discuss China’s rare earth exports to the US at the Apec summit, with Liang saying Trump may have made the 10-month remark to “calm the market a little bit” in case he made no progress with Xi this week.

title_en: Anthropic’s record US$81.3 billion IPO arms US AI giant for price war with Chinese rivals
content_en:
Anthropic’s debut sets a benchmark on profitability and enterprise revenue for the planned IPOs of Chinese AI labs Moonshot AI and DeepSeek.
AI giant Anthropic raises US$81.3 billion in a historic public debut. Photo: Reuters
Anthropic’s record-shattering US$81.3 billion initial public offering (IPO) is handing the US artificial intelligence powerhouse a massive war chest to wage a global price war, piling fresh valuation and monetisation pressure on lower-cost Chinese rivals, according to analysts.
The San Francisco-based creator of the Claude chatbot priced its shares at US$83 apiece on Wednesday, above its marketed range of US$70 to US$78, giving the firm a market capitalisation of around US$1.5 trillion ahead of its Nasdaq debut on Thursday under the ticker ANT.
The base offering of 980 million shares, comprising about 956.4 million new shares and 23.6 million from existing investors, eclipses SpaceX’s US$75 billion listing five months ago to become the largest IPO in history.
Anthropic is also raising an additional US$26 billion via a private placement at the IPO price, backed by investors like tech giants Google and Microsoft, according to regulatory filings.
A harsher benchmark for Chinese IPO hopefuls
The blockbuster debut underscores Wall Street appetite for frontier AI despite recent market turmoil. Analysts say the windfall gives Anthropic the financial firepower to undercut Chinese challengers such as DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Z.ai, which have gained global traction with cheaper, open-weight models.
Felix Wang, managing director and global technology sector head at Hedgeye Risk Management, said Anthropic’s public listing could weigh on Chinese AI valuations by giving global institutional investors a liquid, marquee alternative.
“The massive price war in [large language models] is still happening,” Wang said, adding that Anthropic’s fresh capital would allow it to compete more aggressively on pricing.
Still, Wang noted that Chinese open-weight models retained a distinct appeal for enterprise clients seeking greater control over deployment, customisation and proprietary data, even if their capabilities trailed top proprietary US systems.
Similarly, Ivan Su, an equity research director at Morningstar, said Anthropic’s listing was unlikely to spark a rally for Chinese peers, pointing to the US firm’s higher margins and access to more advanced chips.
“We wouldn’t expect positive sentiment around Anthropic to carry over to Chinese names,” he added.
The logo of the Kimi K3 AI model from Moonshot AI is displayed on a smartphone screen. Photo: AFP
For Chinese AI labs eyeing their own public listings, such as Moonshot AI in Hong Kong or DeepSeek on Shanghai’s Star Market, Anthropic’s debut set a clear benchmark on profitability and enterprise revenue, said Poe Zhao, a Beijing-based tech analyst and founder of Hello China Tech.
“Once they file, investors will immediately check how close their gross profit is to covering R&D and how much revenue comes from recurring enterprise customers rather than low-price traffic,” Zhao said.
Many Chinese developers have prioritised user acquisition through free consumer apps and heavily discounted application programming interfaces, which “means heavy usage arrives as a compute bill before it arrives as revenue”, Zhao said.
Chinese AI labs must pivot faster towards usage caps, tiered pricing and paid enterprise contracts, he added.
Wall Street’s stress test on frontier AI
Beyond its ripple effects in China, Anthropic’s listing serves as a confidence booster for a broader tech sector rattled by soaring AI infrastructure costs and questions over return on investment.
Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at US merchant bank Yorkville Ives & Co, described the offering in a Wednesday note as a “big near-term win for the tech sector” that “should help restore some investor confidence that the AI revolution growth thesis is not waning”.
He projected that between US$3 trillion and US$4 trillion would be poured into AI-related capital expenditure over the next few years, with Anthropic playing a central role in that buildout.
Even so, analysts cautioned that Anthropic faced a steep financial balancing act as a public company. The IPO was the “clearest public market test yet of frontier model economics”, said Yang Wang, principal analyst at Counterpoint Research.
The Claude logo is shown in this illustration taken on November 18, 2026. Photo: Reuters
Despite reporting an annualised revenue run rate of around US$81 billion, Anthropic carried computing commitments of about US$450 billion through 2030, Wang noted.
“The central question is therefore whether revenue growth, cash generation and inference efficiency can keep pace as those obligations become payable and productive,” he said.
Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan said in a research note that the US$83 offer price still sat below the firm’s fair value estimate of US$92 per share, underpinned by Anthropic’s strong footing in enterprise coding and cybersecurity.
However, Khan warned that the company needed to manage the “enormous cost of developing and running its models” amid an uncertain competitive landscape.
Hedgeye’s Wang echoed that caution, suggesting “investors may be extrapolating early-stage growth rates too far into the future” while underestimating long-term model commoditisation and AI safety regulations.
Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers led by CEO Dario Amodei, Anthropic has seen its top line surge this year on the back of booming enterprise adoption of its coding assistant, Claude Code.
According to its prospectus, Anthropic generated US$33.24 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, roughly 13 times its haul from a year earlier.
Net losses widened to US$104 billion over the same period, up from US$25.1 billion a year prior, driven largely by accounting adjustments tied to convertible notes and derivative liabilities.
By Chong Ming Lee

title_en: How a little-known Beijing AI safety group became an adviser to China’s tech giants
content_en:
The second in a three-part series profiles organisations at the forefront of efforts to balance innovation and safety in China’s AI industry.
Team members of Concordia AI, which has become an adviser to China’s tech giants, pictured in Beijing on November 4. Photo: Simon Song
As Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump meet this week in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Apec meeting, the question of how to manage the risks of frontier AI systems is expected to be a major agenda item. In the second of a three-part series profiling Chinese organisations at the forefront of AI safety efforts, we take a look at a small social enterprise that has become a trusted adviser to China’s hottest AI firms.
In 2020, tucked inside Beijing’s traditional hutongs – narrow alleyways lined with old courtyard homes – Brian Tse and Ng Kwan Yee laid the groundwork for what would become one of China’s leading AI safety organisations.
Tse, as Concordia AI’s founder and CEO, and Ng, as its head of international AI governance, were driven by a single conviction: artificial intelligence would evolve faster than humanity could control it.
Back then, ChatGPT was unheard of, and the notion of rogue AI models launching autonomous cyberattacks felt like pure sci-fi.
Six years later, the stakes have transformed. As the US and China race for AI dominance, fears of runaway systems, automated cyber warfare and biothreats have pushed AI safety from a niche concern to the forefront of global geopolitics.
The Beijing-based organisation has grown alongside the technology it monitors. Its now 18-person team includes people formerly with tech giants including Microsoft, ByteDance and Baidu, some of whom walked away from lucrative careers to tackle AI’s emerging risks.
Brian Tse, founder of Concordia AI, pictured in its Beijing office on November 4. Photo: Simon Song
Concordia has signed official partnership agreements with leading Chinese developers including DeepSeek, Z.ai and MiniMax, as well as Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies. It has also briefed executives at Silicon Valley AI labs, US government officials and Washington-based think tanks on China’s approach to AI safety.
And now, as Beijing sharpens its safety focus, the organisation’s core mission is growing more crucial: keeping ever-more-powerful systems from slipping out of human control.
An early conviction
As a teenager determined to make a difference, Tse drew up a list of humanity’s greatest existential threats, from climate change to nuclear weapons.
While studying machine learning at Beijing’s elite Tsinghua University in 2016, he watched Google’s AlphaGo stun the world and realised AI was accelerating towards a whole new league of risk.
“As a young person, maybe it’s something that I could try to learn quickly and try to contribute,” he said.
Ng Kwan Yee, pictured in Concordia AI’s office in Beijing on November 4. Photo: Simon Song
After stints at private equity and banking firms alongside early work in AI governance, Tse returned to Beijing around 2020. Convinced that China would emerge as a major AI power, he set out to establish an independent safety body connecting researchers, companies and policymakers.
He found a like-minded partner in Ng, who had worked in AI governance research. Their early efforts focused on raising awareness of risks many struggled to grasp because the technology remained largely confined to frontier developers. Still, Tse feared the technological race would eventually outgrow humanity’s ability to control it.
“The economic and the commercial incentive for driving AI forward is going to outpace our wisdom and our institutions to govern this technology,” he said.
From research to industry
When US chatbots brought generative AI into the mainstream, and the subsequent rise of Chinese challengers like DeepSeek intensified the global race, Concordia’s role shifted.
Today, as autonomous AI agents begin handling complex tasks without human supervision, the organisation has moved beyond policy research and awareness-building, increasingly engaging directly with China’s tech firms and regulators.
Two former employees of Chinese tech giants, Cheng Yuan and Fang Liang, helped drive that transition, bringing experience in navigating the industry’s commercial and regulatory priorities.
(L-R) Fang Liang and Cheng Yuan, pictured at the office of Concordia AI in Beijing on November 4. Photo: Simon Song
“Before I joined, Concordia’s work was mainly focused on research and policy recommendations,” said Cheng, who previously worked on compliance and content safety at ByteDance, including for TikTok. “There was relatively little direct support or cooperation with domestic large-model companies.”
Cheng now oversees corporate engagement for Concordia, assisting AI companies with risk-management frameworks and overseas regulatory requirements.
Meanwhile, Fang, who spent five years at Baidu working on technology standards and policy, leads Concordia’s safety work by engaging policymakers on national standards.
That industry bridge has produced tangible results.
In September, Concordia partnered with GLM model developer Z.ai – also known as Zhipu AI – to release a risk-management framework for open-weight models, those with underlying parameters that can be downloaded and modified by users.
The framework proposed a six-stage process to manage risks before and after release, addressing concerns that safeguards can be stripped away once models become publicly available.
Concordia has also engaged government-backed standardisation bodies, including presenting recommendations to Chinese policymakers at the National Science and Technology Ethics Committee.
Its close engagement with the industry has not stopped it from highlighting shortcomings in China’s AI safety practices.
“The biggest weakness for me is the transparency of Chinese frontier developers,” said Ng, whose job description includes engagement with foreign policymakers and academics on AI safety standards.
Between mid-2025 and mid-2026, only five of China’s top 10 model developers disclosed safety evaluations in their technical reports, according to Concordia, raising doubt about whether they were taking AI safety seriously.
Not just a job, a moral choice
For safety research engineer Wang Jinge, joining Concordia was a moral imperative.
When ChatGPT took the world by storm in late 2022, Wang was helping Microsoft bring AI to its search engine. A software developer on Microsoft’s China team, Wang watched AI advance at a pace that left him both astonished and uneasy.
“The speed of AI development was far beyond what I had imagined,” he said, adding that he felt AI could replace his job.
In late 2023, Wang wrote a science-fiction story imagining a future in which AI escaped human control, hoping to spark conversations about safety risks.
Wang Jinge works at Concordia AI in Beijing on November 4. Photo: Simon Song
“I wanted to discuss the risks of AI with other people, but not many people around me were aware of them,” he said.
Wang soon grew restless at Microsoft. Despite working on products used by millions, he felt his individual contributions were too small to steer the technology’s trajectory.
“In China, we have a saying that you’re just a screw in the machine,” he said. “You can only do a very small part of the work, and you can’t have a very big influence.”
In 2024, he quit without a firm plan, travelling around China as a digital nomad, exploring the emerging field of AI safety before finding his way to Concordia.
At the nimble social enterprise, he found the sense of agency he lacked at Microsoft: “We have more initiative, and the work we do can have a greater impact,” he said.
Bridging the US-China divide
Beyond its domestic work with developers, Concordia faces an uphill battle abroad: convincing the West that China takes AI safety seriously.
At international conferences, Ng said she frequently encountered the assumption that tighter regulation would hamper US developers in the AI rivalry with China.
“It’s not like China’s going to race ahead if the US regulates,” she said, pointing to China’s existing AI regulations.
As she was often one of just a few Chinese representatives in the room, she hoped Concordia’s expansion would bring more Chinese perspectives into international discussions.
“I can’t represent 1.4 billion people,” she said. “It’s a big responsibility.”
The organisation has expanded beyond Beijing, establishing an office in Singapore in 2024. In July, it became the first Chinese organisation invited by the European Union’s AI Office to participate in a workshop for prospective independent evaluators of advanced AI models. The initiative comes as the EU pushes for greater transparency and accountability through its General Purpose AI Code of Practice, which calls on developers posing systemic risks to publish safety frameworks and conduct risk assessments.
Concordia is funded primarily by donations from organisations and family offices in China, Singapore and Europe, with a smaller share of revenue coming from consulting fees paid by AI companies.
For Ng, who has watched Concordia grow from two people working in Beijing’s hutongs, the expansion has brought mixed feelings.
“In a way, Concordia is really my baby,” she said, describing a mixture of excitement and trepidation about its future.
Ultimately, though, Ng said she hoped Concordia would become obsolete by helping make AI safety as routine as safeguards in aviation or the automotive industry.
“I hope we don’t exist.”
By Chong Ming Lee

title_en: Elon Musk quietly developing ‘1 or 2’ Philippine islands, Manila envoy says
content_en:
Philippine envoy Jose Manuel Romualdez cited frequent, low-key visits by the tech billionaire, though Musk and his companies have yet to comment.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk attends the “A New Golden Age” summit at the US Institute of Peace in Washington, in October. Photo: Reuters
Elon Musk may be developing one or two islands in the Philippines, according to the country’s ambassador to the United States, who said the world’s richest man was “very interested” in the Southeast Asian nation.
Jose Manuel Romualdez said on Thursday that he had been told Musk was developing the islands, although he did not identify their locations or provide details about the projects.
“From what I’m told, Elon Musk comes here quietly very often because he has one or two islands, I’m told, that he’s developing,” Romualdez said. “That’s a big sign. The richest man in the world is actually very interested in the Philippines.”
Philippine ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez answers questions from reporters in Manila in February. Photo: AP
Neither Musk nor his companies have confirmed any island purchases or development projects. This Week in Asia has reached out to Tesla and SpaceX for comment.
The Philippine constitution generally bars foreigners from owning land, although they can lease property or undertake development projects through arrangements that comply with local ownership laws.
Romualdez said Musk had landed in Manila on his private plane at about 11.30am on Wednesday, before leaving for Shenzhen – where he joined US President Donald Trump for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit – according to local broadcaster ABS-CBN.
The ambassador also said Musk had expressed interest in exploring business opportunities in the Philippines, according to Manila-based newspaper the Daily Tribune.
“He loves the Philippines,” Romualdez said. “I had one conversation with him and I think that you could see that he has quite a lot of knowledge about the Philippines.”
Musk has steadily expanded his business footprint in the Philippines in recent years. Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet service, launched in the country in early 2023, making the Philippines the first Southeast Asian nation where the service went online.
As of February this year, the Philippines was Starlink’s sixth-largest market, accounting for 4.2 per cent of its 9.2 million customers globally, local newspaper The Philippine Star reported, citing an Ookla study.
Tesla, Musk’s electric vehicle maker, has also performed strongly since entering the Philippines in November 2024. It sold 3,460 vehicles in the first nine months of this year, making it the country’s second-best-selling battery electric vehicle (BEV) brand among industry association members, according to motoring website Zigwheels.
Electric vehicles charge at the Tesla centre in Manila in January 2025. Photo: AFP
Overall BEV sales in the Philippines grew by 337 per cent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, the Manila Bulletin reported, citing a joint report by the Chamber of Automotive Manufacturers of the Philippines and the Truck Manufacturers Association, which excludes non-member brands such as BYD.
By SCMP’s Asia desk

title_en: Qatar-gifted Boeing 747 makes China debut as Air Force One in Shenzhen
content_en:
Trump flew to Apec with an older presidential jet on hand for support, becoming the first sitting US president to visit the Chinese tech hub.
President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on November 18 at Manila’s Ninoy Aquino International Airport. Photo: AP
All three US presidential Boeing 747s touched down in Manila earlier this week, the first stop on Donald Trump’s Asia tour.
The US Air Force typically deploys a backup aircraft on major overseas trips, but seeing the entire fleet at a single foreign airport was an unusual sight.
The jumbo jets are best known for flying as Air Force One, the call sign used by any US Air Force aircraft carrying the sitting president.
The fleet includes two older Boeing 747-200s, designated VC-25As, that entered presidential service in 1990 and wear the traditional pale blue and white livery. The third jet, a Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar and designated the VC-25B Bridge, was unveiled in June in a red, white and dark-blue livery chosen by Trump. It first flew as Air Force One on July 1.
According to a White House travelling press-pool report, Trump boarded the Qatar-donated plane on Wednesday afternoon, while the two other planes that have served as Air Force One were on hand as support planes.
The Qatar-donated Boeing 747-8 serving as interim Air Force One taxis past a welcoming delegation on November 18 after bringing Donald Trump to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Photo: AFP
Two of the US presidential Boeing 747s arrived in Shenzhen late Wednesday afternoon as Trump travelled to China for the Apec summit. He is the first sitting US president to visit the Chinese tech hub.
One of the older VC-25A jets was seen parked nearby as Trump disembarked from the Qatar-donated aircraft, according to live footage broadcast by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
It remains unclear whether the second older jet also travelled to China or was deployed elsewhere.
The two older VC-25As are extensively modified Boeing 747-200B aircraft, with one having the tail number 28000 and the other 29000.
The Pentagon accepted the 747-8 aircraft, originally used by the Qatari royal family, in May last year before it was converted into an interim presidential aircraft. At its unveiling, Trump said it was “considered the world’s most luxurious plane”.
By Albee Zhang

title_en: Xi, Trump and Putin meet for landmark trilateral talks at Apec
content_en:
The meeting between the Chinese, US and Russian leaders caps a year of intensive diplomacy amid wars and nuclear arms-control debates.
Breaking News
Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin began a historic trilateral meeting on Thursday afternoon, marking the first-ever three-way summit between the leaders of the world’s major nuclear powers.
The meeting is taking place in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.
Ahead of the trilateral talks, Xi held separate bilateral meetings with Putin and Trump.
In his talks with Putin on Wednesday, Xi highlighted the resilience of bilateral relations, saying China-Russia ties “stand as firm as a mountain amid wind and rain”.
The Shenzhen talks cap a year of intensive high-level diplomacy between Beijing and both Washington and Moscow.
[embedded media]
Before his trip to China, Trump said he wanted to focus on nuclear arms control and the war in Iran when sitting down with his two counterparts.
Beijing, however, has long resisted pressure to join trilateral nuclear arms-control negotiations with Washington and Moscow, arguing that its nuclear arsenal remains far smaller than those of the other two powers.
Russia and the United States together hold around 83 per cent of all stockpiled nuclear warheads. However, Washington has repeatedly expressed concern over Beijing’s nuclear build-up in recent years.
Chinese state media have also pushed back against Western characterisations of the summit as a “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 Allied conference where major powers carved up post-war spheres of influence – noting that Beijing opposes “joint governance by major powers” while advocating stronger coordination and cooperation among major countries.
The three-way summit takes place against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine and the Iran war that erupted in February – a conflict that has triggered major disruptions to global energy and oil supplies.
More to follow...
By Amber Wang

title_en: ‘Toy paradise’: Elon Musk says his 6-year-old son loves China
content_en:
The Tesla chief is visiting Shenzhen as part of a US business delegation accompanying President Trump to the Apec summit.
While the billionaire entrepreneur has been a regular visitor to major Chinese cities like Shanghai and Beijing, this is his first public visit to Shenzhen. Photo: Yuyuan Tantian
During a high-profile trip to the southern tech hub of Shenzhen, Elon Musk said his young son loved China because the country “makes almost everything” – including his toys.
In a short video released on Thursday, the SpaceX and Tesla chief executive described himself as a “huge fan” of both China and its technology in a meeting with Ren Hongbin, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade.
Musk then turned to his six-year-old son, X Æ A-Xii, who was seated beside him.
“X, Do you love China?” he asked.
“Yes,” the boy blurted out, prompting immediate laughter from both men.
The exchange was shown in a 24-second video clip released by Yuyuan Tantian, an influential social media account affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV.
[embedded media]
“China makes everything, almost everything,” Musk continued. “China is a toy paradise. His toys are made here,” he added, noting that his son had always wanted to visit the country.
While the billionaire entrepreneur has been a regular visitor to major Chinese cities such as Shanghai and Beijing, this is his first public visit to Shenzhen.
He is part of a US business delegation accompanying President Donald Trump for the two-day Apec summit.
Meanwhile, his son is already an internet darling in China, having won over fans when he joined his father on Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May.
[embedded media]
At that time, the boy, dressed in a Chinese-style silk jacket, was filmed carrying a shoulder bag resembling a tiger’s face and bouncing along hand in hand with his father in the Great Hall of the People.
The jacket and the bag soon sold out quickly on e-commerce platforms.
By Laura Zhou

title_en: Apec summit finds Marco Rubio again admiring Chinese architecture
content_en:
After his viral thumbs-up in Beijing in May, the US secretary of state followed David Perdue’s gaze upwards in Shenzhen.
Marco Rubio, pictured with the Chinese ambassador to the US Xie Feng and US ambassador to China David Perdue . Photo: CNBC
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was once again generous in his admiration for China’s grand architecture, this time at the Apec summit’s welcome dinner ahead of Thursday’s main meeting.
At the Shenzhen International Communication Centre on Wednesday night, Chinese President Xi Jinping and first lady Peng Liyuan welcomed US President Donald Trump and other leaders to the southern tech hub.
A video showed Rubio speaking to China’s ambassador to the United States, Xie Feng, and US ambassador to China David Perdue, as they waited for the state leaders to enter the hall.
Perdue suddenly looked up in apparent awe at the hall’s ceiling, spreading his arms wide as if to take in its scale.
Following his gaze, Rubio looked upwards and appeared to smile in agreement.
The ceiling that drew their attention featured a strikingly futuristic black lattice of gently curving bands against a white surface. Tiny spotlights glimmered overhead, the ceiling’s dark geometry contrasting with the warm tones of the banquet hall below.
Onstage, an LED screen glowed in shades of orange and red. Warm light bathed the upper part of the hall, and the stage backdrop showed flowers rendered in a Chinese ink-wash style.
Round tables with cream tablecloths and floral centrepieces recalled the banquet Xi hosted during Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May. Cream-coloured screens decorated with traditional Chinese landscape paintings lined the walls.
The Apec welcome banquet was held at the Shenzhen International Communication Centre. Photo: Reuters
It was not the first time the US secretary of state had been visibly impressed by Chinese interior design.
In May, when Xi hosted Trump at the Great Hall of the People, a video of Rubio appearing to admire the reception hall quickly went viral.
The footage showed the secretary of state gazing up at the ornate ceiling of the East Hall of the Great Hall, near Tiananmen Square. The vast building is used for state ceremonies and legislative sessions.
Rubio pointed upwards, moving his fingers as though following the contours of the design, before giving a thumbs-up.
He then turned to Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and gestured towards the ceiling again. On Weibo, a hashtag saying Rubio had given “a thumbs-up to Chinese aesthetics” gained traction.
The East Hall, on the building’s second floor, covers about 1,120 square metres (12,056 square feet). Its ceiling draws on traditional Chinese architecture.
[embedded media]
In May, Rubio became the first sitting US secretary of state to visit China after being sanctioned by Beijing.
China sanctioned him twice in 2020, when he was a US senator: first in July, in retaliation for US sanctions over alleged human rights abuses in Xinjiang, and again in August, after Washington sanctioned mainland Chinese and Hong Kong officials over the handling of the 2019 Hong Kong protests.
By Cao Jiaxuan

title_en: Homo erectus teeth found in China’s rainforest topple theory of human evolution
content_en:
Remains from distant ancestors of modern humans were found in an isolated forest once thought to have been the sole domain of homo sapiens.
Some of the teeth, believed to date back to between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, were found in the Naxian cave. Photo: IVPP-CAS
In Chongzuo, Guangxi, at the southernmost tip of China, steep limestone peaks rise abruptly, disappearing into the humid and dense tropical rainforest.
For tens of thousands of years, this green labyrinth of interwoven vegetation has not only swallowed sunlight and footprints but also preserved the secrets of ancient humans.
In Baxian Cave and Naxian Cave on the west bank of the Zuojiang River, archaeologists identified nine tiny ancient human teeth among more than 18,000 mammalian fossils.
Eight of them belong to Homo erectus – an ancient relative of modern humans, Homo sapiens.
Homo erectus existed on Earth for nearly two million years, far longer than our Homo sapiens ancestors. By various means, archaeologists have inferred that the owners of these teeth lived between 184,000 and 324,000 years ago.
This discovery challenges a long-standing consensus in anthropology: that the perilous, isolated tropical rainforest was a zone only Homo sapiens could conquer.
This research was conducted jointly by teams from China, Australia and Europe, and the findings were written up in two papers published in the latest issue of the leading academic journal Nature, released on November 19.
“These findings change how we think about Homo erectus,” author and palaeontologist Professor Zhang Yingqi, from the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, wrote in a press release.
“Finding Homo erectus evidence for the first time among rainforest fauna challenges all our assumptions about their ability to adapt to environmental changes,” he added.
The nine human teeth found in Naxian and Baxian Caves – eight of which have been confidently identified as Homo erectus. Photo: IVPP-CAS
China has extensive evidence of Homo erectus, including the Zhoukoudian cave system in Beijing, where the remains of the so-called Peking Man, who lived between 400,000 and 780,000 years ago, were found.
However, such sites are mainly located in northern China, while very little evidence of Homo erectus has been found in southern China.
The two caves in Guangxi where the latest find was made are linked by a 15km (9-mile) karst valley corridor, surrounded by steep limestone hills, caves and patches of tropical vegetation.
Tropical rainforests are a harsh environment, where it is difficult to find food, navigate and survive. The rainy conditions also make fossil preservation more difficult – yet the limestone caves of Guangxi’s karst landscape happened to preserve these fossils.
More than 18,000 mammal fossils were unearthed from the two caves, including those of the extinct elephant-like Stegodon and the Guangxi giant antelope.
Among them, archaeologists identified nine teeth of human origin. Based on their morphology and ancient protein characteristics, eight were determined to belong to Homo erectus.
The ninth tooth (PA1796) differs morphologically from Homo erectus and does not have the derived amino acid sequence characteristic of Homo erectus.
This indicates that PA1796 does not belong to Homo erectus. However, it cannot currently be determined whether it is a Denisovan or another archaic human population.
By testing for strontium – a chemical element in tooth enamel linked to local geology – in the teeth of these individuals, researchers found that they may have travelled across surprisingly vast karst forest areas during childhood, rather than remaining within a small area.
[embedded media]
Based on the strontium isotope data from three sets of teeth in the study, these Homo erectus individuals moved between the local limestone karst and more distant areas during childhood, travelling distances of up to 250km.
This movement extended as far as present-day northern Vietnam, forming a migration corridor between southern China and Southeast Asia.
Before this, Homo sapiens were thought to be the only species capable of adapting to such extreme environments. In West Africa, there is evidence that Homo sapiens survived in tropical rainforests 150,000 years ago.
In Southeast Asia, the expansion of rainforest during the Middle to Late Pleistocene is generally believed to be associated with the disappearance of archaic non-Homo sapiens hominins.
The world’s last Homo erectus were found on the alluvial plains of Java dating back to 100,000 years ago.
Archaeologists determined the age of the latest fossils through five independent methods, dating them to between 184,000 years and 324,000 ago – indicating that Homo erectus inhabited the two caves roughly contemporaneously.
This finding also extends the reliable record of Homo erectus in China beyond previous discoveries such as the He County site in Anhui (410,000 years ago) and the Nanjing site (640,000 years ago), confirming that southern China was a key habitat for late-surviving Homo erectus populations.
“While there has been growing recognition that our own species, Homo sapiens, adapted to rainforests around the world between 100,000 and 13,000 years ago, this is the first clear, direct evidence we have for another hominin living within these habitats,” said Professor Patrick Roberts of the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, Germany, according to EurekAlert.
The South China Morning Post has contacted the author for comment.
You can read the two papers here and here.
By Shi Huang

Eight of them belong to Homo erectus – an ancient relative of modern humans, Homo sapiens.
Homo erectus existed on Earth for nearly two million years, far longer than our Homo sapiens ancestors. By various means, archaeologists have inferred that the owners of these teeth lived between 184,000 and 324,000 years ago.
This discovery challenges a long-standing consensus in anthropology: that the perilous, isolated tropical rainforest was a zone only Homo sapiens could conquer.
This research was conducted jointly by teams from China, Australia and Europe, and the findings were written up in two papers published in the latest issue of the leading academic journal Nature, released on November 19.
“These findings change how we think about Homo erectus,” author and palaeontologist Professor Zhang Yingqi, from the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, wrote in a press release.
“Finding Homo erectus evidence for the first time among rainforest fauna challenges all our assumptions about their ability to adapt to environmental changes,” he added.
The nine human teeth found in Naxian and Baxian Caves – eight of which have been confidently identified as Homo erectus. Photo: IVPP-CAS
China has extensive evidence of Homo erectus, including the Zhoukoudian cave system in Beijing, where the remains of the so-called Peking Man, who lived between 400,000 and 780,000 years ago, were found.
However, such sites are mainly located in northern China, while very little evidence of Homo erectus has been found in southern China.
The two caves in Guangxi where the latest find was made are linked by a 15km (9-mile) karst valley corridor, surrounded by steep limestone hills, caves and patches of tropical vegetation.
Tropical rainforests are a harsh environment, where it is difficult to find food, navigate and survive. The rainy conditions also make fossil preservation more difficult – yet the limestone caves of Guangxi’s karst landscape happened to preserve these fossils.
More than 18,000 mammal fossils were unearthed from the two caves, including those of the extinct elephant-like Stegodon and the Guangxi giant antelope.
Among them, archaeologists identified nine teeth of human origin. Based on their morphology and ancient protein characteristics, eight were determined to belong to Homo erectus.
The ninth tooth (PA1796) differs morphologically from Homo erectus and does not have the derived amino acid sequence characteristic of Homo erectus.
This indicates that PA1796 does not belong to Homo erectus. However, it cannot currently be determined whether it is a Denisovan or another archaic human population.
By testing for strontium – a chemical element in tooth enamel linked to local geology – in the teeth of these individuals, researchers found that they may have travelled across surprisingly vast karst forest areas during childhood, rather than remaining within a small area.
[embedded media]
Based on the strontium isotope data from three sets of teeth in the study, these Homo erectus individuals moved between the local limestone karst and more distant areas during childhood, travelling distances of up to 250km.
This movement extended as far as present-day northern Vietnam, forming a migration corridor between southern China and Southeast Asia.
Before this, Homo sapiens were thought to be the only species capable of adapting to such extreme environments. In West Africa, there is evidence that Homo sapiens survived in tropical rainforests 150,000 years ago.
In Southeast Asia, the expansion of rainforest during the Middle to Late Pleistocene is generally believed to be associated with the disappearance of archaic non-Homo sapiens hominins.
The world’s last Homo erectus were found on the alluvial plains of Java dating back to 100,000 years ago.
Archaeologists determined the age of the latest fossils through five independent methods, dating them to between 184,000 years and 324,000 ago – indicating that Homo erectus inhabited the two caves roughly contemporaneously.
This finding also extends the reliable record of Homo erectus in China beyond previous discoveries such as the He County site in Anhui (410,000 years ago) and the Nanjing site (640,000 years ago), confirming that southern China was a key habitat for late-surviving Homo erectus populations.
“While there has been growing recognition that our own species, Homo sapiens, adapted to rainforests around the world between 100,000 and 13,000 years ago, this is the first clear, direct evidence we have for another hominin living within these habitats,” said Professor Patrick Roberts of the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, Germany, according to EurekAlert.
The South China Morning Post has contacted the author for comment.

title_en: UN intellectual property agency pledges deeper cooperation with Hong Kong
content_en:
WIPO plans closer work on dispute resolution, education and commercialisation as the city looks to expand its IP-backed lending pilot.
Paul Chan, centre, attends the Business of IP Asia Forum. Photo: Handout
The United Nations agency for intellectual property (IP) has pledged to deepen cooperation with Hong Kong on dispute resolution, education and commercialisation as the city’s government plans to expand a pilot scheme for lending backed by intangible assets.
At the Business of IP Asia Forum on Thursday, Shen Changyu, deputy director general of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), said the agency stood ready to help Hong Kong use IP to advance its ambitions in finance, trade and technology.
Beijing positioned Hong Kong as a regional IP trading centre in China’s 15th five-year plan.
Hong Kong’s own five-year blueprint and the policy address in September set out pledges to promote IP financing and strengthen local capacity to value IP assets.
“We are pleased to see the emphasis placed on building Hong Kong as a regional IP trading centre, promoting technology transfer and commercialisation, and building a wider IP trading ecosystem,” Shen said.
WIPO previously partnered with the government-backed Hong Kong Productivity Council to establish the Hong Kong Technology and Innovation Support Centre, which provides IP support services. Shen said the agency would build on that partnership by exploring further opportunities for cooperation.
“These include international dispute resolution, IP education and training, greater use of WIPO’s global IP services, exchanges for young talent, and support for local businesses in IP commercialisation and financing. I am confident that these efforts will bring more tangible and impactful results in the years ahead,” he said.
At the same event, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said most Asian economies were active in creating IP but still paid more to use it than they earned from it.
“Asia has learned how to create. The task for the coming decade is to capture more of the value of what it creates,” he added.
Chan pointed to difficulties in valuing IP, using it to secure financing and trading it across borders. He said the government aimed to expand Hong Kong’s IP Financing Sandbox and was consulting industry professionals on how artificial intelligence could affect the creation and use of IP.
Paul Chan speaking at the forum, where he outlined Hong Kong’s plans to expand its pilot scheme for intellectual property-backed lending. Photo: Handout
“What Hong Kong can offer is a place to test ideas. And we will share our experience with our partners on the mainland and around the world,” he said.
Launched in December, the sandbox allows banks to test lending against IP assets in a controlled environment. The first seven loans of HK$1 million to HK$39 million (US$4.9 million) were backed by assets such as patents and trademarks. The borrowers came from sectors including construction, toy manufacturing and medical devices.
During a panel discussion at the forum, Cheng Ying-ying, head of banking supervision at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, said the regulator was preparing for the next phase of the sandbox.
“So we aim to broaden participation to more banks and also more enterprises from diverse sectors. We are currently considering the appropriate arrangements to facilitate the participation of new interested enterprises,” she said.
Cheng added that sandbox participants had identified two priorities for expanding IP financing in Hong Kong: improving the valuation process and strengthening valuation expertise at local banks. She called for more standardised documentation to make valuations easier to process.
“Standardised templates for IP valuation can streamline information submission. This reduces the back and forth between the borrower, the banks and the valuation firms. It makes the process faster and smoother,” she said.
Fellow panellist Anita Ou, head of enterprise banking at HSBC’s Hong Kong commercial banking division, said banks assessing loan applications often contended with differences in how valuation firms assessed IP assets. HSBC handled three of the seven loans under the sandbox.
“Banks would like to see a more consistent methodology and approach, when it comes to valuation, to be more standardised, I would say, for banks’ credit underwriting,” she said.
“We would like to have sort of better understanding and consistency in the approach and the assumptions being applied in the valuation report.”
Ou said high upfront valuation costs were another hurdle, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which had to pay for a valuation without any guarantee that their loan applications would be approved.
She welcomed the government’s recent initiative to subsidise IP valuations for SMEs, saying it would ease the cost burden and help businesses access financing.
By Leopold Chen

title_en: Greater Bay Area has ‘enormous’ potential, John Lee tells Xi at Apec
content_en:
Chief executive says Hong Kong will deepen integration into the Greater Bay Area and accelerate the Northern Metropolis megaproject.
John Lee briefly spoke with Chinese President Xi Jinping and put on a red scarf for a group photo during Apec summit in Shenzhen. Photo: Sam Tsang
Hong Kong’s leader has pledged to deepen Greater Bay Area development and accelerate the Northern Metropolis megaproject after attending Apec meetings, where he briefly spoke with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Thursday outlined strategies for deepening Hong Kong’s integration into the bay area through infrastructure development, aligning rules and standards, and promoting cross-border mobility and exchanges.
He also secured agreements and held bilateral talks with leaders from seven of the 21 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies – Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, Thailand, Chile, Peru and Singapore.
Concluding his three-day visit to Shenzhen for the Apec summit, Lee told the media that he had used the opportunity to brief Xi on Tuesday’s Apec CEO Summit panel discussion on the development of the bay area.
“I told President Xi that participants responded very positively to the Greater Bay Area’s development prospects,” Lee said. “There were lively discussions and attendees agreed that the region’s growth potential is enormous.”
He added that Hong Kong would continue to leverage its advantage in connecting mainland China with the world under “one country, two systems”, fulfilling its roles as a “superconnector” and “super value-adder” to better integrate into and serve the country’s overall development, while contributing to cooperation and growth across the Asia-Pacific.
Lee highlighted the five outcomes achieved during the summit, saying he had used the opportunity to consolidate ties with Asean countries. He said leaders from the economic bloc had reaffirmed their support for Hong Kong’s application to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) as soon as possible.
During the Apec gathering, Hong Kong also deepened exchanges with other member economies, expanded trade networks with emerging markets and promoted Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area internationally, Lee said.
He added that as China was hosting Apec this year, Hong Kong had contributed its strengths through active participation and by hosting the finance ministers’ meeting for the first time.
Lee arrived in Shenzhen on Tuesday for the summit, which drew more than 2,000 global business leaders, politicians and media representatives over two days. It was followed by the highly anticipated 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting on Wednesday and Thursday.
Attending the morning meeting at which Xi delivered a speech, Lee briefly spoke with the Chinese leader and put on a red scarf for a group photo. During the meeting, he sat between Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.
John Lee (front row, centre) attends the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. Photo: Handout
Lee said Hong Kong also sent its largest delegations, with 54 business leaders taking part in the CEO Summit.
Lee highlighted the development opportunities and business prospects under Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the Northern Metropolis megaproject, which aims to transform 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land near the city’s border with Shenzhen into an engine for technological development and economic growth.
The city leader also encouraged Southeast Asian companies to use Hong Kong as a springboard to expand into mainland China.
Hong Kong also signed an agreement with Chile to establish a bilateral working holiday scheme, making Chile the programme’s first partner country in South America.
Hong Kong, along with Macau, Shenzhen and eight other cities in Guangdong, forms the Greater Bay Area economic powerhouse. Xi called on other bay areas across the Asia-Pacific region to form a world association of bay areas, including Tokyo, New York and San Francisco.
In his keynote address at the Apec CEO Summit on Wednesday, Xi also called for stronger economic connections and deeper exchanges among major coastal innovation centres worldwide.
The leaders’ meeting concluded at lunchtime.
Additional reporting by Vivian Au

title_en: US and China have mutual interest in getting oil through Strait of Hormuz: Trump
content_en:
Agriculture trade, Ukraine and nuclear weapons also on the agenda as leaders of world’s two largest economies meet.
US President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping pose for a photo during a bilateral meeting in Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Apec Summit in Shenzhen on Thursday. Photo: Pool/AFP
Talks between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping have concluded after Trump spoke of their mutual interest in the flow of oil supplies and that he would press China on agricultural purchases.
Before the meeting got under way on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, Trump said both Washington and Beijing had “an interest in ensuring that energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz” and that “Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon”.
“We both feel that very strongly on both points,” he said.
[embedded media]
While Trump said the two leaders had made their relationship “fair”, he said he would ask Xi to “do some more for our farmers”, citing China’s “insatiable appetite”.
Trump said Washington’s ties with Beijing had previously been “lopsided”.
“Our [previous] presidents didn’t do their job. We’ve made it a fair relationship. That’s what we want. That’s all we ask,” Trump said.
After Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May, China agreed to purchases of at least US$17 billion of American farm goods, and restored access for US beef and poultry. In September, during Xi’s state visit to Washington, the two countries agreed on a US$30 billion tariff reduction framework, covering certain products, including agricultural goods.
While expectations for a breakthrough on trade or other sticking points were low, the meeting at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen’s northwest offered the leaders of the world’s two largest economies a chance to air their concerns about a bilateral relationship still strained by trade frictions.
President Donald Trump, left, seated next to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meets holds talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday. Photo: AP
Trump hinted at possible deliverables from his sit-down with Xi, saying “something will come out”. He said the two countries were “looking to both help” end the war in Ukraine.
“Ukraine would like to see it ended,” he said. “[Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s going to be coming here a little bit later. We’ll have a … trilateral … I look forward to that.”
Trump met Putin just before meeting Xi, with the Kremlin saying they discussed the Ukraine war and bilateral relations. The Trump-Xi talks will be followed by an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Putin.
The unprecedented three-way talks between the US, China and Russia have alarmed Europe, fearing Ukraine’s future could be decided without Kyiv or its European allies at the table. Ahead of the talks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told NBC News that the war could be ended in the trilateral meeting.
“If they want to end the war in reality, don’t play any games, they can,” he said in the interview. “If China and the United States will put sanctions, or will say that they will put sanctions, stop export-import trade between Russia and these countries, that’s the end of the war.”
The Trump administration has repeatedly pressed China — Iran’s most important economic partner — to use its leverage to help end the Iran war, including by persuading Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump received a grand red-carpet welcome from Xi when he arrived in the southern Chinese coastal city on Wednesday. It was the first time in nearly seven decades that China’s top leader had personally greeted a visiting foreign head of state upon arrival.
Trump later told Fox News that his welcome showed a “high level of respect”, again playing up his close ties with Xi. “He’s a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” he said.
“That’s a big win for us. It’s a big win for China too.”
[embedded media]
The talks on Thursday came weeks after Trump’s Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the US midterm elections and days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy – a claim Beijing has dismissed as a smear.
Xi and Trump have already met twice this year, in Beijing in May and in Washington in September.
More to follow …
By Dewey Sim
