title_en: Crackdowns failed to stop Southeast Asia’s scam centres. Here’s what advocates want next
content_en:
With world leaders in Asia, campaigners are hoping to refocus efforts to uproot hubs near the Thai borders with Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos.
A Thai soldier patrols an  abandoned scam centre in O’Smach town on the Thai-Cambodian border, on September 7. Photo: AFP
Campaigners in Asia are taking advantage of the presence of global leaders in the region this week to urge governments to redouble efforts to uproot the scam centres whose bosses continue to swindle billions of dollars from hideouts in Myanmar and other parts of the Mekong.
In a reminder of the scale of the scam crisis, Malaysian lawmakers on Monday heard that their citizens have lost 6.95 billion ringgit (US$1.6 billion) to scams in the last three years, while the Global Anti-Scam Alliance reported on November 9 that 60 per cent of Thais fell victim to scams in the last year alone, costing them 110 billion baht (US$3.2 billion).
Despite high-profile crackdowns triggered by pressure from China and the US, scam gangs remain operating just over the Thai border in ungovernable areas of Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos. All that has changed is that the networks – who crime experts say are mainly run by Chinese criminals – have splintered into smaller groups.
With US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping after joining the Asean Summit in Manila, anti-scam campaigners are keen to keep the global momentum on tackling the scourge.
China-born scam suspect Li Xiong is escorted off a China Southern Airlines plane after being extradited from Cambodia on April 1. Photo: China’s Ministry of Public Security . AFP
Jay Kritiya, a coordinator at the Civil Society Network for Human Trafficking Victim Assistance, which has helped rescue hundreds of scam workers from inside Myanmar, urged global leaders to be clear-eyed about the perpetrators of the global scam crisis – and the enablers, including social media platforms.
“These criminal networks are linked to Chinese mafia syndicates,” she wrote in an open letter. “The Chinese government must take responsibility for pursuing its nationals involved in these operations. All affected governments must cooperate across borders, rather than allowing criminals to exploit jurisdictional gaps and political divisions.”
The financial crime is compounded by a human rights crisis, with thousands of foreign nationals tricked and trafficked into scam hubs to target their compatriots online. Others travel willingly to operate elaborate bogus romance and fake investment schemes often involving the transfer of hard-to-trace cryptocurrency.
Tensions were raised after the Chinese embassy in Thailand urged Chinese nationals to be on the alert against scam syndicates in the kingdom on October 16. The warning landed badly among many Thais, who insist that the kidnappings are carried out by the Chinese themselves, who use their compatriots as forced labour in the scam hubs they control across the Thai border or for ransom.
Lured by fake police
The latest example of how ordinary people are ensnared by scam gangs unfolded late last week, when a 19-year-old Chinese student was lured to Thailand after a Chinese call centre scam gang acting as local police persuaded him to leave his studies in Australia.
He arrived in Bangkok on Friday after days of 24-hour surveillance in Australia by the scammers, Thai immigration police said, and was taken to a hotel in Pattaya the next day. Once there, he was coerced into recording videos pretending he had been assaulted to extort money from his family in China, whom the criminals contacted over WeChat.
The criminals “threatened his family and demanded a ransom of 10 million baht while threatening to physically harm him if the money was not paid”, the police said. The man was freed on Tuesday and reunited with his father after Thai authorities located him following his parents’ appeal for help.
[embedded media]
In her letter, Kritiya said trafficking victims should be urgently rescued from scam hubs and protected, irrespective of their nationality. She urged greater screening of young people travelling to the scam hotspots.
“Social media platforms and internet service providers must also be held accountable for their role in enabling recruitment and online fraud,” she added.
But a truly transnational crime, which sees millions of dollars laundered through real estate and other investments from New York to London, and from Singapore to Bangkok, requires a global policing effort, according to the campaigner.
“Governments must dismantle the criminal networks behind these operations, pursue their financiers and protectors, seize their assets, and hold everyone responsible to account, including individuals and armed groups that enable these businesses to operate,’’ she said.
Scams were discussed at the East Asia Summit, an expansion of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations talks, in Manila this week. In a joint statement issued after the meeting, the leaders pledged to address underlying drivers of the crime – including “poverty, lack of social protection interventions, outdated domestic laws … corruption and limited economic opportunities”.
By Aidan Jones

title_en: ‘Productive ageing’: China is rethinking how it can ease strains of demographic shift
content_en:
The nation aims to turn its ageing population into an economic asset.
An elderly woman exercises at a park in Beijing. Photo: AFP
China’s top leadership has called for an active response to the country’s deepening demographic shift, vowing to tap older people’s social participation and consumer demand to support the slowing Chinese economy.
The country’s growing group of older adults was no longer framed solely as dependents, but as economic participants and contributors, according to an official readout of the National Conference on Ageing, held in Beijing on Wednesday and Thursday.
Besides stronger social security, elderly care and health services for older people, China needed to expand their social participation and “vigorously develop the silver economy”, President Xi Jinping was quoted as saying in a message to the conference.
Premier Li Qiang told the gathering that meeting the “value-realisation needs” of seniors meant “actively expanding the space for their participation in economic and social development,” the readout said.
The conference was convened at a time when economists fear falling birth rates and a rapidly ageing population would drag future growth of the world’s second-largest economy. Both demographic shifts typically lead to a shrinking workforce and pressure on the pension and healthcare insurance systems.
The last time top officials held a meeting of this level on this theme was in 2021, when population growth nearly stalled before entering a downward trend.
China is now regarded as a deeply ageing society, with people aged 65 and above accounting for nearly 16 per cent of the total population in 2025. Last year also marked a turning point as the 65-plus population surpassed the population aged 14 and under for the first time, meaning the burden of supporting the elderly exceeded that of raising children, according to government data.
“[We should] take a dialectical view of the profound impact of population ageing and fully recognise China’s unique strengths in responding to it,” said Li at the conference.
Seniors exercise in China’s central Hunan province. Photo: Xinhua
Calling for “productive ageing”, he urged cadres to take into account both the basic care for the elderly and opportunities for them to continue contributing to the economy.
China’s older population is markedly skewed towards the so-called younger-old: those aged 60 to 69 account for more than half of all older people, according to official figures.
The traditional retirement age is 60 for men and 50 or 55 for women, depending on job category. Since January 2025, a gradual delay has been under way, set to reach 63 for men and 55 or 58 for women over 15 years.
But the contribution of the younger-old to the economy might be marginal, as some say the country is “old before it is rich”.
“China will experience ageing far worse than Japan has, because Chinese consumers are not rich enough,” said Anthony Fox, data scientist at World Data Lab, a Vienna-based data analytics company.
With far poorer consumers than Japan’s, he projected in a recent research note that by 2050, most of China’s 390 million over-65s would shop on modest budgets.
In the near term, China would have one-fifth of its population aged 65 and above by 2032, a mark Japan reached in 2005, he said. But by that time, Chinese consumers would spend only about three-fifths per person of what Japanese consumers spent in 2005, at purchasing power parity.
By Mandy Zuo

title_en: China’s abundant electricity is not yet a decisive AI edge
content_en:
More electricity does not necessarily mean it gets cheaper or that it is generated in the right place and at the right time for AI demand.
Construction workers conduct high-altitude operations on the 500-kilovolt line project from Xiangjian to Ludao in Anhui province, China, on December 16, 2025. Photo: Xinhua
As Washington continues to tighten controls over advanced chip exports, China faces greater obstacles to accessing high-performance processors. The fall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, a prominent advocate for selling chips to China, adds another layer of uncertainty.
Some observers believe China’s abundant electricity can help offset chip constraints in the artificial intelligence (AI) race. Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, has said China’s ability to scale up electricity generation gives it a decisive edge in the AI race and predicted that the country will outpace every rival in computing power.
The statement is only half right. While China builds power plants and grids faster than anyone else, more electricity does not necessarily lead to cheaper electricity, and it is not always generated in the right place at the right time to meet AI demand.
The United States is facing an unexpected surge in electricity demand. After decades of flat consumption, its grid is struggling to keep pace with the expansion in data centres and utility prices are being rapidly driven up.
Electricity prices in data-centre-heavy areas such as Virginia have risen by as much as 267 per cent in five years. Adding generation capacity has proved difficult, with financing, supply chain and siting issues leaving many approved projects unbuilt.
China is far more accustomed to large-scale investment and expansion in its energy system. Its electricity consumption reached 10.37 trillion kilowatt-hours last year, nearly eight times the level in 2000, driven by energy-intensive manufacturing. Data centres consume only 1.6 per cent of electricity, a small addition in an ever-expanding market. Beijing’s ability to mobilise investment lets it absorb AI demand with relative ease.
[embedded media]
But building electricity generation capacity quickly does not mean delivering it cheaply. Anders Hove of the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies notes that electricity prices for Chinese businesses are not low by international standards.
The International Energy Agency finds that, once transmission and other charges are included, prices for China’s energy-intensive industries are as high as those in the US, sometimes even higher. One industry estimate puts prices for large energy users in Guangdong and Jiangsu at 0.6-0.75 yuan per kWh (roughly 9-11 US cents), close to the industrial average of about 10 US cents in Virginia.
Hove points to two features of China’s power system. The first is the cost of surplus capacity. After the power shortages of 2021-22, China relaxed approvals for coal plants, adding 78 gigawatts of coal capacity in 2025 alone. Much of it was not built where power is most needed.
Provinces secure their own supply for political and economic reasons, and keep building even where capacity is excessive. For years, users have paid for idle plants through a capacity payment; related system charges doubled on commercial and industrial bills in the first quarter of this year.
The second is a rigid market. Despite heavy investment in transmission lines, trading remains constrained by provincial boundaries, and power plants run on administered prices and dispatch decisions rather than real-time market signals.
[embedded media]
Beijing began addressing this last year, notably through a transmission-pricing policy that aims to better integrate the grid, but changing how provinces generate and trade power will take years. A grid with weak price signals delays in responding to AI’s fluctuating needs.
China’s western regions offer an attractive solution to surging AI energy demand. They have abundant wind and solar resources, ample land and significant unused renewable energy generation capacity. In January and February, solar-power utilisation rates in Tibet, Qinghai, Gansu and Xinjiang ranged from only 60.8 per cent to 85.6 per cent, while the rest went to waste.
To harness this potential, Beijing has ordered the AI industry to shift computing westwards, closer to where the renewable resources are. In 2022, it designated eight national computing hubs, including in Inner Mongolia, Gansu, Guizhou and Ningxia, and demanded new data centres be built there.
Where the model works, the economics can be attractive. In Inner Mongolia, the Ulanqab Low-Carbon Computing Base Project by Centrin Data combines 200 megawatts of wind and 100MW of solar generation with energy storage, supplying a data centre through a dedicated power line. Local authorities put the delivered electricity price at 0.32 to 0.36 yuan per kWh, with operating costs 30 to 50 per cent below those in major eastern cities.
[embedded media]
Yet the strategy is limited by the time sensitivity of AI use. AI training and other batch-processing tasks can be located farther away, but latency-sensitive services, which need data to travel quickly between users and servers, must stay relatively close to population centres. Much of the computing demand comes from China’s eastern population and business centres, where electricity prices stay relatively high.
China avoids the permitting delays, local opposition and grid bottlenecks that have slowed data centre development in the US, and it excels at mobilising investment. But that has yet to become a decisive edge for AI.
As chip restrictions tighten, China will increasingly need its electricity to compensate for constraints elsewhere in the AI supply chain. But the decisive question lies in whether power can reach computing facilities at an attractive price and the right time.
By Xuandi (Aaron) Wang

title_en: Japanese PM Takaichi tries to break ice with Xi by thanking him for hosting Apec summit
content_en:
Relations have been in the deep freeze for over a year and Takaichi had only brief interactions with the Chinese leader in Shenzhen.
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke briefly with Xi Jinping when they shook hands ahead of the Apec leaders’ meeting. Photo: Pool AFP via AP
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi thanked Chinese President Xi Jinping for inviting her to the Apec summit and congratulated him on successfully hosting the event on Thursday.
Speaking at a press conference at the end of her visit to Shenzhen, Takaichi described her brief interactions with the Chinese leader.
Unlike other leaders, she did not have a one-on-one meeting with Xi, but after a quick handshake at Wednesday’s welcome banquet, she spoke to him for around 10 seconds on Thursday during a much longer handshake at the leaders’ meeting.
“At last night’s banquet and today’s leaders’ session, I was greeted by President Xi and we shook hands and exchanged greetings,” she said.
“Yesterday I expressed my gratitude for the invitation, and today I offered my thanks and congratulations on the hosting of last night’s banquet and today’s leaders’ session.”
The Wednesday handshake was the first since relations soured dramatically after Takaichi angered Beijing with her comments suggesting that a military conflict in Taiwan Strait could constitute an existential crisis for Japan, justifying a military response.
The Japanese prime minister received a modest reception when arriving in Shenzhen on Wednesday afternoon, with only a small honour guard and no dancers or musical performances, in sharp contrast to how other foreign leaders were welcomed to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
Xi did not speak during either handshake with Takaichi, and on Thursday he only nodded as she talked.
[embedded media]
When asked about the reception for Takaichi, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Thursday that Beijing made “adequate protocol arrangements” for all parties in accordance with international practice.
Takaichi said Tokyo would continue to seek a stable, mutually beneficial strategic relationship with Beijing, while pursuing dialogue to protect their respective national interests.
She added that the four documents governing relations with China “remain unchanged”.
The documents – the 1972 Joint Communique that normalised relations, the 1978 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, the 1998 Joint Declaration and the 2008 Joint Statement – are the bedrock of the relationship between the two countries.
The 1972 communique said Japan “fully understands and respects” Beijing’s stance that Taiwan is an inalienable part of the People’s Republic of China.
Beijing has never renounced the use of force to reunite Taiwan with the mainland, while Japan, in common with most countries, does not recognise the island as independent.
“Precisely because there are some outstanding issues and challenges between Japan and China, we need all the more to engage in useful communication and dialogue based on the foundation accumulated over the long term,” Takaichi said.
[embedded media]
The 2008 Joint Statement enshrined the concept of mutually beneficial and stable ties, and it remains a key element of Tokyo’s approach to Beijing.
Different prime ministers, including Fumio Kishida in 2023, have expressed their commitment to that approach.
Takaichi herself pledged to work towards that goal when she met Xi shortly after taking office in October last year – a week before she made her comments about Taiwan.
By Alyssa Chen

title_en: India ‘missed the bus’ on manufacturing in the 1980s. Can it now catch up with China?
content_en:
China’s continued industrial dominance and the AI threat mean India may need to follow a different economic model, analysts say.
Electric vehicles at a manufacturing facility in India’s Telangana state in October. Photo: AFP
Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar’s recent statement that his country “missed the bus” on building up its manufacturing and industrial base in the 1980s, when China was forging ahead, has reignited debate over how India can catch up with its neighbour.
Analysts say India still has room to expand its manufacturing sector, but China’s continued industrial dominance and the threat artificial intelligence poses to India’s service-led economy mean New Delhi may need to follow a different economic model.
At a Hindustan Times Leadership Summit on Saturday, Jaishankar referred to a visit by former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi as the inflection point when the two countries’ economic fortunes diverged.
“When Rajiv Gandhi went to China in 1988, India and China’s economies were the same size. But China in the 1980s made a huge push towards modernisation and industrialisation. I’m sorry to say India in the 1980s simply missed the bus,” Jaishankar said.
He added that although India introduced economic reforms in the 1990s, it failed to sustain them across sectors and build industrial capacity at the required pace.
Jaishankar said India now needed to catch up with China by focusing on areas of competitive strength through a strategy of “leapfrogging”, rather than competing directly in every sector.
Through this strategy, India had ramped up manufacturing capacity in industries such as mobile phones, Jaishankar said.
External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar says India has ramped up manufacturing capacity through a strategy of “leapfrogging”. Photo: EPA
China rapidly scaled export-oriented manufacturing, infrastructure and investment, pulling well ahead from the 1990s onwards. India has relied on services, IT and domestic consumption, with a larger share of its workforce still in agriculture and informal sectors.
“India is one of the fastest-growing major economies. It has unused productive resources, especially human resources, which, if well utilised, can maintain a high growth and reduce the gap with China,” said Amitendu Palit, an economist specialising in international trade and investment policies at the National University of Singapore’s Institute of South Asian Studies.
“However, India’s challenge will be to make the growth inclusive and increase per capita income.”
India reported GDP growth of 7.8 per cent year on year in the first quarter of the financial year that began on April 1, according to government data, remaining the world’s fastest-growing major economy despite challenges posed by soaring oil prices and trade tensions with the US.
However, India’s GDP per capita is substantially lower than that of two Asian economic giants, China and Japan – roughly 5.6 times lower than China and nearly 13 times lower than Japan, according to 2026 International Monetary Fund estimates.
Palit said several sectors in India, such as biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, edutech and tourism, “have good potential for growth” but would need to be “supported by strong regulations – on pricing, intellectual property and labour conditions”.
India’s trade deficit with China has also risen to record levels.
According to the Business Standard newspaper on Sunday, India’s trade deficit with China reached a record US$83 billion in the first seven months of the financial year that began April 1, up 30 per cent year on year, and is projected to hit US$150 billion for the full financial year.
Palit said the trade deficit would be difficult to address until China had a decisive cost advantage in goods that India did not produce enough of and ended up importing.
Containers are transported by train near the Deendayal Port in Kandla, in the western state of Gujarat. India’s trade deficit with China has reached record levels. Photo: Reuters
India’s key imports from China include electronics, industrial machinery, chemicals and pharmaceutical raw materials.
“India can hope to reduce the deficit only if it can increase exports to China,” Palit said.
Raw materials, intermediate goods and industrial inputs, alongside growing electronics and engineering products, are among India’s main exports to China.
Jamus Lim, an associate professor of economics at ESSEC Business School Asia-Pacific, noted that despite its GDP gains, India struggled to replicate China’s manufacturing-led rapid growth experience.
He pointed to two challenges with this approach.
“First, the Chinese economy has stubbornly refused to relinquish its low-value-added manufacturing base, despite high and rising unit labour costs; and second, rapid advances in AI threaten to undermine the business process outsourcing base that India has relied on as an alternative growth engine,” he said.
While China maintained its manufacturing edge through productivity improvements, Lim said that with sufficient government support, India “may yet be able to fill a niche” in manufacturing and assembly as Chinese business costs continued to rise over time.
India has actively pursued manufacturing growth as global companies adopted a “China Plus One” strategy amid supply chain disruptions during the Covid pandemic, combining policy incentives for a range of sectors and a large domestic market to attract investments.
N.R. Bhanumurthy, director of Madras School of Economics, said India could derive value from building up manufacturing and exporting goods despite scepticism about whether the same model that served China well in the eighties and nineties would work.
“India seems to be catching up in some of those areas,” he said.
India has seen rapid export growth in areas including electronics and smartphones. Photo: DigiTimes
India has seen rapid export growth in specific areas – particularly electronics and smartphones – alongside gains in sectors like pharmaceuticals, engineering goods and toys. However, this expansion often relies heavily on upstream Chinese components and machinery.
Bhanumurthy said the push towards manufacturing big-ticket items such as defence equipment and factory machinery would be important as revenue from the services sector, which India traditionally relied on, could decline due to AI adoption.
Other industry observers said a manufacturing boost alone could yield limited success for India.
“India should perhaps focus more on things higher up the value chain such as research and development and innovation, whether it be in food security, health or education,” said Samit Sinha, an independent brand consultant and industry veteran.
“That is where the country has a chance to come up with something the world needs”, but that would require a fundamental change in the education system to encourage creativity and innovation, Sinha added.
Biswajit Dhar, an independent development economist, concurred, saying the need for labour-intensive industries would lessen over time.
“You need to start with the education system. Skill formation is something we have not given enough attention to,” Dhar said. “It has to start from the roots to foster a culture of innovation.”
By Biman Mukherji

title_en: Danish lawmakers approve US-Greenland security deal
content_en:
The deal paves the way for more US bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for the island to become part of the US.
The Danish parliament ratifies the US-Greenland agreement in the Parliament Hall at Christiansborg in Copenhagen on Thursday. Photo: via Reuters.
Denmark’s parliament on Thursday approved a hard-wrought agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The vote follows months of pressure by US President Donald Trump seeking to control Greenland, a semi-autonomous territory of Denmark, a Nato ally.
The trilateral deal – between Trump and the Danish and Greenlandic leaders – paves the way for more US bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the US.
The 109-0 vote in the Folketing amounts to a final step: The deal was expected to enter into force once Denmark and Greenland had signed on.
Greenland’s parliament approved the deal earlier this month, also with no opposition.
The text of the agreement says it will enter into force once Denmark and Greenland tell the US “in a diplomatic note” indicating that their parliaments had completed all necessary steps.
The US ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the “strong support” in the Danish parliament for ratification of the deal “paving the way for it to enter into force.”
“The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernises our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of Nato,” he wrote on social media.
Glacier and snow-covered mountains are seen from a commercial airliner as it prepares to land at Greenland’s Narsarsuaq in 2009. Under the deal, the US can set up “defence areas” at Narsarsuaq. Photo: Reuters
The aim is to bolster the US military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.
Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed the deal in September in New York, after months of quiet, behind-the-scenes negotiations to address his security concerns and Danish and Greenlandic fears of a possible US takeover.
Under the deal, which builds on a defence agreement dating to 1951, the United States can expand its military presence on the island and “modernise and expand” its activities at the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest.
The US can also set up “defence areas” at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east of Greenland, and can establish additional defence areas in the territory and strengthen its military operations or sites.
By Associated Press

title_en: Alibaba’s AI bet paying off as cloud services drive 10% revenue jump
content_en:
CEO Eddie Wu says AI-related product revenue has recorded triple-digit growth for 13 consecutive quarters.
The logo of Alibaba is seen at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on July 6, 2023. Photo: TNS
Alibaba Group Holding’s external recurring revenue tied to AI cloud and computing surged 67 per cent during the quarter ended September 30, lifting total revenue 10 per cent to a better-than-expected 271.5 billion yuan (US$40.5 billion) as the company doubles down on full-stack AI capabilities.
The tech and e-commerce giant’s AI Cloud and Compute Services segment, comprising its cloud computing business and chip design unit T-Head, which filed for an initial public offering in Hong Kong in September, rose 53 per cent to a revenue of 61 billion yuan during the three months, marking the fastest growth since late 2020.
“AI-related product revenue delivered triple-digit growth for the thirteenth consecutive quarter,” said CEO Eddie Wu Yongming in the statement. The 67 per cent growth rate was largely driven by the increasing adoption of AI-related products, it said.
Toby Xu, the chief financial officer, said: “As AI monetisation continues to ramp up, we will maintain disciplined investments in AI capabilities with a focus on return on invested capital while targeting to achieve positive free cash flow.”
Alibaba’s capital expenditure (capex), mainly to support its AI infrastructure buildout, reached 50.5 billion yuan during the period, down from 67.7 billion last quarter.
Meanwhile, free cash flow – a measure of operating cash flow minus capex – had an outflow of 34.5 billion yuan, compared with an outflow of 44.7 billion yuan in the June quarter. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
The latest results came as the ongoing saga surrounding Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang raised the possibility of tighter US export controls, which could make it more difficult for Chinese tech companies to access advanced US chips and hamper the development of artificial intelligence models including Alibaba’s flagship Qwen family.
But Alibaba’s intense focus on AI lifted its overall financial performance during the quarter.
Total revenue increased 10 per cent year on year to 271.5 billion yuan, surpassing a Bloomberg consensus estimate of 270.5 billion yuan, and net income rose 213 per cent to 64.4 billion yuan, beating the 24.3 billion yuan projection.
Adjusted Ebita (earnings before interest, taxes and amortisation) – a key measure of operating profitability – grew 260 per cent to 32.6 billion yuan year on year.
Other Chinese big tech companies, meanwhile, also reported quarterly revenue declines on Thursday. Short-video platform Kuaishou reported an 11.1 per cent decline in revenue to 31.6 billion yuan and a net loss of 959 million yuan. Research and development spending rose 41.9 per cent, mainly on increased investment in its Kling AI video-generation business.
Video gaming giant NetEase’s revenue fell 1.8 per cent to 27.9 billion yuan, with games and related services revenue down 1.7 per cent. Net profit attributable to shareholders slipped 2.5 per cent to 8.4 billion yuan.
Alibaba’s AI Labs and Applications segment – covering AI model labs, the Qwen Consumer Business Group and workplace AI agent platform QwenWork – generated 4.4 billion yuan in revenue, a 51 per cent year-on-year increase.
Earlier this week, the company launched Qwen4-Max, its most advanced AI model, which it said was better than earlier models at addressing AI-enabled cyberattacks and offered superior reasoning capabilities while bringing down inference costs.
Alibaba’s core e-commerce business, the other key pillar of the 27-year-old company, reported a 2 per cent rise in revenue to 197.2 billion yuan, as the company navigates a cautious domestic consumer market.
The company’s shares lost 5.5 per cent to HK$80.55 on Thursday in Hong Kong, ahead of the earnings release.
By Ann Cao, Minxiao Chang

title_en: South Korea court orders retrial of ex-PM Han in 2024 martial law case
content_en:
He was handed a 23-year jail term in January and an appeal court then reduced the sentence to 15 years in May.
Former South Korean prime minister Han Duck-soo (middle) arrives at the Seoul Central District Court for his first sentencing trial in the insurrection case, in Seoul in January. Photo: via AP
South Korea’s top court overturned former prime minister Han Duck-soo’s 15-year sentence on Thursday for aiding a martial law declaration that briefly suspended civilian rule, sending the case back to a lower court.
The 2024 decree issued by the president at the time, Yoon Suk-yeol, plunged the country into chaos, but lasted only around six hours as opposition lawmakers scrambled to overturn it in a vote.
Han, one of several top officials sentenced over the short-lived martial law bid, was handed a 23-year jail term in January for engaging in the declaration, which the court said threatened “the constitutional order” and amounted to insurrection.
An appeal court then reduced the sentence to 15 years in May, citing Han’s “more than 50 years as a public official before the martial law declaration”.
People in Seoul watch a TV news report on South Korea’s Seoul Central District Court ruling on charges against former PM Han Duck-soo, in January. Photo: Reuters
Both Han and prosecutors appealed against that ruling, taking the case to the Supreme Court, which on Thursday found there was insufficient evidence to sustain one of his insurrection convictions, ordering a retrial.
While the “martial law in this case was, in itself, unconstitutional and unlawful”, to “hold an individual liable for ‘engaging in essential duties during an insurrection’, it must be strictly proven that the defendant … harboured an intent to subvert the constitutional order”, the court said in a statement sent to AFP.
The court found that Han’s proposal to convene ministers before the martial law, allegedly to create the appearance that Yoon’s declaration had undergone cabinet deliberation, did not constitute insurrection as there was insufficient evidence of intent to subvert the constitutional order.
The Supreme Court, however, upheld Han’s conviction for playing a role in the insurrection after martial law was declared, including by seeking cabinet ministers’ signatures and discussing plans to blockade parliament and cut power and water supplies to certain media outlets.
The lower Seoul High Court will now retry the case based on the Supreme Court’s legal interpretation.
Supporters of former South Korean president Yoon Suk-yeol stage a rally outside the Seoul High Court in Seoul in April. Photo: AP
In the aftermath of the martial law, Han’s former boss Yoon was impeached and removed from office by the Constitutional Court in April 2025.
A presidential election two months later brought Lee Jae Myung to power.
Han, a 77-year-old career technocrat, has been imprisoned since his original sentence in January.
During the course of the trial, he had denied wrongdoing, insisting he had never supported or helped the martial law declaration.
After Yoon was removed from office, Han assumed his post as acting president and was at one point seen as a strong conservative contender in the snap election.
He resigned from the caretaker role in May last year to pursue a presidential bid, which soon collapsed when Yoon’s People Power Party refused to nominate him as its standard-bearer.
By Agence France-Presse

The court found that Han’s proposal to convene ministers before the martial law, allegedly to create the appearance that Yoon’s declaration had undergone cabinet deliberation, did not constitute insurrection as there was insufficient evidence of intent to subvert the constitutional order.
The Supreme Court, however, upheld Han’s conviction for playing a role in the insurrection after martial law was declared, including by seeking cabinet ministers’ signatures and discussing plans to blockade parliament and cut power and water supplies to certain media outlets.
The lower Seoul High Court will now retry the case based on the Supreme Court’s legal interpretation.
Supporters of former South Korean president Yoon Suk-yeol stage a rally outside the Seoul High Court in Seoul in April. Photo: AP
In the aftermath of the martial law, Han’s former boss Yoon was impeached and removed from office by the Constitutional Court in April 2025.
A presidential election two months later brought Lee Jae Myung to power.
Han, a 77-year-old career technocrat, has been imprisoned since his original sentence in January.
During the course of the trial, he had denied wrongdoing, insisting he had never supported or helped the martial law declaration.
After Yoon was removed from office, Han assumed his post as acting president and was at one point seen as a strong conservative contender in the snap election.
He resigned from the caretaker role in May last year to pursue a presidential bid, which soon collapsed when Yoon’s People Power Party refused to nominate him as its standard-bearer.

title_en: Who’s who in Shenzhen: the priorities revealed by Xi-Trump-Putin summit rosters
content_en:
From closest aides to policy specialists and diplomats, each leader’s negotiating team has been carefully chosen.
(From left) Russian President Vladimir Putin, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anton Siluanov, Presidential aide Yury Ushakov and Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO - Special Presidential Representative for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries Kirill Dmitriev wait before a meeting with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China. Photo: Pool via EPA
In high-stakes summitry, seating charts and delegation rosters often speak louder than boilerplate communiques.
And, as the unprecedented China-US-Russia trilateral meeting unfolds in Shenzhen, the strategic agendas of the three powers can be discerned by the security and economic tsars, top diplomatic strategists and influential technocrats flanking the three leaders.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ forum in southern China on Thursday.
Xi, Trump and Putin were seated at a round table for the historic meeting, with all the supporting staff in the background.
Xi was accompanied by his closest party gatekeepers, including his security apparatus chief and veteran diplomatic hands – a line-up that highlighted the multidimensional nature of the trilateral summit’s agenda.
[embedded media]
Xi’s inner circle and policy heavyweights
According to state media outlets, in top place of the ruling Communist Party hierarchy sat Cai Qi, a member of the Politburo Standing Committee and Xi’s chief of staff – a trusted lieutenant overseeing the operation of the party’s top echelon and China’s security affairs.
Also present on the Chinese side were two Politburo members: Foreign Minister Wang Yi, China’s top diplomat, and Vice-Premier He Lifeng, Beijing’s point man on economic and trade affairs.
On Wednesday at Kylin Villa, the lakeside resort in Shenzhen’s northwest, Xi and Putin held more than two hours of talks across two distinct formats: a 13-a-side expanded session followed by a closed-door working breakfast with just two aides per leader.
[embedded media]
When the talks narrowed to the restricted working breakfast, Beijing’s bench was reduced to Cai and Wang, underscoring their standing as Xi’s principal domestic and diplomatic gatekeepers.
Beijing’s presidential coordination and policy deliberation units were represented at Thursday’s trilateral summit by Tang Fangyu, director of the party’s Central Policy Research Office, and Lu Luhua, secretary to the president.
Reflecting the strategic importance of economic ties among the three powers, Xi also brought a slate of financial and commercial chiefs: National Development and Reform Commission chairman Zheng Shanjie, Finance Minister Lan Foan – also chairing the Apec finance ministers’ meeting – and Commerce Minister Wang Wentao.
Rounding out the Chinese side were deputy foreign minister Ma Zhaoxu, along with Xie Feng and Zhang Hanhui, ambassadors to Washington and Moscow, respectively, and the host province’s top official – Politburo member and Guangdong Communist Party secretary Huang Kunming.
Washington trade hawks and new operations chief
The US delegation reflected a markedly different structure. Five cabinet-level foreign policy, trade and economic principals were paired with a tight-knit circle of White House operational and communications loyalists.
On the policy side, Washington’s line-up was anchored by Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio.
[embedded media]
Alongside him were the four heavyweight officials driving Washington’s China policy, including tariffs, industrial and macroeconomic strategy: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and US ambassador to Beijing David Perdue.
Also present was a concentration of senior White House staff led by newly appointed assistant to the president and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and his deputy, Dan Scavino.
The remainder of the US roster serving in the background underscored the tight logistical, protocol and messaging control around the presidency.
They included Beau Harrison, who oversees operations, as well as White House communications director Steven Cheung and staff secretary Ben Moss, along with speechwriting director Ross Worthington, Oval Office operations director Walt Nauta, and director of the chief of staff’s office and deputy assistant to the president Alina Bulazel.
Also present on the working team were special assistants to the president Chris Ambrosini and Margo Martin – who also serves as a communications adviser – as well as executive assistant to the president Natalie Harp and US chief of protocol Monica Crowley.
Moscow’s security, economic technocrats
Putin fielded a calibrated delegation blending foreign policy and security veterans with the technocrats entrusted with steering Russia’s sanctions-tested economy and bilateral ties, according to presidential assistant Yuri Ushakov’s announcement on Monday.
On the diplomatic and security front, Putin was accompanied by the veteran Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov as well as Defence Minister Andrey Belousov and foreign policy aide Ushakov.
[embedded media]
The Kremlin’s administrative and messaging power was represented by two deputy chiefs of staff from the Presidential Executive Office: economic strategist Maxim Oreshkin and presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov.
Economic, fiscal and energy cooperation formed the core of the ministerial contingent, led by three deputy prime ministers – Tatyana Golikova, Dmitry Chernyshenko and Anton Siluanov, who also serves as finance minister – alongside Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov and Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilev.
Moscow also signalled an emphasis on non-security exchanges by including Health Minister Mikhail Murashko, Science and Higher Education Minister Valery Falkov and Culture Minister Olga Lyubimova.
For Thursday’s closed-door working breakfast opposite Cai and Wang, Putin retained only Lavrov and Ushakov, relying on the seasoned pair to handle the most sensitive strategic discussions.
Taken together, the three rosters illustrate the dual nature of the diplomacy unfolding in Shenzhen.
While expansive economic and ministerial benches point to intensive wrangling over trade, finance and industrial policy, Washington’s reliance on an insular White House core – and the retreat by Beijing and Moscow into two-aide breakfast sessions – suggests the decisive geopolitical bargains remain tightly held at the very top.
By William Zheng

title_en: While locals lie low, visiting Apec leaders explore Shenzhen’s streets and shops
content_en:
Foreign dignitaries attending summit make time to explore fruit stores and take tai chi lessons in Chinese metropolis.
Social media users posted about Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast at a leading Chinese fruit chain retailer shop in Shenzhen to discuss deals. Photo: Jimu
Shenzhen residents may have been kept at a distance from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit their city hosted, but some had the opportunity to encounter dignitaries who made time to explore the Chinese metropolis.
Social media users posted on Wednesday that they saw Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast at a shop for Pagoda, a leading Chinese fruit chain retailer, discussing business deals with local fruit importers.
Pagoda opened its first store in 2002 and has risen to become China’s top fruit retailer, operating more than 6,000 outlets nationwide as of June this year.
Other visiting dignitaries took interest in the city’s lively commercial scene.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast was seen at a shop for Pagoda, a leading Chinese fruit chain retailer, in Shenzhen on Wednesday. Photo: Jimu
On Wednesday afternoon, Thananon Charnvirakul, wife of Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, browsed at popular shopping centre Upper Hills, according to a Futian district government account, while the night before, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was spotted walking through the central financial district.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum picked a more traditional pastime. On Tuesday night, she took an hour-long tai chi lesson from a local coach, the Shenzhen Evening News reported.
“I have learned more in this hour than the past year combined,” Sheinbaum was quoted as saying.
In recent days, foreign visitors have frequented places Shenzhen is famous for, such as Huaqiangbei, home to the world’s largest electronics marketplace. Media reported an increased flow of people to the commercial district this week.
David Kershenobich Stalnikowitz, Mexico’s health secretary, stopped by to examine neck and leg massage devices and other wellness appliances.
“Unlike during the meetings, he seemed especially down-to-earth,” a Beijing News report said of the senior Mexican official. “He not only examined the product features and tried them out but also compared prices carefully.”
For most in Shenzhen, life in the city proceeded largely as usual, though tighter restrictions caused some inconveniences.
[embedded media]
On Wednesday and Thursday, during Apec meetings held in the newly built Shenzhen International Communication Centre, pavements leading to the venues were temporarily sealed off, a South China Morning Post reporter observed.
Deliveries were temporarily unavailable in the area when the meetings were under way. Residents nearby were told the rooftops were off limits, and the SCMP reporter saw plain-clothes security personnel at almost every residential community in the area as well as in nearby parks.
The city’s main roads remained open, but only a few cars drove past, as Shenzhen officials had encouraged residents to use public transport.
More than 1.5 million cars – about one-third of the total number in the city – had voluntarily registered to stay off the roads this week, the authorities said.
Many Shenzhen residents simply left the city ahead of the leaders’ meeting, having been encouraged to do so by the government.
Shenzhen had designated a four-day “autumn break” for primary and secondary schools that coincided with the Apec gathering, and the local railway authority previously estimated about 1 million outbound trips would be made.
Despite the restrictions, some residents could still be seen on the streets, taking photos of Apec signs and newly planted flowers.
Others joked on social media that they had “dressed up”, putting on their finest clothes and make-up for the foreign guests, just as the city had.
By Phoebe Zhang

title_en: AI models favour US and UK accents, score Chinese and Nigerian ones lowest, study finds
content_en:
The models rated the content of the same scripts differently, with implications for the use of AI in hiring, education and immigration tests.
One of the study’s co-authors says caution is needed as people are turn to audio AI models as third-party evaluators in contexts like hiring, oral exams in education and English tests in immigration. Photo illustration: Shutterstock
Ask an artificial intelligence model to grade a job interview or test answers, and a person’s accent may change the score.
That is according to new University of Washington research that looked at how some of the most advanced AI models rated English speakers with different accents, both on what they said and how they said it.
In the scripted tests, every speaker said the same words, and AI models transcribed the accented speech accurately, meaning the models understood the accents just fine. But the models still scored speakers differently, revealing a bias in how they rated accents.
American- and British-sounding speakers ranked highest, speakers with Indian accents were in the middle and those with Chinese and Nigerian accents scored lowest, according to the findings.
The AI models even rated the content of identical scripts differently, despite being told to judge only what was said.
They understood the speakers, but they just had this implicit notion of hierarchy among them based on accentOrevaoghene Ahia, study co-author
“People are now trusting audio AI models as sort of third-party evaluators, for hiring, for oral exams in education, for certain English tests in immigration – contexts where fairness really matters,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering and a co-author of the study, which was presented in October at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.
“Caution is definitely necessary,” Ahia added.
The researchers tested Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Flash, OpenAI’s GPT-Audio-1.5 and Qwen3-Omni, made by the Chinese tech giant Alibaba. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.
The models were among the most advanced available when the team ran its tests in the spring. Newer versions have since been released.
For part of the test, AI-generated “synthetic voices” read identical scripts with the five different accents, mimicking job-interview answers, conference presentations and English test responses.
The models listened and rated each recording from one to seven on delivery and content.
To make sure the results held up with natural speech, the researchers also had people with each accent deliver the same scripted interview answers. For both synthetic and human voices, the AI models ranked American and British accents highest.
Even Alibaba’s model, listening to people’s interview answers, gave British speakers the best delivery scores and Chinese speakers the worst.
Results did not meaningfully differ between men’s and women’s voices, Ahia said.
[embedded media]
The models’ written explanations of the rankings said American and British speakers were “clear” and “excellent”, whereas Chinese and Nigerian speakers were “mumbling” or “difficult to understand”.
“They understood the speakers, but they just had this implicit notion of hierarchy among them based on accent,” Ahia said of the AI models.
The research also found AI cannot be trusted to self-report its bias. Models admitted that accents shaped ratings in only about 10 per cent to 30 per cent of explanations.
Gifts from Google and OpenAI partly funded the research, but Ahia said the companies had no role in the work.
While developers of AI models measure their accuracy, Ahia said this was not enough and that testing for fairness across accents should be a standard step.
The research team next wants to study more accents and how AI handles audio in emergency response scenarios, like emergency call dispatch centres. Ahia said that work is still in its early stages because the data is sensitive.
Local governments are already using audio AI tools on nonemergency and emergency dispatch lines.
By Tribune News Service

title_en: China-centred order or host duties? Experts weigh in on Xi-Trump-Putin seating
content_en:
Table placement at historic Shenzhen summit divides analysts over whether Beijing was asserting dominance or simply following protocol.
Presidents Putin, Xi and Trump participate in a trilateral meeting in the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen on Thursday. Photo: AP
The seating arrangement at Thursday’s historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen sparked debate among former US officials and analysts over whether the optics reflected standard host protocol or a deliberate bid by China to place itself at the centre of the discussions.
“A stunning image of a China-centred order: a would-be G3 with Xi presiding,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as senior director for China and Taiwan affairs at the White House National Security Council during the Joe Biden administration.
He said the staging made Beijing’s intended hierarchy “unmistakable”, with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the centre facing the cameras and US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on either side.
“The American president appears as one of two guests in a world convened by Beijing,” he wrote on social media.
“There’s nothing equilateral about this triangle. Xi has put himself at the apex.”
Gewirtz, now a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Institute of Global Politics, acknowledged that “a seating plan obviously doesn’t establish a new international order”.
[embedded media]
Still, he argued that the arrangement offered “a powerful picture of the order Beijing would like others to imagine”.
Sourabh Gupta, resident senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, pushed back against that reading, noting that “the host will always enjoy centrality concerning the seating provision”.
“It comes with the territory,” Gupta said, dismissing comments from a few commentators as an overreaction that “speaks to their lack of confidence more than anything else”.
Even so, Gupta noted there was “an element of signalling by Beijing” in opting for a circular table rather than a triangular one that would have made the three leaders appear “polycentric”, calling the choice “almost certainly a deliberate staging”.
Isaac Stone Fish, chief executive and founder of business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, echoed concerns over the optics of the photo.
“Wow. China, the Chinese flag, and Xi Jinping at the centre. American presidents should never allow themselves to be photographed like this.”
The unprecedented three-way talks – held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit – brought together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, resulting in a joint statement focused on United Nations reform, nuclear risk reduction, global energy supplies and the jurisdiction of international courts.
In the joint statement, the US and Russian leaders also thanked China for hosting what they described as a “historic trilateral Summit”.
Gupta noted that despite initial hesitation from Beijing, which generally “prefers to keep matters on the bilateral track” and was “the least gung-ho going into the meeting”, the outcome worked in China’s favour.
“In the end, it has come out looking the adult supervisor of the three,” he said.

title_display: China-centred order or host duties? Experts weigh in on Xi-Trump-Putin seating
content_display:
Table placement at historic Shenzhen summit divides analysts over whether Beijing was asserting dominance or simply following protocol.
Presidents Putin, Xi and Trump participate in a trilateral meeting in the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen on Thursday. Photo: AP
The seating arrangement at Thursday’s historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen sparked debate among former US officials and analysts over whether the optics reflected standard host protocol or a deliberate bid by China to place itself at the centre of the discussions.
“A stunning image of a China-centred order: a would-be G3 with Xi presiding,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as senior director for China and Taiwan affairs at the White House National Security Council during the Joe Biden administration.
He said the staging made Beijing’s intended hierarchy “unmistakable”, with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the centre facing the cameras and US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on either side.
“The American president appears as one of two guests in a world convened by Beijing,” he wrote on social media.
“There’s nothing equilateral about this triangle. Xi has put himself at the apex.”
Gewirtz, now a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Institute of Global Politics, acknowledged that “a seating plan obviously doesn’t establish a new international order”.
[embedded media]
Still, he argued that the arrangement offered “a powerful picture of the order Beijing would like others to imagine”.

title_en: Xi, Trump and Putin ‘peace declaration’ suggests summit is more than a photo op
content_en:
Three leaders also outline cooperation in worldwide energy markets, nuclear non-proliferation and global governance after historic meeting.
Left to right: Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are seen after a photo op session at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen on Thursday. Photo: pool via Reuters
What was teased for weeks as an unprecedented three-way photo opportunity ended up rattling the geopolitical landscape on Thursday with the release of a China-US-Russia joint “peace declaration” outlining areas of cooperation in worldwide energy markets, nuclear non-proliferation and global governance.
At the conclusion of the first-ever three-way meeting in Shenzhen between Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the trio issued a statement that called for reform of the United Nations, weakening of the International Criminal Court, an increase in oil supplies and dialogue to reduce nuclear risks.
Xi called the meeting positive, constructive and “fruitful”, Putin termed it “open and candid”, while Trump said it was “a Great and Highly Consequential Trip”.
Dialogue and negotiation are essential to resolve differences worldwide, Xi added, according to a Xinhua readout. “As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace,” he said.
Trump’s decision during the two-day Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit to huddle with and craft a formal statement involving Washington’s long-standing adversaries suggested that the lame duck US president will continue to surprise, upend and challenge global norms.
[embedded media]
Trump enjoys far more leeway in foreign affairs than at home, particularly after his party was trounced in the US midterm elections two weeks ago.
The declaration also underscored China’s central role as host and conduit in whatever the potential three-way partnership may evolve into. That followed from Beijing’s long-term, if at times uneasy, collaboration with Moscow and its increasingly equal economic, military and technological standing with Washington.
“Trump’s trip has been a victory for Xi,” said Jonathan Stivers, a commissioner on the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, who criticised Trump for being soft on Beijing. “The summit was used to portray a strong China to both global and domestic audiences.”
Strength and depth of three-way arrangement questioned by analysts
While the idea of such a three-way agreement would have been unthinkable before Trump won his first presidential election in 2016, the strength and depth of Thursday’s announced arrangement remains wobbly even as it has unsettled traditional US allies and partners.
“The trilateral summit produced mostly warmed-over statements of support for lowest common denominator topics such as UN reform, increasing supply of refined oil products and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Jeremy Chan, senior analyst with the Eurasia Group. “That said, the symbolism and rhetoric surrounding the trilateral summit should not be discounted.”
Chan added that he expected more to follow. “All three leaders would welcome further trilateral engagements, including as early as next month at the G20 summit in Miami.”
The main points outlined in Thursday’s declaration amounted to low-hanging fruit, analysts said.
While the trio called for increased oil production leading to lower energy prices “for the benefit of all nations”, there was no mention of ending the Iran war that Trump launched in February or Ukraine war that Putin started over four years ago that have distorted global markets.
Likewise, reforming the UN has been bandied about for decades, leaving it unclear whether any overhaul would follow Washington’s more ruthless approach of cutting off funding or Beijing’s more potentially organised culling, in keeping with its bid to expand its soft power and global footprint.
Containing the spread of nuclear weapons, likewise, makes a good headline. But the US and Russia walked away from the only remaining containment agreement in February, even as Beijing has sought to build up its nuclear arsenal before coming to the bargaining table.
And while Trump likely has Iranian containment in mind, Washington is not likely to back Chinese opposition to the Australia-United Kingdom-US, or Aukus, agreement under which the three allies would jointly develop nuclear-powered submarines.
Also unclear is how Russia-China cooperation would fare if their common distrust of the US were less pronounced – and whether their three-way cooperation can outlast Trump.
[embedded media]
During the past two years, the mercurial US president has managed to quiet and intimidate China hawks from both parties. But this will almost certainly change once Democrats take control of the US Congress in January, even as their prospects of taking the presidency in 2028 improve.
The three countries also took aim at the International Criminal Court, calling for immunity from prosecution for officials from sovereign states. They also warned The Hague-based institution not to abuse its authority. The three have bridled at suggestions that their actions have amounted to crimes against humanity even as Putin is wanted by the court.
Thursday’s announcement has spurred headlines and raised concerns in foreign capitals. While any improvement in US-China trade tensions and major-power relations could benefit the global economy and security, the three-way pronouncement unnerved global leaders amid fears it could usher in a new order they had little role in shaping.
“What is clear is that on European security issues, there is no discussion without the Europeans, without the Ukrainians,” said an official in the French presidential office. “And I note, by the way, that the Chinese are saying the same thing.”
In a social media post, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she and Trump had a “frank exchange of views” on security issues involving the Indo-Pacific and Ukraine when he briefed her after his meetings.
“Erstwhile US allies and partners were neither in the room nor consulted before the discussion,” said Chan, a former US diplomat in Shenyang, China.
“Brussels and Tokyo will breathe a sigh of relief that Trump did not give the store away to Xi and Putin. But anxiety over the US will remain high in Europe and Japan for the duration of Trump’s presidency.”
No need for other global leaders to be concerned, expert says
Global leaders should avoid becoming alarmed, however, said Cui Hongjian, director of the Centre for EU and Regional Development Studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, even as he acknowledged their concern.
“The China-US-Russia trilateral summit did not include Europe, and I think that will have a rather complex psychological effect on Europe,” Cui said. “Of course, I think this worry is unnecessary.”
Under Chinese diplomacy, this sort of high-level meeting is mainly a way to outline broad objectives, he added. “China does not seek to discuss specific issues in this setting, because the parties have not yet reached a high degree of consensus on them.”
It was not immediately clear whether the threesome would organise regular meetings or an institutional structure. Xi suggested it might, while Putin was more non-committal.
“Its goal is to find mutually acceptable solutions for the three of us, primarily in the area of security,” Putin told reporters. “However, we have not agreed to meet regularly in this format.”
The three leaders added that a nuclear war “cannot be won and must never be fought”, even as Xi urged Washington to “do the right thing” on Taiwan and Trump called for greater Chinese cooperation on agriculture, energy and artificial intelligence.
Countries should abandon the “Cold War mentality” and enhance economic and trade cooperation rather than pursue decoupling, Xi said, according to CCTV. “Global energy security faces severe challenges, and the three nations can strengthen communication to safeguard the stability of energy supply chains.”
Additional reporting by Ji Siqi, Xiaofei Xu and Han Li
By Mark Magnier

title_en: Trump bought up to US$265,000 of Nvidia stock in September, disclosure shows
content_en:
The trades took place weeks before reports surfaced of CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese spy.
US President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after presenting him with the National Medal of Science in Washington in October. Photo: Reuters
US President Donald Trump bought as much as US$265,000 in Nvidia stock and sold as much as US$15,000 worth of the stock in September, weeks before reports surfaced of CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese spy, according to Trump’s latest financial disclosure released on Thursday.
US lawmakers have been asking questions about Trump’s knowledge of Huang’s personal life, and the ‌president has said he “was amazed” by the allegations against Huang, who is among the president’s closest allies in Silicon Valley.
Trump administration officials are currently weighing policies that could shape Nvidia’s future, including rules governing exports of its advanced chips.
Nvidia faces heightened scrutiny after news reports surfaced that Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman accused of spying for Beijing. Reuters has not independently confirmed that the woman is a spy.
The Nvidia trades were among hundreds the president made in September, according to the disclosure signed by Trump on November 1 and made ⁠public by the US Office of Government Ethics on Thursday.
In August, Trump bought as much as US$1.6 million worth of Nvidia shares and sold as ‌much as US$1 million worth, Reuters previously reported.
[embedded media]
Trump also bought as much as US$315,000 in SpaceX stock in September, according to the same disclosure. SpaceX is a US military contractor run by Trump’s former adviser Elon Musk.
The company has billions ‌of dollars’ worth of contracts with the US government, and its fortunes are often tied to approvals from federal agencies. Trump ⁠has traded SpaceX stock over the course ⁠of his second term as president, including in June and July 2026.
Reuters could not immediately determine the precise amount of Trump’s trades because federal officials use ranges to declare the value ‌of their assets on their financial disclosure forms.
White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement that third-party financial institutions independently manage the president’s portfolio and replicate “recognised indexes, ‌such ‌as the Schwab 1000”.
“Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio ‌is invested or when investments are bought or sold,” Ingle said.
Nvidia is the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips, widely used to develop cutting-edge ⁠AI systems. The US has for years sought to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, driven by concerns that China could use them ⁠to build weapons or superior AI tools.
Nvidia executives, including Huang, have argued for broader access to China. Chinese companies and researchers have also repeatedly found ways around the US export restrictions.
On Monday, the Trump administration said it would further limit China’s access to advanced ‌AI chips from companies such as Nvidia ‌by restricting shipments of advanced chips to Southeast Asian countries, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models.
The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed in 2025 on Huang’s relationship with the woman and on intelligence that she was giving information to the Chinese government, and that he chose not to act on the findings.
Questioned about the Times’ reporting, Trump said he “was amazed” by the allegations against Huang.
By Reuters

title_en: FCC votes to ban Chinese telecoms from direct access to US phone numbers
content_en:
The action will affect China Mobile, China Telecom, China Unicom and other IP-enabled service providers.
US FCC Chairman Brendan Carr speaks during a press conference in Washington in July. Photo: Reuters
The US ⁠Federal Communications Commission voted on Thursday ⁠to ban Chinese telecoms firms from direct access to US phone numbers on national security grounds – a measure designed to prevent scam-related robocalls.
The action will bar China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom and other IP-enabled service providers from ‌direct access. The FCC previously barred the three firms from providing international telecommunications services to the US.
For telecoms firms providing Voice over Internet Protocol – technology that converts voice into digital data and sends it over broadband connections – direct access is a much cheaper option and makes it easier to offer advanced features.
The FCC is also barring ⁠IP-enabled service providers that use equipment from companies on the FCC’s list that pose national security ‌risks, including Huawei Technologies and ZTE.
The Trump administration has continued an extensive crackdown on Chinese telecoms over the past year. The FCC last month voted ‌to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics starting from December 2028.
[embedded media]
Also ⁠in October, HKT, ⁠a leading Hong Kong telecoms carrier and subsidiary of PCCW Ltd, agreed to halt its operations in the US under pressure from the FCC by September 2027.
The telecoms crackdown has sparked a strong reaction from Beijing. China said on ‌Friday that it ‌firmly opposed the FCC action on labs, warning it would take necessary countermeasures “if the ‌US side persists in acting unilaterally”.
Other measures under consideration by the FCC include barring Chinese telecoms ⁠firms from connecting to US networks and from operating their data centres in the US.
Reuters ⁠reported this week the FCC plans to press ahead with efforts to block imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over ‌fibre-optic cables at the speed ‌of light within data centres, over national security concerns.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr said on Thursday that he had no update on the issue.
Concerns about the potential for spying and other harms to arise from Chinese access to US telecoms data and infrastructure have grown in recent years.
By Reuters

title_en: 4 UK men guilty of sex crimes against drugged woman in case with echoes of Pelicot
content_en:
Joanne Young’s then spouse, Philip Young, advertised her for sex online to strangers over more than a decade.
Joanne Young gives a statement outside Winchester Crown Court in England on Thursday. Photo: PA via AP
Four British men were convicted on Thursday of raping or sexually abusing a woman who was drugged by her then husband in a case with echoes of that of Gisele Pelicot, the French woman who became a global symbol in the fight against sexual violence.
Joanne Young, like Pelicot, decided to waive her legal right to anonymity after discovering that her husband at the time had repeatedly drugged her and ‌advertised her for sex online to strangers over more than a decade.
Philip Young, a 50-year-old former local councillor, pleaded guilty in January to more than 50 charges against his ex-wife, including 11 counts of rape and charges relating to recording the abuse and publishing it online hundreds of times.
“This abuse has cost me my life as I knew it,” Joanne Young said outside court. “The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.”
Police discovered the abuse only after an account linked to Philip Young posted bestiality images online in 2024 and then seized his devices, containing videos and images of the abuse.
Philip Young is seen in a custody photograph. Photo: Wiltshire Police via AFP
Young’s crimes have striking similarities to those of Dominique Pelicot, who admitted drugging ⁠his then-wife Gisele and inviting dozens of men to rape her, prompting a 2024 trial that horrified the world and spurred France to revamp its rape law.
Britain’s National Crime Agency said this year it ‌had uncovered a “truly international network” of drug-facilitated rape and sexual assault, which it said was organised online and had members across the world.
Law enforcement officials from 10 countries, including the US, are now working on a global operation to target drug-facilitated sexual assaults.
Joanne Young said her case “raises serious questions about how the law deals ‌with consent”, adding: “I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in the future.”
The men found ⁠guilty following a trial at Winchester Crown Court, ⁠in southern England, had responded to adverts posted by Philip Young, who admitted drugging his wife and inviting strangers to have sex with her, watching and filming while it happened.
Richard Clive Wilkins, 62, was convicted of rape and assault by penetration, Norman ‌Macksoni, 48, was also convicted of rape, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, was found guilty of sexual assault and assault by penetration, while Mohammed Hassan, 38, was convicted of one count of sexual assault.
In defences echoing those of many of the 50 co-defendants of Dominique Pelicot who ‌were convicted ‌in France, they said they thought Joanne Young consented and that it was a shared fantasy with her then husband.
Custody photos show (clockwise from top left) Richard Wilkins, Norman Macksoni, Connor Sanderson-Doyle and Mohammed Hassan. Photos: Wiltshire Police via AFP
She had sat in court as prosecutor Sarah Jones said her ex-husband had posted images ‌online, showing his then wife tied to her bed and blindfolded, as he “sought strangers to come and sleep with his wife – any age, any race”.
After the verdicts were announced, Judge Pushpinder Saini said she had ⁠shown “amazing bravery”.
A fifth man, Dean Hamilton, 47, had previously admitted rape, assault by penetration and sexual assault.
All five, along with Philip Young, will be sentenced next month, and Saini said they faced a ⁠significant custodial sentence.
The Pelicot trial horrified the world, but it now appears to be far from an isolated case.
Specialist Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor James Foster said the case “marks the first time in England that a jury has convicted men of sexually assaulting a woman, who had been drugged in abuse organised by her husband”.
In April, law ‌enforcement bodies from 10 countries, coordinated by Europol, the ‌EU’s law enforcement agency, set up “Project Medusa” to tackle the issue, led by investigators from Britain and Germany, and including the US, France and Canada.
Those involved have since launched 113 investigations linked to that operation, leading to 57 arrests and 158 safeguarded victims, Europol said in June.
The Crown Prosecution Service said British police had spoken with investigators who worked on the Pelicot case and that the toxicology expert whose evidence was used in France had also worked on the case involving Joanne Young.
“I live with a pain that’s hard to put into words … it is terrifying that this could happen to anyone,” Young said.
By Reuters

title_en: Nasa’s Voyager 1 phones home from an awe-inspiring 1 light-day away
content_en:
The call was received exactly 24 hours after it was sent at the speed of light from more than 26 billion kilometres away.
Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft entering interstellar space is depicted in an artist’s concept. Image: Nasa/JPL-Caltech via Reuters
Nasa’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity’s first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.
Flight controllers received the spacecraft’s call on Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That is how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometres) at the speed of light.
“Travelling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveller,” Nasa’s Joe Westlake, the heliophysics division director, said in a statement.
It marked another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977.
It swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our “pale blue dot” in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998 and crossed from the sun’s sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012.
People take part in the “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day” celebration, marking Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth, at Caltech in Pasadena, California, on Tuesday. Photo: AFP
Nasa could not confirm this newest distance record until the signal reached the control team at California’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But that did not stop the space agency from wishing everyone a “Happy Voyager light-day … day!” via social media the day before.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” JPL director Dave Gallagher said in a statement.
Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are Nasa’s longest-operating space missions, still churning out data despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring.
Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn plus Uranus and Neptune was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It will not reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.
Both spacecraft are doing well for their 49 years of age, ploughing through space at 38,000 mph (61,000km/h) with plutonium for power.
Picture-taking ended long ago, but they typically send back bits of precious data almost every day on their never-before-explored environment.
The Voyager Golden Record Album is seen in an undated image. Photo: Nasa/JPL-Caltech via AP
No science or engineering data has been received from Voyager 1 since Saturday, according to Nasa.
However, the carrier signal that normally conveys that data kept coming and, along with flight path calculations, allowed the team to confirm the light-day milestone.
Controllers are trying to figure out why the flow of science and engineering data stopped.
Each carries a so-called Golden Record brimming with the sounds of Earth.
The project was led by the late Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, who also coined the phrase “pale blue dot” for Voyager 1’s farewell glimpse of Earth.
Nasa expects the gold-plated phonographic records – time capsules for anyone or anything that might encounter them – to last more than 1 billion years.
By Associated Press
